R243.decision_summary: R243: `window-size manual` + `resize-window` — the value R241 declined to offer, behind a reason that was a true statement about cost and said nothing about what the omission cost. That reason: `manual` needs a stored size and a verb that writes it, and an option value naming a rule nothing performs is this front's recurring defect. Every word holds. Probed first — R241's own rule, and R242's finding that a true reason can hide a defect — the omission's cost turned out to be measurable and irreversible from the user's side: a session with panes at 100x30 and nobody attached was reflowed to 80x24 the instant any client attached, went to 60x20 when that client resized, and STAYED at 60x20 after it detached, because the honest answer with nobody watching is to leave the panes alone. A long-running program's wrap width was set by whoever last glanced at the session, permanently, with no value of the option able to hold it. Reading also moved the design off the prior round's own wording: the stored size is NOT per session. It is `tile`'s second argument and `tile`'s first is a WINDOW's tree, so the rectangle belongs beside the tree it measures — on `Window`, in the snapshot, restored with the arrangement. The other decision is what `manual` means with nothing pinned, and it is not `None`: `None` means no window, which sends both frontends to their no-window fallback of sizing panes from their own surface — the two-authority defect R242 removed, re-reachable by one `set-option`. It defers to the DEFAULT policy instead, which also makes `set-option window-size manual` on its own a change the user cannot see.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-terminal/src/registry.rs: `Window::manual_size` / `set_manual_size`, plus `resize_window` on `Session` and `SessionRegistry` beside `rename_window`, and a read-only `SessionRegistry::window` to match `window_mut`. The field lives on the WINDOW, not the session, and the reason is a property of the function that consumes it: a pane's size is `tile(tree, window)`, and `tile`'s tree is a WINDOW's, so the rectangle it is laid out over belongs beside the tree it measures. R241's own sentence about what `manual` would need said "a per-session size", and that was the one word in it worth correcting. The setter deliberately does NOT bump `layout_revision`: that number says a client's projection of the ARRANGEMENT is stale, and the arrangement is untouched here — the same tree over a different rectangle. Bumping it would invalidate every client's layout cache to deliver news about something else.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/snapshot.rs: `WindowSnapshot::manual_size`, `#[serde(default)]` so the addition is additive (the rule `argv` and `remote` already follow — a pre-field snapshot loads un-pinned, which is exactly what those daemons did). It has to be here because a reboot is precisely the moment there is no client to ask: every pane already carries its own `cols`/`rows`, but those are READINGS taken at snapshot time and the first client to attach overwrites them, while this is a DECISION no set of pane sizes can reconstruct (they are a tiling of it, not it).

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `WindowSize::Manual`, and `arbitrate` takes a third input. THE design decision of the round is what it answers with `manual` set and nothing pinned: not `None`. `None` means "no window", which sends both frontends to their no-window fallback of sizing panes from their own surface — the two-authority defect R242 removed, re-reachable by one `set-option`. It defers to `WindowSize::DEFAULT` instead, so `set-option window-size manual` on its own is a change the user cannot see: they have named a source and the source is empty until `resize-window` writes it. The `Latest | Manual` arm that implements the deferral is held to `DEFAULT` by its own test rather than by a comment.

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `retile` reads the pin off the window it is about to tile, and takes the scope and the pin under ONE registry lock. Two locks would let a window switch land between them and lay one window's tree out over another window's pinned rectangle — the same class as the lock-in-a-match-scrutinee R242 paid for, one indirection along.

crates/sprag-host/src/wire.rs + workspace.rs: `RESIZE_WINDOW_ACTION` (`{window?, cols?, rows?}`) — both dimensions pin, neither un-pins, and HALF is refused whole, the rule `client/size` already follows. It writes a stored fact and touches no PTY; the panes follow through the invoke BOUNDARY's re-derivation, so a pinned window and a derived one reach the panes by one path. Thirteen actions became fourteen and the boundary did not have to learn anything.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `sprag resize-window -t SESSION [window] {-x COLS -y ROWS | -u}`. tmux's relative forms and its `-a`/`-A` are NOT offered, and the reason is a fact rather than a size preference: each computes a new rectangle from a current one, and this CLI holds neither input — reading them here would put a SECOND arbitration in a client, which is the defect this whole front has been removing. The verb pins under ANY policy and NAMES the gap on stderr when the policy in force is not `manual`, read from the user's own file. Refusing the natural order (pin, then choose to use it) would fail for no mechanical reason, and a stored value that silently does nothing is what this front keeps finding.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `manual` joins `WINDOW_SIZE_VALUES` on the same terms as the other three, because it now names a rule the daemon performs. What it does with an empty source is `arbitrate`'s to state, not the table's: an empty source is not an unperformed rule.
verification_bullets: THE COST OF THE OMISSION WAS MEASURED BEFORE ANY DESIGN, and the numbers are what shaped the round. A live daemon, one pane, no config: boot 40x6; a client attaches and resizes to 100x30, pane 100x30; the client DETACHES, pane holds 100x30 and the window goes null; a second client attaches at its terminal's own 80x24 and the pane becomes 80x24 INSTANTLY, before the user has done anything; it resizes to 60x20, pane 60x20; it detaches, and the pane STAYS 60x20. So the program the user had arranged at 100x30 was reflowed by a transient client and left there, and no value of `window-size` could hold it. R241 had recorded `manual` as needing machinery; this is what not having it cost.

THE PTY GATE IS TWO REAL CLIENTS' WORTH OF MACHINERY ON ONE LIVE SESSION, and every number in it is chosen so no fallback can be mistaken for a pass: the pin (111x33) is not the boot pane (40x6), not the attaching client's pseudoterminal (80x24) and not the area it resizes to (60x20). Claim 1 is the discriminating one — with NO client attached, the pin moves the panes, and every other policy answers "no window" in that state, so this alone separates a `manual` the daemon performs from a value the table accepts. Then a real `sprag-tui` on a real pseudoterminal attaches and reports 60x20, and the panes stay pinned; the wait is on `sprag list-clients` showing the client's own area, because "the pane did not move" means nothing until the report has LANDED. It holds through a settle window, and it survives the DETACH, which is its own re-derivation path.

THE UN-PIN IS ITS OWN GATE, and it is the only direction that can tell a governed report from an absent one: `-u` with a client attached hands the window back and the panes take the CLIENT's area — which is also the live proof that `manual` with nothing pinned defers to the default policy rather than answering "no window".

THE GUI IS GATED SEPARATELY AND THE CLAIM IS NOT THE SAME ONE. R242 proved a window is IN the arbitration; this proves the one policy that takes the arbitration AWAY from it still governs it, which a reasoning-only argument would have skipped — a GUI reports what its panes measured, `manual` ignores that report, and "the pin wins" depends on the client not re-asserting its own measurement. Five checks in the live headless smoke, pinned 20 cols and 8 rows LARGER than the window measured for itself: the pin becomes the session's window over the client's report, every pane grows past what the window measured, the window paints PART of every pinned pane, the pin is not pulled back, and `-u` returns every pane to exactly what the window measured.

SIX REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, FIVE RED. `arbitrate` ignoring the pin fails a unit test, both PTY gates, the CLI gate and three of the five smoke checks. `retile` not READING the pin (passing None) fails both PTY gates — 22 of the suite's 24 still pass, so that call is the whole path. The pin not RESTORED, and separately not CAPTURED, each fail the registry round-trip with `None` where `Some((123, 45))` was asserted — both ends of the chain proved separately. The CLI's note removed fails the CLI gate on an empty stderr.

THE SIXTH REVERT-PROOF PASSED, AND IT IS RECORDED AS A LIMIT RATHER THAN FIXED. Deleting the `announce` from the `resize_window` action leaves the whole PTY suite green, including the two tests written for that action, because the re-derivation resizes panes, a pane resize marks it dirty, and the dirty path bumps. That is R241's `client/size` finding repeating one action along. The announce is kept for the earlier, contracted wake and because every sibling action announces, and its doc now says it is not independently falsifiable and why — the chain it would otherwise rest on holds only while a window change always changes some pane's size, which is false for a window of nothing but floats and false for a re-pin the tiling absorbs.

THE CLI GATE CAUGHT A REAL MISTAKE IN ITS OWN FIRST DRAFT, and the mistake is the invariant working. It gave the isolated config home to the CLI alone, so the verb stored the pin and printed no note — its own view of the file said `manual` — while the daemon went on arbitrating under the default and the panes never moved. No option crosses the wire, so the DAEMON reads `window-size` itself and the test has to hand it the same file. The gate now flips the policy through the real `set-option`, which also shows the daemon picking the change up with nothing restarted.

THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, repeatedly with the input changed. `show-options window-size` off no daemon; the refusal listing all four values for a word that names no rule; the file after `set-option`. Then a live daemon: pinning with no client attached moved the pane 80x24 -> 120x40 -> 90x25 -> 100x28 by name; `-u`; half a size, a zero, `-u` with dimensions and an unknown window each refused with their own reason. Then a real reboot with `--daemon`: `manual_size` on disk, and the pane back at 111x33. That last reading was CONFOUNDED and the confound was found rather than reported as a pass — the snapshot's own per-pane `cols`/`rows` were also 111x33, so it could not tell a live pin from a restored reading. The discriminating measurement forces the pane elsewhere and watches the next action boundary pull it back (111x33), with the un-pinned control staying where it was put (40x10).

carry_forward_bullets: A REASON THAT NAMES ITS OWN COST IS STILL NOT A MEASUREMENT OF WHAT THE OMISSION COSTS. R241 declined `manual` because it needs a stored size and a verb, and because an option value naming a rule nothing performs is this front's recurring defect. Both true, and the second is a rule worth keeping. What neither says is that without it a long-running program's wrap width is set by whoever last glanced at the session and left — measured, three attaches deep, and irreversible from the user's side. This is R242's finding a second time in a row, which makes it a habit rather than an anecdote: when a previous round's boundary is the thing you are building against, probe the FAILURE, not the reason.

A STORED THING BELONGS BESIDE THE FUNCTION THAT CONSUMES IT, AND THAT IS WHERE THE DESIGN CAME FROM RATHER THAN FROM THE PRIOR ROUND'S WORDING. R241 wrote "a per-session size" and it reads as settled. But a pane's size is `tile(tree, window)` and `tile`'s tree is a WINDOW's, so the rectangle is a window's fact; the DERIVED window is session-wide only because clients attach to sessions, which is a constraint on the derivation and not on a declaration. Granularity is a property of the consumer, not of the surrounding vocabulary.

The setter deliberately does NOT bump `layout_revision`: that number says a client's projection of the ARRANGEMENT is stale, and the arrangement is untouched here — the same tree over a different rectangle. publishable_verification_bullets: THE COST OF THE OMISSION WAS MEASURED BEFORE ANY DESIGN, and the numbers are what shaped the round. THE UN-PIN IS ITS OWN GATE, and it is the only direction that can tell a governed report from an absent one: `-u` with a client attached hands the window back and the panes take the CLIENT's area — which is also the live proof that `manual` with nothing pinned defers to the default policy rather than answering "no window".

Then a live daemon: pinning with no client attached moved the pane 80x24 -> 120x40 -> 90x25 -> 100x28 by name; `-u`; half a size, a zero, `-u` with dimensions and an unknown window each refused with their own reason. R244.decision_summary: R244: `resize-window`'s derived and relative forms — the correction of an exclusion R243 wrote in the same round as the finding that condemns it. R243 left tmux's `-a`/`-A` and `-U`/`-D`/`-L`/`-R` out with the sentence 'each computes a new rectangle from a current one, and the CLI holds neither input; they belong in the action, where the stored size and the clients' reports both already are'. Every clause is true and the conclusion does not follow: that is a description of WHERE THE WORK GOES, and R234's rule already says a fix inside sprag's own crates is not blocked. So the work went where the sentence said it belonged. A `SizeRequest` (exact / adjust / fold-the-clients / clear) crosses the wire as a DESCRIPTION and the daemon resolves it, which is not merely convenient — the descriptions reduce to machinery that already exists, so `-a`/`-A` cannot come to disagree with the `smallest`/`largest` policies about what 'the largest client' means, and a relative resize moves exactly the rectangle every client is reading. The same argument then forced something not planned: the action must ANSWER the resolved rectangle, because a caller that could not compute the request cannot report the result either. Two things had to stay apart rather than collapse into one 'no size': a description that names no rectangle (refused) and a request to un-pin (honoured), because merging them turns `resize-window -R 10` on an unwatched window into a silent un-pin.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `SizeRequest` — `Exact` / `Adjust {cols, rows}` / `Clients(WindowSize)` / `Clear`, with `resolve(current, reports)`. Three of the four are DESCRIPTIONS rather than rectangles, and they reduce to machinery that already exists: `Clients` IS `arbitrate` (so `-a`/`-A` cannot disagree with the `smallest`/`largest` policies about what "the largest client" means), and `Adjust` moves whatever the arbitration currently answers. Neither introduces geometry of its own, which is the whole reason they belong on this side of the wire.

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `NoBasis` is a DISTINCT outcome from `Clear`, and keeping them apart is the load-bearing decision of this slice. Both could be spelled "no size", and collapsing them would make `resize-window -R 10` on a window nobody is watching silently UN-PIN it — the opposite of what was asked. An adjustment saturates at one cell at both ends (`i64` arithmetic then clamped, so no `u16` wrap can answer a huge window to a request for a smaller one) because it names a DIRECTION: at the edge, "narrower" honestly means the narrowest. `-x 0` is refused instead, at the CLI, where the number was typed.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: `size_request` tells the four spellings apart, the ONE place that happens, and refuses a request carrying two rather than ordering them by a precedence nobody stated. `from: "manual"` is refused: it is the one policy that folds no clients, so as a SOURCE it names nothing. The action's relative BASIS is the arbitrated window falling back to the pin — not a guess but the only rectangle anybody has declared when the policy does not read it and no client is attached, which is what makes `-x 100 -y 30` then `-R 20` work on a detached session.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the action now ANSWERS the rectangle it pinned (`null` for an un-pin). Three of the four spellings are descriptions the caller cannot resolve — that is why they are resolved here — so a caller told only "accepted" would have to guess what it had asked for, or read the window back and race the next change. `scoped_window_action` returns the answer instead of discarding it.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `-a`/`-A` and `-L`/`-R`/`-U`/`-D N`, with the five spellings mutually exclusive and opposing directions on one axis refused. Each relative flag names an EDGE and pushes it, so `-L`/`-U` shrink and `-R`/`-D` grow — `resize-pane`'s convention under tmux's flag names. The adjustment is REQUIRED with its flag: tmux's bare `-U` defaults to 1 and takes its count as a trailing positional, which sprag cannot copy because the window target here is a leading positional and window names are integers by default, so `resize-window -U 5` would be genuinely ambiguous between "5 shorter" and "window 5".

crates/sprag-tui/tests/pty_round_trip.rs: `DEADLINE` 15s -> 45s, and the reason is measured rather than argued. Its own doc already said it is "a deadline for a HANG, not a guess at how long the work takes", and 15s was not that: the slowest legitimate wait in the file needs 9-13s in ISOLATION on a quiet machine, so it passed only by fitting. The doc now carries the numbers behind it, including where the time goes.
verification_bullets: THE GATE FOR `-a`/`-A` IS TWO REAL CLIENTS ON REAL PSEUDOTERMINALS, CROSSED so the fold answers a rectangle NEITHER of them reported: 100x24 and 80x30 give `-A` = 100x30 and `-a` = 80x24. A daemon that answered by picking a whole client is caught, and a CLI that had computed the fold itself would have needed both areas over the wire plus its own arithmetic. The CLI's printed line is part of the assertion — it must contain the rectangle the DAEMON worked out. Then the second client is resized and the pin does NOT follow it, which is the whole difference between `resize-window -A` and `window-size largest`; a daemon that had merely switched policies moves here.

THE RELATIVE BASIS IS GATED WITH NOTHING PINNED UNDER A DERIVED POLICY, so the basis can only be the window the CLIENTS gave: a 90x28 client, then `-R 12 -U 6` must answer 102x22. That also pins the direction convention, which is the thing a reader gets wrong — `-U` SHORTENS, and a gate written to "up means taller" fails. The same test then shows the stored rectangle sitting INERT under `latest` and becoming live the moment `window-size manual` names it, with nothing re-sent.

AN UNRESOLVABLE REQUEST IS REFUSED AND THE PIN SURVIVES IT, gated live: `-a` with no client that has reported an area, against a window pinned at 77x21, and the assertion is that the pin is still 77x21 afterwards. This is the `NoBasis`-is-not-`Clear` distinction as a user-visible claim rather than a type-level one.

SIX REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL RED. `Clients` answering the current size instead of folding fails 2 unit tests and both fold gates. The relative basis taken from the pin instead of the arbitrated window fails the relative gate. An unresolvable request answering `Ok(None)` instead of `NoBasis` fails a unit test and the live pin-survives gate. The action answering `null` instead of the rectangle fails the CLI relative gate and both fold gates. The exclusivity arm replaced by a precedence order fails the action-level test. The relative basis' fallback to the pin removed fails the action-level test.

THAT NEW TEST THEN CAUGHT A REAL DEFECT ON ITS FIRST RUN, which is why it is worth having: a relative resize was REFUSED when a pin existed but the policy did not read it and no client was attached, because the arbitration honestly answers "no window" there. The pin is the one rectangle anybody has declared for that window, so refusing to move it made `resize-window -x 100 -y 30` followed by `-R 20` fail on a detached session. Fixed by falling back to the pin, with the revert measured red.

A TEST ALSO CAUGHT `-a -A` SILENTLY MEANING `-A`. Both spellings land in one slot, so the mode count could not see the contradiction and the second flag overwrote the first; it surfaced as the daemon's no-basis refusal instead of an argument error. Now refused with its own message, and the assertion records why it exists.

THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, against a live daemon with `window-size manual`: `-x 100 -y 30` -> 100x30; `-R 20` -> 120x30; `-U 5` -> 120x25 (SHORTER); `-L 30 -D 10` -> 90x35 (two axes in one call); `-L 9999` -> 1x35, saturating rather than wrapping. HEAD was 16/16 on the failing test, so it looked like a regression; instrumenting it showed the test spends 9-11 of its 12 seconds waiting for an 88-character command to be echoed, at roughly 100-124ms per character (measured with a throwaway probe: 1 char 222ms, 10 chars 384ms, 20 chars 2.1s, 40 chars 5.0s). The test was already using 9-13s of a 15s cap in ISOLATION; the new tests' parallel load tipped it. `DEADLINE` is 45s now, with the numbers in its doc, and the PTY suite is 10/10 green at 29 tests.

AN ATTEMPTED FIX TO THAT TEST WAS REVERTED RATHER THAN SHIPPED HALF-UNDERSTOOD. Replacing the 88 keystrokes with a birth-argv split made it fail deterministically: pane 0 received the click sequence as RAW TEXT. That also showed the wait it replaced was not what its comment claimed — it reads the CLIENT's mouse mode, which two tracking panes satisfy in microseconds, so it says nothing about the pane being clicked. Both facts are recorded; neither is fixed here, because a mouse gate is not the place for a change whose failure mode I could not yet explain.

The same reasoning then forces something I had not planned: the action must ANSWER the resolved rectangle, because a caller that could not compute the request also cannot report the result. R245.decision_summary: R245: `history-limit` — the scrollback depth becomes the user's, and the round's own elegant coupling turned out to be a defect. Two things were confused under one name before this: `SCROLLBACK_CAP = 1000`, a hard-coded const the emulator enforced, and `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY`, an operator's env knob whose default was DERIVED from that const to mean "persist everything the pane still holds". Making the first configurable breaks the second's derivation silently — a pane set to keep 50,000 lines would come back from a reboot holding 1,000 — so the persistence default became "no ceiling" rather than a number, and the operator's variable stayed the authoritative bound it was. The design decision that took the longest was one I got WRONG first and caught before shipping: since a pane now owns a limit, narrowing the save budget to it reads like the tighter, more correct bound. It is not. A saved history is the scrollback PLUS the visible screen, so that narrowing cuts the live screen out of a full pane's save and leaves a pane set to keep NO scrollback restoring blank. The zero case is also why the options table's `Number` kind grew a floor instead of keeping its blanket refusal of zero: for a SIZE zero is nonsense, for a RETENTION COUNT it is a decision, and one kind cannot answer both.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-vt/src/port.rs: `Screen` carries a `history_limit`, and `Screen::new` takes it as a PARAMETER. That is the load-bearing shape choice: the three internal callers are exactly the places a derived screen must inherit the limit (`resized`, `reflowed`, the alt screen), so a signature that demands the value cannot be silently forgotten by a fourth added later — where a default-then-setter would let one through and evict a user's raised history on the next resize only. `SCROLLBACK_CAP` is renamed `DEFAULT_SCROLLBACK_LINES` because the name would otherwise lie: once it is configurable it is a default, not a cap.

crates/sprag-vt/src/port.rs: the physical-row ceiling stops being a `const` and becomes `scrollback_physical_ceiling(lines)`, derived per screen. Held at the old 8x1000 it would have capped a pane configured for 50,000 lines at 8,000 physical rows, so the memory guard would silently stop tracking the setting it sits beside and the option would look broken on wide wrapped output. It saturates rather than wrapping.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `OptionKind::Number` gains a `min`, and the `history-limit` entry floors at 0 while `gui-font` floors at 1. Zero is not one thing — a glyph of no pixels is not a smaller glyph, but a pane that remembers nothing is exactly what a user asking for it wants, and tmux's `history-limit 0` takes it. A floor rather than a `zero: bool` because that is the honest shape of the constraint and costs a future option with a real minimum nothing. The refusal message now NAMES the floor that was missed instead of saying "above zero" for every option.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/workspace.rs: `HistoryLimitSource`, an `Arc<dyn Fn() -> usize>` the pool consults at each BIRTH, shared by `sibling()` exactly as `next_id` is. A source rather than a number so a user editing `history-limit` gets it on their next pane rather than their next daemon — `default-command`'s rule. Held on the pool rather than passed to `spawn` because this crate owns the only two places a pane is ever born, and a caller that had to pass the limit is one that could forget; a sibling that defaulted would give a session's second window shallower history than its first.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs + config.rs: `history_limit_lines()` reads the option per birth, and `Host::new` AND the restore path both install the source. Two installs and not one, because a restore builds a whole new set of pane pools — a registry seeded on only one path is the asymmetry R237 named, where a setting is honoured on one birth and silently ignored on another.

crates/sprag-host/src/history.rs: `DEFAULT_HISTORY_LINES` becomes `NO_HISTORY_CEILING = usize::MAX`. The old default was `SCROLLBACK_CAP` and its doc said it meant "everything the pane still holds" — true only while every pane's retention was the same constant. The encoder already saturates at what the screen holds, so an unset ceiling persists exactly that with no arithmetic, and `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY` stays the operator's authoritative bound over any `config.toml`, which is what keeps the module's own "an option is not the place for an operator's control" invariant intact.
verification_bullets: THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND READ, and the three-way live measurement is what makes each number mean something rather than one reading that could have come from anywhere. One daemon, one pane, 3,000 lines fed, `capture-pane` counted: UNSET retains 1023 with the oldest at line1978; `history-limit 0` retains 23 with the oldest at line2978; `history-limit 5000` retains 3000 with the oldest at line1. No two are the same and each is explainable — 1023 is the 1000-line default plus a screenful, 23 is the visible screen ALONE, 3000 is everything fed. A pane whose limit never reached the emulator lands on 1023 in all three.

THE ZERO READING IS THE ONE THAT CAUGHT MY OWN DEFECT. 23 lines retained at `history-limit 0` is the visible screen surviving, and it is the number that would have been 0 had the per-pane save cap I first wrote shipped: a saved history is the scrollback PLUS the visible screen, so bounding the save by a RETENTION limit blanks a restored pane. Found by asking what `history_bytes` actually encodes rather than trusting that the tighter bound was the better one, and the coupling was deleted rather than tuned.

THE REBOOT HALF WAS MEASURED WITH ITS OWN CONTROL, because a restore reading can be confounded by the thing beside it (R243). Same feed, a real `kill-server` and daemon restart: RAISED goes 3000 before -> 3000 after with the oldest still line1, while the UNSET control goes 1023 -> 1022. Had the persistence default stayed the old 1000-line constant, the raised pane would have come back at ~1000 — the control is what separates "the ceiling was lifted" from "a restore replays everything regardless".

SEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, AND TWO OF THEM PASSED FIRST. Red immediately: `trim_scrollback` reading the default instead of the per-screen limit (2 unit tests), `sibling()` not inheriting the source, `reflowed` re-defaulting, the birth ignoring the pool's source (3 tests), and `Host::new` not installing it (the live CLI gate). The two that PASSED are the ones worth recording, and both were closed rather than noted.

THE FIRST PASSING REVERT-PROOF: `resized()` re-defaulting the limit left the whole suite green, because that path is the fallback only the alt screen and a degenerate size take, and an alt screen holds no scrollback for a wrong limit to evict. Rather than declare it unfalsifiable, `Screen::resized` is `pub(crate)` and the new test calls it DIRECTLY — it carries scrollback across verbatim WITHOUT trimming, so a re-defaulted limit sits dormant and evicts on the next push instead of at the resize, which is the delay that makes such a bug hard to attribute. The revert is red now.

THE SECOND PASSING REVERT-PROOF WAS ON CODE I DELETED, which is why it was worth running at all: re-adding the per-pane save cap passed the ENTIRE workspace suite. So a future author could reintroduce the defect that blanks a zero-retention pane and nothing would catch it. `a_pane_retaining_no_scrollback_still_captures_its_visible_screen` now spawns a real pane with a zero source and asserts `pane_histories` still captures the screen; with the cap re-added it fails, and nothing else in the suite moves.

THE DAEMON-BORN GATE DRIVES A REAL DAEMON, because a test over `Workspace` proves a pool honours a source without proving anything installs one. `a_daemon_born_pane_retains_the_users_history_limit` boots a host on an isolated config home with `history-limit = 12`, feeds 200 lines, and waits on the CONTENT the assertion reads rather than a timer. 12 is neither the 1000-line default nor the screen height, so no fallback passes it.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets (0), the rustdoc gate, workspace 1411 -> 1426 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 29 each, live GUI pixel smoke 117 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.

THE DOC GATE WAS NEARLY REPORTED GREEN WITHOUT RUNNING. `.githooks/doc-gate.sh` only DEFINES `doc_gate()`, so sourcing it exits 0 having done nothing — which is exactly what a pass looks like. Caught by this project's own rule that silence is not a passing gate, and re-run as `. doc-gate.sh && doc_gate`, which prints its command and documents 15 crates.
carry_forward_bullets: THE TIGHTER BOUND WAS THE WRONG BOUND, AND THE ONLY THING THAT CAUGHT IT WAS ASKING WHAT THE FUNCTION ACTUALLY ENCODES. Once a pane owned a `history-limit`, narrowing the save budget to it looked like the strictly more correct choice — per-pane instead of global, tighter instead of looser, and it made a pleasing symmetry with the retention path. It would have blanked every restored pane set to keep no scrollback, because a saved history is the scrollback PLUS the visible screen and no retention limit bounds that second half. The general shape: when a new per-thing value appears, the places that ALREADY take a number are not automatically places that should take THIS number. Read what the consumer's number means before handing it a better one.

AN ELEGANT COUPLING IS A CLAIM ABOUT TWO THINGS BEING THE SAME, AND IT GETS READ FROM THE CODE LIKE ANY OTHER. This is [[verify-before-you-write-it-down]] pointed at a design rather than a comment: I had written the cap, its doc, and its justification before checking `history_bytes`. All three were coherent and all three were wrong together, which is what coherence costs — a wrong premise elaborated carefully looks more right, not less.

A REVERT-PROOF ON CODE YOU DELETED IS WORTH RUNNING. The per-pane cap was gone from the tree, so there was nothing to prove; running it anyway asked the real question — if someone re-adds this, does anything object? Nothing did, across the whole workspace. A decision recorded only in a doc comment is one the next author can undo in one line, so the ones that were hard to get right earn a test even when the current code is correct without it.

ZERO IS A DECISION FOR SOME SETTINGS AND AN ABSENCE FOR OTHERS, AND ONLY THE SETTING KNOWS WHICH. `OptionKind::Number` refused zero for every option on the reasoning that a caller must never be handed a size of nothing — sound for `gui-font`, wrong for `history-limit`, where zero is precisely what tmux takes and what `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY=0` already meant on the neighbouring axis. The `Command` kind's doc had already drawn this distinction for the empty string; the numeric kind just had not been asked yet. A shared validator that encodes one option's judgement as a universal rule is a constraint waiting to be wrong.

A CONSTANT'S NAME IS A CLAIM AND CONFIGURABILITY FALSIFIES IT. `SCROLLBACK_CAP` was accurate while it was a hard cap and became a lie the moment it was a default, so it was renamed rather than left to mislead every future reader. Same for `DEFAULT_HISTORY_LINES`, whose doc claimed it meant "everything the pane still holds" — true only while every pane held the same amount, and repaired by making the default an absent CEILING rather than a count.

SOURCING A GATE SCRIPT IS NOT RUNNING IT. `.githooks/doc-gate.sh` defines a function and runs nothing, so `. doc-gate.sh` exits 0 having documented no crate — indistinguishable from a pass. [[silence-is-not-a-passing-gate]] caught it. Worth carrying because the same shape holds for any helper that is sourced for its definitions: the exit code of the source is a claim about the FILE PARSING, not about the work.

STILL NOT BUILT, and the reason is a mechanism rather than a preference: re-applying a changed `history-limit` to panes ALREADY ALIVE. A pane's retention lives in its emulator from birth, and lowering the limit on a live pane would DESTROY retained output as a side effect of editing a config file. Offering that safely needs a verb the user aims at a pane, which is a different feature from an option — not a scope cut, since the option itself is complete and matches tmux's own model. The two R244 leads are untouched: the ~124ms-per-keystroke input cost (the bigger, user-facing one) and the mouse gate whose wait verifies the client's mode rather than the pane being clicked.

Held at the old 8x1000 it would have capped a pane configured for 50,000 lines at 8,000 physical rows, so the memory guard would silently stop tracking the setting it sits beside and the option would look broken on wide wrapped output. It saturates rather than wrapping.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `OptionKind::Number` gains a `min`, and the `history-limit` entry floors at 0 while `gui-font` floors at 1. Zero is not one thing — a glyph of no pixels is not a smaller glyph, but a pane that remembers nothing is exactly what a user asking for it wants, and tmux's `history-limit 0` takes it. A floor rather than a `zero: bool` because that is the honest shape of the constraint and costs a future option with a real minimum nothing. The refusal message now NAMES the floor that was missed instead of saying "above zero" for every option.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/workspace.rs: `HistoryLimitSource`, an `Arc<dyn Fn() -> usize>` the pool consults at each BIRTH, shared by `sibling()` exactly as `next_id` is. A source rather than a number so a user editing `history-limit` gets it on their next pane rather than their next daemon — `default-command`'s rule. Held on the pool rather than passed to `spawn` because this crate owns the only two places a pane is ever born, and a caller that had to pass the limit is one that could forget; a sibling that defaulted would give a session's second window shallower history than its first.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs + config.rs: `history_limit_lines()` reads the option per birth, and `Host::new` AND the restore path both install the source. Two installs and not one, because a restore builds a whole new set of pane pools — a registry seeded on only one path is the asymmetry R237 named, where a setting is honoured on one birth and silently ignored on another.

crates/sprag-host/src/history.rs: `DEFAULT_HISTORY_LINES` becomes `NO_HISTORY_CEILING = usize::MAX`. The old default was `SCROLLBACK_CAP` and its doc said it meant "everything the pane still holds" — true only while every pane's retention was the same constant. The encoder already saturates at what the screen holds, so an unset ceiling persists exactly that with no arithmetic, and `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY` stays the operator's authoritative bound over any `config.toml`, which is what keeps the module's own "an option is not the place for an operator's control" invariant intact.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND READ, and the three-way live measurement is what makes each number mean something rather than one reading that could have come from anywhere. One daemon, one pane, 3,000 lines fed, `capture-pane` counted: UNSET retains 1023 with the oldest at line1978; `history-limit 0` retains 23 with the oldest at line2978; `history-limit 5000` retains 3000 with the oldest at line1. No two are the same and each is explainable — 1023 is the 1000-line default plus a screenful, 23 is the visible screen ALONE, 3000 is everything fed. A pane whose limit never reached the emulator lands on 1023 in all three.

THE ZERO READING IS THE ONE THAT CAUGHT MY OWN DEFECT. 23 lines retained at `history-limit 0` is the visible screen surviving, and it is the number that would have been 0 had the per-pane save cap I first wrote shipped: a saved history is the scrollback PLUS the visible screen, so bounding the save by a RETENTION limit blanks a restored pane. Found by asking what `history_bytes` actually encodes rather than trusting that the tighter bound was the better one, and the coupling was deleted rather than tuned.

THE REBOOT HALF WAS MEASURED WITH ITS OWN CONTROL, because a restore reading can be confounded by the thing beside it (R243). Same feed, a real `kill-server` and daemon restart: RAISED goes 3000 before -> 3000 after with the oldest still line1, while the UNSET control goes 1023 -> 1022. Had the persistence default stayed the old 1000-line constant, the raised pane would have come back at ~1000 — the control is what separates "the ceiling was lifted" from "a restore replays everything regardless".

SEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, AND TWO OF THEM PASSED FIRST. Red immediately: `trim_scrollback` reading the default instead of the per-screen limit (2 unit tests), `sibling()` not inheriting the source, `reflowed` re-defaulting, the birth ignoring the pool's source (3 tests), and `Host::new` not installing it (the live CLI gate). The two that PASSED are the ones worth recording, and both were closed rather than noted.

THE FIRST PASSING REVERT-PROOF: `resized()` re-defaulting the limit left the whole suite green, because that path is the fallback only the alt screen and a degenerate size take, and an alt screen holds no scrollback for a wrong limit to evict. Rather than declare it unfalsifiable, `Screen::resized` is `pub(crate)` and the new test calls it DIRECTLY — it carries scrollback across verbatim WITHOUT trimming, so a re-defaulted limit sits dormant and evicts on the next push instead of at the resize, which is the delay that makes such a bug hard to attribute. The revert is red now.

THE SECOND PASSING REVERT-PROOF WAS ON CODE I DELETED, which is why it was worth running at all: re-adding the per-pane save cap passed the ENTIRE workspace suite. So a future author could reintroduce the defect that blanks a zero-retention pane and nothing would catch it. `a_pane_retaining_no_scrollback_still_captures_its_visible_screen` now spawns a real pane with a zero source and asserts `pane_histories` still captures the screen; with the cap re-added it fails, and nothing else in the suite moves.

THE DAEMON-BORN GATE DRIVES A REAL DAEMON, because a test over `Workspace` proves a pool honours a source without proving anything installs one. `a_daemon_born_pane_retains_the_users_history_limit` boots a host on an isolated config home with `history-limit = 12`, feeds 200 lines, and waits on the CONTENT the assertion reads rather than a timer. 12 is neither the 1000-line default nor the screen height, so no fallback passes it.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets (0), the rustdoc gate, workspace 1411 -> 1426 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 29 each, live GUI pixel smoke 117 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.

THE DOC GATE WAS NEARLY REPORTED GREEN WITHOUT RUNNING. `.githooks/doc-gate.sh` only DEFINES `doc_gate()`, so sourcing it exits 0 having done nothing — which is exactly what a pass looks like. Caught by this project's own rule that silence is not a passing gate, and re-run as `. doc-gate.sh && doc_gate`, which prints its command and documents 15 crates.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: THE TIGHTER BOUND WAS THE WRONG BOUND, AND THE ONLY THING THAT CAUGHT IT WAS ASKING WHAT THE FUNCTION ACTUALLY ENCODES. Once a pane owned a `history-limit`, narrowing the save budget to it looked like the strictly more correct choice — per-pane instead of global, tighter instead of looser, and it made a pleasing symmetry with the retention path. It would have blanked every restored pane set to keep no scrollback, because a saved history is the scrollback PLUS the visible screen and no retention limit bounds that second half. The general shape: when a new per-thing value appears, the places that ALREADY take a number are not automatically places that should take THIS number. Read what the consumer's number means before handing it a better one.

AN ELEGANT COUPLING IS A CLAIM ABOUT TWO THINGS BEING THE SAME, AND IT GETS READ FROM THE CODE LIKE ANY OTHER. This is [[verify-before-you-write-it-down]] pointed at a design rather than a comment: I had written the cap, its doc, and its justification before checking `history_bytes`. All three were coherent and all three were wrong together, which is what coherence costs — a wrong premise elaborated carefully looks more right, not less.

A REVERT-PROOF ON CODE YOU DELETED IS WORTH RUNNING. The per-pane cap was gone from the tree, so there was nothing to prove; running it anyway asked the real question — if someone re-adds this, does anything object? Nothing did, across the whole workspace. A decision recorded only in a doc comment is one the next author can undo in one line, so the ones that were hard to get right earn a test even when the current code is correct without it.

ZERO IS A DECISION FOR SOME SETTINGS AND AN ABSENCE FOR OTHERS, AND ONLY THE SETTING KNOWS WHICH. `OptionKind::Number` refused zero for every option on the reasoning that a caller must never be handed a size of nothing — sound for `gui-font`, wrong for `history-limit`, where zero is precisely what tmux takes and what `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY=0` already meant on the neighbouring axis. The `Command` kind's doc had already drawn this distinction for the empty string; the numeric kind just had not been asked yet. A shared validator that encodes one option's judgement as a universal rule is a constraint waiting to be wrong.

A CONSTANT'S NAME IS A CLAIM AND CONFIGURABILITY FALSIFIES IT. `SCROLLBACK_CAP` was accurate while it was a hard cap and became a lie the moment it was a default, so it was renamed rather than left to mislead every future reader. Same for `DEFAULT_HISTORY_LINES`, whose doc claimed it meant "everything the pane still holds" — true only while every pane held the same amount, and repaired by making the default an absent CEILING rather than a count.

SOURCING A GATE SCRIPT IS NOT RUNNING IT. `.githooks/doc-gate.sh` defines a function and runs nothing, so `. doc-gate.sh` exits 0 having documented no crate — indistinguishable from a pass. [[silence-is-not-a-passing-gate]] caught it. Worth carrying because the same shape holds for any helper that is sourced for its definitions: the exit code of the source is a claim about the FILE PARSING, not about the work.

STILL NOT BUILT, and the reason is a mechanism rather than a preference: re-applying a changed `history-limit` to panes ALREADY ALIVE. A pane's retention lives in its emulator from birth, and lowering the limit on a live pane would DESTROY retained output as a side effect of editing a config file. Offering that safely needs a verb the user aims at a pane, which is a different feature from an option — not a scope cut, since the option itself is complete and matches tmux's own model. The two R244 leads are untouched: the ~124ms-per-keystroke input cost (the bigger, user-facing one) and the mouse gate whose wait verifies the client's mode rather than the pane being clicked.

R246.decision_summary: R246: the keystroke cost R244 registered, priced — and its headline number falsified before anything was built on it. R244 measured typed input at roughly 100-124ms PER CHARACTER through a real client on a real pseudoterminal and carried it forward as "the bigger, user-facing" lead. That is a DEBUG build's number. The same probe in release is ~5ms/char, and the same probe in debug on this box now reads ~304ms/char — sixty times apart in one direction and two and a half times apart between two runs of the "same" measurement, which is what a number nobody can reproduce looks like. The reproducible facts are counts and ratios taken inside one run (R221's rule), and they say a keystroke does cost something worth removing: the SAME forty characters delivered as one PASTE land in 12ms against typing's 200ms, cost the daemon 1 grid projection against 22 and 1,920 cells against 42,240, and put exactly the same text on the screen. Bisected per stage inside one client's life, the per-keystroke config re-read is 4.8us and reconcile/follow are microseconds; what scales is BUILDING the pane's change list, O(cells) and once per keystroke — 1.14ms at 80x24, 7.02ms at 160x48, 17.9ms at 240x64, more than a 60Hz frame to echo one character on a large terminal, against 4.2ms of actual flushing across the whole burst. The fix rests on a guarantee that already existed: `ProjectionToken`'s per-row damage stamps are the ones pinion's `TextGrid` already gates on, which is why `sprag-vt` stamps EVERY row on a palette change. So the client rebuilds only the rows whose stamp moved, and everything the stamps cannot see — the alternate screen, a width change, a row-count change, a moved arrangement, a blanked surface — rebuilds the pane whole.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-tui/src/paint.rs: `PaintCache` + `PanePaint`, and `pane_changes` splits into a row-limited `pane_rows_changes` the cache drives. ONE call for the whole frame rather than one per pane, which is not a style choice: the arrangement check has to see every pane's rectangle at once, and a per-pane entry point is one a caller painting in a loop can forget. The cache compares the WHOLE arrangement rather than each pane's own rectangle, because a pane's rectangle being unchanged does not say another pane has not written over it — and the cheapest way never to have to make that argument is not to rest on it.

crates/sprag-tui/src/paint.rs: `comparable` names what a row stamp cannot see, and each field is one the token already carries for that reason: the alternate screen (both screens keep their own counters, so equal stamps across a switch mean nothing), the column count (a resize COPIES surviving rows' stamps, documented in `ProjectionToken`), and the row count. The CURSOR is deliberately excluded — it moves on nearly every keystroke and is painted separately from the same grid, so treating it as a whole-pane invalidation would rebuild every frame and save nothing.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs: `HostClient::pane_cells_and_token`, defaulted to `(pane_cells(..), None)`. The pairing is the whole point of the method: a client reading the cells and then the token reads two facts a frame apart, and a fetch landing between them pairs OLD cells with a NEW token — after which every row those cells still owe goes unpainted until something else stamps it. `None` means "cannot say" and every caller must read it as "rebuild everything", which is also the honest answer for a non-zero offset, since the token summarises the LIVE screen and says nothing about a projection windowed into scrollback.

crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: the `WireHost` override reads both out of ONE `lock_cache`, split into a free `cells_and_token` so the pairing can be asserted without a daemon. The poll thread replaces a pane's frame and its token together, so one lock is what makes the pair describe one frame.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: `paint` builds the frame's `PanePaint` list, takes the cursor from the SAME buffers, and hands the list to the cache; `Clear::Yes` calls `cache.forget()` in the same breath as the `ClearScreen`. `sprag-grid` is promoted out of `[dev-dependencies]` — a production `use` from a dev-only dependency does not build, and the crate's GPU-free gate is unaffected since its closure is pinion-core + sprag-vt, both already here.

crates/sprag-tui/tests/pty_round_trip.rs: `a_click_in_the_second_pane_arrives_in_that_panes_own_columns` waits on the DAEMON's per-pane `mouse` key instead of the client's mirror, and on the split shell having taken its terminal before typing at it. Both were latent: the client's mirror is the MAXIMUM over the panes, so with two tracking children it says nothing about either, and a shell's startup `tcsetattr` purges type-ahead exactly as this client's does. R244 measured the first and could not land a fix; making a keystroke cheap removed the ~11 seconds of typing that had been standing in for both waits.
verification_bullets: THE HEADLINE NUMBER WAS FALSIFIED BEFORE ANY DESIGN, by asking what ELSE produces it. R244's probe was rebuilt and run under both profiles on this box: 40 characters typed take 12.15s in debug (~304ms/char) and 0.20s in release (~5ms/char), with the release figure stable at 215 / 203 / 200ms across three runs. R244's own debug reading was 4.97s for the same 40 characters, so the debug measurement is not even reproducible against itself. Nothing was designed against the falsified number, and R244's `DEADLINE` 15s -> 45s decision still stands, because the test suite does run in debug.

THE CONTROL IS A PASTE, AND IT IS WHAT MAKES EVERY OTHER NUMBER MEAN SOMETHING. The same forty characters as one bracketed paste produce identical output, identical echo, identical painting and identical work for the harness's own emulator — the only difference is how many times the client's input loop runs. Typed 200ms against pasted 12ms, and the paste is FLAT from n=1 to n=40 (10.8 / 10.2 / 14.7ms) while typing is linear. That single comparison exonerates the harness, the output volume and the daemon in one reading.

THE DAEMON AND THE SOCKET WERE PRICED OUT SEPARATELY, three layers on one box: 40 key actions over a RAW connection with nobody attached cost 117us each; the same over a raw connection with a client attached cost 787us each; through the client they cost milliseconds. So an attached client makes any request dearer, and the client's own loop is dearer still — but neither is the term that grows.

R217's METER PUTS A COUNT ON IT. Same 40 characters, same screen: typed costs the daemon +22 projections and +42,240 cells, pasted costs +1 and +1,920. Twenty-two times the grid work for the identical result, reproduced 3/3 on the paste side at exactly +1 / +1,920.

THE PER-STAGE BREAKDOWN WAS TAKEN INSIDE ONE CLIENT'S LIFE, because the end-to-end spread across runs is 30-50% and a stage's SHARE is worth more than any duration (R221). The per-keystroke config re-read is 203us over 42 keys — 4.8us each, and NOT the cost, though its own doc claimed a `metadata` call where the code does a full `read_to_string`. `reconcile` is 40us and `follow` 15us over the whole burst. Splitting `paint` into building the change list and flushing it settles it: build is 96-99% of paint at every size (25.1 / 210.5 / 448.4ms) against a flush of 0.9 / 1.7 / 4.2ms, and build per repaint climbs 1.14 -> 7.02 -> 17.9ms as the pane goes 1,920 -> 7,680 -> 15,360 cells.

THE WIN IS MEASURED ON THE SAME BINARY WITH THE SKIP DISABLED, which is the revert-proof and the before-number in one reading. 40 keystrokes: 160x48 goes 295ms -> 80-105ms, 240x64 goes 947ms -> 101-109ms, and the cost stops scaling with the pane's area (105 / 108, 80 / 108, 86 / 101 across three runs at the two sizes). The PTY suite's own wall clock fell from ~12s to ~5.7s.

SEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED; FOUR RED AT ONCE, AND THE THREE THAT PASSED ARE THE ONES WORTH RECORDING. Red: ignoring the screen kind and ignoring the column count each fail `what_the_stamps_cannot_see_rebuilds_the_pane_whole`; a silent pane keeping its token fails `a_pane_that_stops_answering_forgets_what_it_said`; dropping the token on the read fails the new `sprag-client` pairing test.

THE FIRST PASSING REVERT-PROOF WAS MY OWN TEST BEING VACUOUS. Deleting the arrangement check left the suite green, because `a_changed_arrangement_discards_the_cache` asserted the FRAME was non-empty and the joining pane's changes were in the same list. Rewritten to read a SURFACE through split-and-undo — a pane returning to a rectangle a neighbour has written over, with the same content and therefore the same stamps — and the revert is red.

THE SECOND WAS A GUARD NOTHING REACHED, AND THE THIRD ATTEMPT AT REACHING IT IS THE ONE THAT COUNTS. `cache.forget()` on `Clear::Yes` survived the whole suite. The first replacement test used a divider drag onto the divider's own column and proved nothing at all: `MouseEdges` emits no edge for a pointer that did not move, so there was no drag and no clear. The case that IS reachable needs a PINNED window — a client's terminal growing past a window that does not follow it clears the surface while every rectangle stays put — and with `forget()` removed that test reads a COMPLETELY BLANK screen, which is what a user with `window-size manual` would have seen on any resize. Green with it, 3/3.

THE THIRD PASSING ONE IS RECORDED AS REDUNDANT RATHER THAN FIXED: `forget()`'s own token clear cannot be falsified, because clearing the arrangement alone already forces the next frame whole (any frame with a pane in it differs from the empty arrangement). It is kept and its doc says so, since that argument holds only while no caller asks for an empty frame and this is a public type.

A REGRESSION THIS ROUND CAUSED WAS FOUND, ATTRIBUTED AGAINST A CONTROL, AND FIXED AT ITS CAUSE. The PTY suite went 2-of-3 RED; at HEAD it was 3-of-3 green in the same session, so it was mine. The failing test types 88 characters at a freshly split shell and then clicks: making a keystroke cheap removed ~11 seconds during which the shell took its terminal and the child enabled tracking. Both waits are now real — the pane's own text for the first, the DAEMON's per-pane `mouse` key for the second — and the suite is 10 consecutive green runs at 30 tests each.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features (0), the rustdoc gate (15 crates, run as `. doc-gate.sh && doc_gate` — R245's lesson), workspace 1426 -> 1437 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green at 30 each. The live GUI pixel smoke is 117 / 0 on 16 of 17 runs; the single failure was two of R243's pinned-window checks, HEAD measured 6/6 green as a control, and this round's diff reaches no GUI code path (the two shared additions are a defaulted trait method and a `WireHost` method the GUI never calls). Recorded as observed rather than explained.
carry_forward_bullets: A MEASUREMENT WITHOUT ITS BUILD PROFILE IS NOT A MEASUREMENT, AND MINE SAT IN THE LEDGER FOR A ROUND. R244 wrote "~100-124ms PER CHARACTER ... through a real client on a real pseudoterminal" and called it user-facing; it was a debug build, release is ~5ms, and re-running the debug probe gave ~304ms — so the recorded figure could not even reproduce itself. The number was RIGHT for the thing R244 was actually doing (explaining why a debug test suite flaked) and wrong for the thing it was carried forward as. When a number leaves the context that produced it, the context has to travel with it.

THE CONTROL THAT SEPARATES THE COST FROM THE APPARATUS WAS ONE LINE. The same 40 characters as a PASTE produce identical output through identical machinery and differ only in how many times the loop runs — so a flat paste against a linear typed cost rules out the harness's emulator, the output volume, the daemon and the socket in a single reading. Before instrumenting anything, look for the input that changes ONLY the variable in question.

THE FIX RESTED ON AN INVARIANT THAT ALREADY EXISTED, AND FINDING THAT OUT WAS THE DESIGN. Per-row skipping looked like it needed a new guarantee, and the hazard it seemed to carry — a palette change re-colouring cells without touching them — turned out to be one `sprag-vt` already stamps every row for, with a doc saying it exists because pinion's `TextGrid` is generation-gated. The right question was not "is this safe" but "who else already needs it to be".

TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WERE VACUOUS AND ONLY THE REVERT-PROOF SAID SO. One asserted a frame was non-empty when a second pane's changes were always in it; the other drove a gesture that produced no event at all. Both LOOKED like coverage and both passed with the code they guarded deleted. A test written from a design cannot falsify it — and the cheapest way to find that out is to delete the thing and watch.

A GUARD NOTHING REACHES IS A GUARD NOTHING PROVES, AND "UNREACHABLE" WAS WRONG TWICE. `cache.forget()` on a clear survived the whole suite because every clear the suite reaches also moves a rectangle. The reachable case needed a PINNED window, and there the failure is a completely blank screen. R244's lesson one notch on: the layer above did not enforce this guard, it merely never exercised it.

MAKING SOMETHING FAST BREAKS THE TESTS THAT WERE USING IT AS A SLEEP. The PTY suite went 2-of-3 red, and both waits it exposed were already wrong: one read the client's mouse mirror (the MAXIMUM over panes) while claiming to read one pane's child, the other typed at a shell before its startup `tcsetattr` had stopped purging type-ahead. R244 measured the first and called the 88 keystrokes "an accidental synchroniser"; this is that observation arriving as a failure. An optimisation's first job is to find every test that was timing on the old cost.

STILL NOT BUILT, and each is a mechanism rather than a preference: the GUI has its own paint path and does not use `PaintCache` (it composites pixels, not `Change`s, so the row-limited form is not the same object). R217's open item 1 — a DAMAGE-DRIVEN fetch, so an unchanged pane costs no frame at all — is untouched and is now the next term, since 22 projections per 40 keystrokes is still 22 more than a paste. `sprag-tui.rs`'s `refreshed` doc claims a `metadata` call where the code does a full `read_to_string`; measured at 4.8us per key, so it is a wrong SENTENCE rather than a wrong cost.

R244's probe was rebuilt and run under both profiles on this box: 40 characters typed take 12.15s in debug (~304ms/char) and 0.20s in release (~5ms/char), with the release figure stable at 215 / 203 / 200ms across three runs. R244's own debug reading was 4.97s for the same 40 characters, so the debug measurement is not even reproducible against itself. Nothing was designed against the falsified number, and R244's `DEADLINE` 15s -> 45s decision still stands, because the test suite does run in debug.

THE CONTROL IS A PASTE, AND IT IS WHAT MAKES EVERY OTHER NUMBER MEAN SOMETHING. The same forty characters as one bracketed paste produce identical output, identical echo, identical painting and identical work for the harness's own emulator — the only difference is how many times the client's input loop runs. Typed 200ms against pasted 12ms, and the paste is FLAT from n=1 to n=40 (10.8 / 10.2 / 14.7ms) while typing is linear. That single comparison exonerates the harness, the output volume and the daemon in one reading.

THE DAEMON AND THE SOCKET WERE PRICED OUT SEPARATELY, three layers on one box: 40 key actions over a RAW connection with nobody attached cost 117us each; the same over a raw connection with a client attached cost 787us each; through the client they cost milliseconds. So an attached client makes any request dearer, and the client's own loop is dearer still — but neither is the term that grows.

R217's METER PUTS A COUNT ON IT. Same 40 characters, same screen: typed costs the daemon +22 projections and +42,240 cells, pasted costs +1 and +1,920. Twenty-two times the grid work for the identical result, reproduced 3/3 on the paste side at exactly +1 / +1,920.

THE PER-STAGE BREAKDOWN WAS TAKEN INSIDE ONE CLIENT'S LIFE, because the end-to-end spread across runs is 30-50% and a stage's SHARE is worth more than any duration (R221). The per-keystroke config re-read is 203us over 42 keys — 4.8us each, and NOT the cost, though its own doc claimed a `metadata` call where the code does a full `read_to_string`. `reconcile` is 40us and `follow` 15us over the whole burst. Splitting `paint` into building the change list and flushing it settles it: build is 96-99% of paint at every size (25.1 / 210.5 / 448.4ms) against a flush of 0.9 / 1.7 / 4.2ms, and build per repaint climbs 1.14 -> 7.02 -> 17.9ms as the pane goes 1,920 -> 7,680 -> 15,360 cells.

THE WIN IS MEASURED ON THE SAME BINARY WITH THE SKIP DISABLED, which is the revert-proof and the before-number in one reading. 40 keystrokes: 160x48 goes 295ms -> 80-105ms, 240x64 goes 947ms -> 101-109ms, and the cost stops scaling with the pane's area (105 / 108, 80 / 108, 86 / 101 across three runs at the two sizes). The PTY suite's own wall clock fell from ~12s to ~5.7s.

SEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED; FOUR RED AT ONCE, AND THE THREE THAT PASSED ARE THE ONES WORTH RECORDING. Red: ignoring the screen kind and ignoring the column count each fail `what_the_stamps_cannot_see_rebuilds_the_pane_whole`; a silent pane keeping its token fails `a_pane_that_stops_answering_forgets_what_it_said`; dropping the token on the read fails the new `sprag-client` pairing test.

THE FIRST PASSING REVERT-PROOF WAS MY OWN TEST BEING VACUOUS. Deleting the arrangement check left the suite green, because `a_changed_arrangement_discards_the_cache` asserted the FRAME was non-empty and the joining pane's changes were in the same list. Rewritten to read a SURFACE through split-and-undo — a pane returning to a rectangle a neighbour has written over, with the same content and therefore the same stamps — and the revert is red.

THE SECOND WAS A GUARD NOTHING REACHED, AND THE THIRD ATTEMPT AT REACHING IT IS THE ONE THAT COUNTS. `cache.forget()` on `Clear::Yes` survived the whole suite. The first replacement test used a divider drag onto the divider's own column and proved nothing at all: `MouseEdges` emits no edge for a pointer that did not move, so there was no drag and no clear. The case that IS reachable needs a PINNED window — a client's terminal growing past a window that does not follow it clears the surface while every rectangle stays put — and with `forget()` removed that test reads a COMPLETELY BLANK screen, which is what a user with `window-size manual` would have seen on any resize. Green with it, 3/3.

THE THIRD PASSING ONE IS RECORDED AS REDUNDANT RATHER THAN FIXED: `forget()`'s own token clear cannot be falsified, because clearing the arrangement alone already forces the next frame whole (any frame with a pane in it differs from the empty arrangement). It is kept and its doc says so, since that argument holds only while no caller asks for an empty frame and this is a public type.

A REGRESSION THIS ROUND CAUSED WAS FOUND, ATTRIBUTED AGAINST A CONTROL, AND FIXED AT ITS CAUSE. The PTY suite went 2-of-3 RED; at HEAD it was 3-of-3 green in the same session, so it was mine. The failing test types 88 characters at a freshly split shell and then clicks: making a keystroke cheap removed ~11 seconds during which the shell took its terminal and the child enabled tracking. Both waits are now real — the pane's own text for the first, the DAEMON's per-pane `mouse` key for the second — and the suite is 10 consecutive green runs at 30 tests each.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features (0), the rustdoc gate (15 crates, run as `. doc-gate.sh && doc_gate` — R245's lesson), workspace 1426 -> 1437 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green at 30 each. The live GUI pixel smoke is 117 / 0 on 16 of 17 runs; the single failure was two of R243's pinned-window checks, HEAD measured 6/6 green as a control, and this round's diff reaches no GUI code path (the two shared additions are a defaulted trait method and a `WireHost` method the GUI never calls). Recorded as observed rather than explained.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: A MEASUREMENT WITHOUT ITS BUILD PROFILE IS NOT A MEASUREMENT, AND MINE SAT IN THE LEDGER FOR A ROUND. R244 wrote "~100-124ms PER CHARACTER ... through a real client on a real pseudoterminal" and called it user-facing; it was a debug build, release is ~5ms, and re-running the debug probe gave ~304ms — so the recorded figure could not even reproduce itself. The number was RIGHT for the thing R244 was actually doing (explaining why a debug test suite flaked) and wrong for the thing it was carried forward as. When a number leaves the context that produced it, the context has to travel with it.

THE CONTROL THAT SEPARATES THE COST FROM THE APPARATUS WAS ONE LINE. The same 40 characters as a PASTE produce identical output through identical machinery and differ only in how many times the loop runs — so a flat paste against a linear typed cost rules out the harness's emulator, the output volume, the daemon and the socket in a single reading. Before instrumenting anything, look for the input that changes ONLY the variable in question.

THE FIX RESTED ON AN INVARIANT THAT ALREADY EXISTED, AND FINDING THAT OUT WAS THE DESIGN. Per-row skipping looked like it needed a new guarantee, and the hazard it seemed to carry — a palette change re-colouring cells without touching them — turned out to be one `sprag-vt` already stamps every row for, with a doc saying it exists because pinion's `TextGrid` is generation-gated. The right question was not "is this safe" but "who else already needs it to be".

TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WERE VACUOUS AND ONLY THE REVERT-PROOF SAID SO. One asserted a frame was non-empty when a second pane's changes were always in it; the other drove a gesture that produced no event at all. Both LOOKED like coverage and both passed with the code they guarded deleted. A test written from a design cannot falsify it — and the cheapest way to find that out is to delete the thing and watch.

A GUARD NOTHING REACHES IS A GUARD NOTHING PROVES, AND "UNREACHABLE" WAS WRONG TWICE. `cache.forget()` on a clear survived the whole suite because every clear the suite reaches also moves a rectangle. The reachable case needed a PINNED window, and there the failure is a completely blank screen. R244's lesson one notch on: the layer above did not enforce this guard, it merely never exercised it.

MAKING SOMETHING FAST BREAKS THE TESTS THAT WERE USING IT AS A SLEEP. The PTY suite went 2-of-3 red, and both waits it exposed were already wrong: one read the client's mouse mirror (the MAXIMUM over panes) while claiming to read one pane's child, the other typed at a shell before its startup `tcsetattr` had stopped purging type-ahead. R244 measured the first and called the 88 keystrokes "an accidental synchroniser"; this is that observation arriving as a failure. An optimisation's first job is to find every test that was timing on the old cost.

STILL NOT BUILT, and each is a mechanism rather than a preference: the GUI has its own paint path and does not use `PaintCache` (it composites pixels, not `Change`s, so the row-limited form is not the same object). R217's open item 1 — a DAMAGE-DRIVEN fetch, so an unchanged pane costs no frame at all — is untouched and is now the next term, since 22 projections per 40 keystrokes is still 22 more than a paste. `sprag-tui.rs`'s `refreshed` doc claims a `metadata` call where the code does a full `read_to_string`; measured at 4.8us per key, so it is a wrong SENTENCE rather than a wrong cost.

R247.decision_summary: R247: the three things R246 wrote down instead of fixing. The owner asked why a known-wrong thing was left wrong, and the answer is that there was no reason — each was inside sprag's own tree and none was blocked. (1) `sprag-tui.rs`'s `refreshed` doc claimed the per-keystroke cost is one `metadata` call where the code does a full `read_to_string`; R246 MEASURED that (4.8us per key), named the wrong sentence in its own carry-forward, and left the sentence in the file — a doc defect discovered, priced, recorded and not repaired. (2) R246 excluded the GUI from the row-gated repaint on the grounds that it composites pixels rather than `Change`s, which is a description of a difference rather than a reading of what the GUI does; read from pinion's own `term_grid.rs`, its consumer remembers the highest generation it has read and re-reads only the rows whose generation exceeds it — so the GUI already HAS the mechanism one layer down, and the exclusion is now a measured fact instead of an assertion. (3) The GUI pixel smoke failed once in seventeen runs and R246 recorded it as observed-not-explained; the cause was not found in ~33 further runs either, but the reason it could not be found is fixable and was fixed — both call sites of the cropped-pane predicate answered a bare `false`, so a failure named neither the pane nor the axis nor whether the grids were empty at all.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: `refreshed`'s doc now says `read_to_string` and says WHY it is the whole file rather than a stat — `ClientConfig::refresh` compares CONTENT, because an editor that rewrites a file unchanged must not count as an edit. The measured 4.8us per key rides with it, and the sentence records that it said `metadata` until R246 read the function it was describing. A cost claim in a doc is a claim like any other.

crates/sprag-gui/src/bin/sprag-smoke.rs: `every_pane_is_cropped` replaces the predicate duplicated at both call sites and PRINTS the last grids it observed when the wait does not hold. The duplication was not the problem; the silence was — a `report.check` handed a bare `false` is a sentence with no observation in it, and a gate that cannot say what it saw cannot be diagnosed by the next person who sees it fail once in thirty runs.
verification_bullets: THE GUI EXCLUSION IS NOW READ RATHER THAN ASSERTED. pinion's `crates/pinion-core/src/term_grid.rs` documents the damage contract on `GridBuffer` itself: a consumer remembers the highest generation it has read and, on its next `scene/snapshot`, re-reads only the rows whose generation exceeds it. So the pixel path already gates on exactly the stamps R246's `PaintCache` gates on — the TUI was the frontend MISSING the mechanism, not the one that needed a bespoke copy of it. That also explains, rather than merely accompanies, why `sprag-vt` stamps every row on a palette change.

THE SMOKE FLAKE WAS NOT REPRODUCED AND THAT IS REPORTED AS ITSELF. 14 consecutive green runs on the instrumented binary plus 2 more before it, on top of R246's 16-of-17 — roughly 32 of 33 green with this round's tree and no second occurrence. No cause was found, no cause is claimed, and the diagnostic is the deliverable: the next occurrence prints the painted and buffer extents for every pane instead of a bare `false`.

Gates green after the fixes: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features (0), the rustdoc gate, workspace 1437 tests passed / 0 failed (unchanged — a doc sentence and a smoke diagnostic add no assertions), the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 30 each, live GUI pixel smoke 117 / 0 on 14 consecutive runs.
carry_forward_bullets: A DEFECT YOU HAVE ALREADY FOUND AND PRICED IS THE CHEAPEST ONE THERE WILL EVER BE TO FIX, AND I FILED IT INSTEAD. The `metadata` sentence was wrong, I knew it was wrong, I had the file open, the fix was one comment — and it went into a carry-forward bullet under STILL NOT BUILT, a heading that is for work with a mechanism behind it and not for things I simply did not do. The tell is the shape of the entry: when a not-built item costs less than the sentence describing it, it is not an exclusion, it is an omission.

AN EXCLUSION THAT NAMES A DIFFERENCE IS NOT AN EXCLUSION THAT NAMES AN OBSTACLE. Saying the GUI composites pixels rather than `Change`s is true and settles nothing; what settles it is that pinion's grid consumer already re-reads only the rows whose stamp advanced, which took one grep of the pinned rev to establish. This is the scope-cut rule at a finer grain than the previous four instances: the reason was not about WHERE the work goes, it was about the two things not being identical — which says nothing about whether the second one needs the work.

A GATE THAT PRINTS NOTHING WHEN IT FAILS IS THE MIRROR OF ONE THAT PRINTS NOTHING WHEN IT PASSES, AND THE PROJECT ONLY HAD A RULE FOR THE SECOND. Silence-is-not-a-passing-gate covers a gate that never ran; this is a gate that ran, failed, and could not say what it had seen — so a once-in-thirty failure is unattributable by construction and gets written up as observed-not-explained. When a rare failure cannot be reproduced, the deliverable is the diagnostic, not the explanation.

STILL NOT BUILT, and this one has a mechanism: R217's open item 1, a damage-driven FETCH. The client re-fetches a whole frame per scene bump, so 40 keystrokes still cost the daemon 22 projections against a paste's 1. That is a change to what crosses the wire and to the fetch gate's shape, not a change to a caller — and it is the next term now that the paint half is row-gated.
