R248.decision_summary: R248: H2's last keybinding slice -- tmux's `-n` root table and `-r` repeat -- and the round began by disbelieving the two sentences that had deferred them. Slice 1 declined `-n` because "a binding with no prefix competes with the pane for every keystroke, so it needs the arbitration slice 4 owns"; that first clause is a definition of `-n` rather than an obstacle and the second is circular, and the place it was pointing at -- a function where a client decides between the table and the pane -- was BUILT BY SLICE 3 as `Keymap::route`. The exclusion outlived its own obstacle by two rounds and nobody re-read it. It declined `-r` because "the loop is a pure select today and adding a timeout to it is a change to the thing R226 measured", which confuses a timer with a deadline: nothing in sprag observes the moment a repeat window closes, because there is no key-table indicator to repaint, so the only reader of "has it expired" is the next keystroke -- and a deadline compared on arrival is indistinguishable from a timer that fires, at a cost of one `Instant::now()` per keystroke in each client and no timeout, thread or tick anywhere. What the round could NOT have reasoned out is the routing ORDER, and both of the two questions that decide it are runtime behaviour tmux's manual does not state. Measured against the 3.2a binary driving a real client on a pseudoterminal: the PREFIX is checked before the root table, so `bind -n C-b` does not fire and the prefix still arms (with a root binding on another key firing as the control, which is what makes that a finding rather than a broken harness); and an unbound key INSIDE a repeat window falls through to the pane rather than being swallowed the way an unbound key after the prefix is, which is why the repeat window is a third `PrefixMode` state instead of a deadline hung off the second. Every repeat re-arms the window from itself, also measured. The one deliberate divergence is `-r` on a ROOT binding: tmux accepts it and it does nothing there, because repeat holds the PREFIX table open and a root binding is reached without the prefix -- so sprag refuses it and names that mechanism, the treatment this file already gives a bare `split-window` in a binding.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/keymap.rs: `KeyTable` (Prefix / Root) and `Bind`, a record of table + key + action + repeat replacing the `(KeySpec, BoundAction)` pair. ONE list for both tables rather than one per table, because the file's `[[bind]]` is one array and `list-keys` shows a user their own declaration order -- two lists would need a merge that reconstructs it. A closed enum rather than a string because a table name arrives from three places (the CLI's `-T`/`-n`, the file's `table = ...`, the defaults) and every one has to refuse an unknown name rather than create a table nobody consults; parsing once is what makes the refusal impossible to forget at the fourth call site.

crates/sprag-host/src/keymap.rs: `Keymap::route` gains the root lookup and takes `now: Instant`. The order is armed-table, then the PREFIX, then the root table, then the pane -- and the middle step is the measured one: the natural implementation looks the root table up first and silently takes a user's prefix away when they bind anything to it. `now` is a parameter rather than a call inside so a repeat window is arithmetic in a test instead of a sleep.

crates/sprag-host/src/keymap.rs: `PrefixMode::Repeating { until }` and `Routed::Act { action, again }`. `again` is carried OUT of the routing rather than computed by the caller so `Routed::next` stays what R237 made it -- the one total definition of the next mode, which two frontends cannot partially implement. A third state rather than a deadline on `AfterPrefix` because the two differ in what an UNBOUND key does, swallow against fall-through.

crates/sprag-host/src/keymap.rs: `set_prefix`'s self-send retarget is scoped to the prefix table on BOTH sides -- the binding that moves, and the binding on the new key that is displaced. A `send-prefix` in the root table is a statement about THAT key rather than about whichever key the prefix currently is.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `repeat-time`, `Number { min: 0 }`, default 500. tmux's own default and tmux's own bound (measured: `0` accepted, `-1` refused). The second option the keymap is built FROM rather than beside, so `config.rs`'s existing rule holds unchanged -- options first, keymap downstream of them.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `[[bind]]` gains `table` and `repeat`, `[[unbind]]` gains `table`, both defaulted. Slice 1 chose an array of tables over a `key = action` map for exactly this ("a map has nowhere to put a second field"), so the format change it was avoiding costs nothing here. `table = "root"` and not `root = true` because the CLI and `list-keys` speak `-T TABLE`, and one concept keeps one spelling.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: the bound-and-unbound contradiction becomes PER TABLE, and the writer's `names` matches table AND key. The second is the load-bearing one: an editor matching on the key alone rewrites the wrong entry, silently, and only for users who took the trouble to bind one key in both tables. `set_or_clear` REMOVES a `table`/`repeat` field that has fallen back to its default, so a rebind that drops `-r` does not leave a line the keymap no longer honours.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `bind-key [-nr] [-T TABLE]` and `unbind-key [-n] [-T TABLE]`, with `-n` and `-T` refusing to CONTRADICT (tmux documents `-n` AS `-T root`, so `-n -T prefix` is two statements about one binding and honouring either would invent a precedence rule the user cannot see). Flag parsing stops at the first unrecognised token rather than at the first dash, because a key spec may BE `-`. `list-keys` prints `-T` and `-r` per line, so every line is still a `bind-key` command a user can paste back.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs + crates/sprag-gui/src/keys.rs: one `Instant::now()` each at the routing call. That is the entire cost of `-r` to both event loops; the terminal client's remains the pure `select` R226 measured, with no timeout on `poll_input`.

crates/sprag-gui/src/input.rs: the keymap's position after the pane gate stops being merely right and becomes load-bearing, with the comment saying so. A prefix binding could never reach a text field -- it needs a prefix keystroke and the mode is taken out above -- but a ROOT binding is on a bare key, so with the lookup any higher a user who bound `F5` and then typed `F5` into a search needle would get a split instead of a search.
verification_bullets: TMUX WAS DRIVEN, NOT READ, AND THE ONE PROBE THAT MATTERS HAS A CONTROL. Eight questions were put to the 3.2a binary on this box, four of them through a real client on a pseudoterminal because they are runtime behaviour the manual does not state. (1) `-n` is an alias for `-T root` -- manual. (2) root and prefix hold one key at once: `bind -n C-b` sits beside `C-b send-prefix` in `list-keys`. (3) THE PREFIX WINS: pressing `C-b` then a prefix-table key ran the PREFIX binding and the root binding on `C-b` never fired. (4) THE CONTROL for (3): a root binding on `C-g` DID fire in the same harness -- without it, "the root binding did not run" is equally explained by root bindings not working at all, and (3) would have been a broken apparatus reported as a finding. (5) An unbound key inside a repeat window reaches the PANE: with a `-r` binding armed, typing `ZQ` put `ZQ` in the shell. (6) Every repeat RE-ARMS: three presses at 0/400/800ms under a 500ms `repeat-time` all reached the binding and none reached the pane. (7) `repeat-time` defaults to 500, takes `0`, refuses `-1`. (8) `bind -n -r` is accepted and stored and does nothing.

THE MEASURED ORDER IS THE ONE REASONING WOULD HAVE GOT WRONG. The natural implementation of a root table looks it up first, which is what the design sketch assumed until probe (3) said otherwise. Had that shipped, a user binding anything to their own prefix key would have lost the prefix entirely -- every command key after it going to the shell -- and no unit test written from the design would have caught it, because the design was the thing that was wrong.

THE PTY GATES DRIVE THE SHIPPED BINARY, AND BOTH WERE MEASURED RED. `a_root_binding_acts_with_no_prefix_and_the_key_never_reaches_the_pane` asserts both halves, and the second is the one easy to get wrong: a client that consulted the root table and ALSO forwarded the keystroke looks correct in every screenshot while typing a control character into the user's shell. With the root lookup removed the gate times out at one pane. `a_repeat_binding_acts_twice_on_one_prefix_and_then_lets_go` types the prefix ONCE and the bound key three times; with `PrefixMode::armed` made unconditionally true for a repeat window, its third claim times out.

THE REPEAT GATE'S BINDING IS `send-prefix`, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT FAILING IS WHY. Written against `split-window` it failed on the third claim for a reason that is worth more than the fix: a split MOVES THE FOCUS to the pane it creates, so the key typed after the lapse went to a freshly born shell rather than to the `cat` the test can read -- and a fresh shell's startup `tcsetattr` purges type-ahead anyway (R246). `send-prefix` changes no focus and spawns no child, so the same keystroke produces two different visible bytes depending on the window: `^B` inside it, a literal `%` after it. One pane, no shell, and the third claim is the one that separates "open for repeat-time" from "open forever".

R249.decision_summary: R249: the round began by disbelieving the item it had been asked to build, and the item was already built. R217's open item 1 -- a damage-driven fetch, so an unchanged pane costs no frame at all -- was carried forward as "still not built, and this one has a mechanism" through R246, R247 and R248, and it had been closed three rounds before that carry-forward began. R218's projection gate (rpc::pane_cells_for) stops a request that cannot read a grid from projecting one, and R220's stale_panes in sprag-client (commit 2aeafb8, 2026-07-28, "a client refetches only the panes that changed") refetches only the panes whose ProjectionToken moved. Both frontends share that one wire client, so both have been behind the gate the whole time; the only whole-set fetches left are boot and session-switch, where there is no prior frame to compare against and nothing to skip. It is gated twice over -- sprag-host/tests/grid_cost.rs at unit level, and the live smoke check that asserts only the pane that CHANGED was re-fetched -- and priced in time by sprag-latency, which reports a display client's poll wake over three panes with one changed at 68.40 us against 191.49 us before the gate. What remains under that name is a different and much smaller thing: a pane that changed by one row still pays a whole-grid projection and a whole grid on the wire, 61.55 us or 0.37 percent of a frame, which sits below the 20-to-30 percent run-to-run band the instrument itself says a duration on this box survives in. It was therefore declined as work with a number rather than with an opinion. The shape is R248's inverted: R248 found an EXCLUSION that outlived its obstacle, and this is an OPEN ITEM that outlived its own completion, re-promoted three times because the sentence was carried rather than re-read. The owner then chose H3, agent state detection, and the remainder of the round is its design -- derived from four measurements taken by driving the shipped binaries with a real agent CLI in a real pane, not from herdr's source. The measurements moved the design off the shape it would otherwise have had: sprag's one structural busy/idle signal, ShellState from OSC 133, is dark on an ordinary shell and would in any case read "running" for an agent's entire life, because an agent is one long command; the agent's own signal is its OSC title, whose LEADING GLYPH is the state and whose suffix is a stale task summary; and an idle agent pane is exactly quiescent, which makes the per-row damage stamps already on the wire an EXACT skip for the detector rather than a heuristic one.
changes_bullets: claudedocs/DESIGN-H3-AGENT-STATE.md: the H3 design, derived from four measurements rather than from a rival's source. Nine decisions, each carrying the reading that forced it; five slices; four exclusions that each name an obstacle rather than a location; and a section of OPEN MEASUREMENTS that slice 1 must take before it closes. claudedocs is gitignored, so this ledger entry is the design's durable half and is written to stand without the file.

DECISION D1/D2: the detector is a PURE crate, sprag-detect, sited beside sprag-grid and run DAEMON-side. Pure because sprag-grid is the exact precedent -- a one-directional read of a sprag_vt::Screen owning no lock, no wire shape and no clock -- which is what makes a verdict testable from a synthetic screen instead of from a live agent. Daemon-side because three consumers need the answer (TUI, GUI, MCP) and a fact each computes for itself is three authorities that disagree under load, the rule R237 already paid for with Routed::next. The clock arrives as a PARAMETER, as in R248's Keymap::route(mode, now), so hysteresis is arithmetic in a test rather than a sleep.

DECISION D4: quiescence is an EXACT gate, not an optimisation. The rules are a pure function of the screen and the title, so if neither moved, re-running them provably yields the same verdict -- and "neither moved" is read from the per-row damage stamps the pane list already carries and every client already compares. The exception is written into the decision rather than discovered later: a pane with a transition PENDING confirmation has the clock as a third input and must be re-evaluated on the tick even when nothing moved, or an agent that goes quiet mid-transition freezes in its previous state forever, which is worse than the flicker hysteresis exists to stop.

R250.decision_summary: R250: H3 slice 1 -- sprag-detect, the pure rule engine that reads what an agent pane is DOING from its screen and its OSC title. The round opened by taking the measurement R249 had recorded as slice 1's blocker rather than as an assumption: the title shown during a MID-SESSION PERMISSION DIALOG. Two probes answered it, and the free one answered it first -- a slash-command picker is a modal choice list that costs no model tokens at all, and its title was byte-identical to the idle title, which is already the whole finding. The paid probe then confirmed it on the real thing: a genuine tool-permission dialog was driven up on a live claude in a live sprag pane, and the title read the IDLE glyph beside a summary of a task that had already finished several turns earlier. So the answer is the one the design named as the branch that changes rule priority: the title cannot separate Blocked from Idle, the bottom-region rule carries that distinction alone, and the blocked rule must outrank the idle rule because on a blocked pane BOTH of them match. That measurement is now a test, and the test asserts the non-vacuity explicitly -- it checks that the idle rule really does match the same screen, because otherwise the priority assertion would be proving nothing. Three independent dialogs were captured in all (first-run trust, a slash-command picker, a tool permission request) and they share exactly one shape: a selection marker followed by a numbered option at the start of a line, with at least one further numbered option below it. The second half of that pattern is not decoration; without it a user's own typed line echoed into the prompt box reads as a dialog, since an echo and a choice list's first row are the same string, and a choice list always offers more than one choice. The crate is pure in the sense sprag-grid is pure -- a one-directional read of a sprag_vt::Screen owning no lock, no wire shape and no clock -- and the screen and the title are SEPARATE parameters rather than one bundled pane, because those two are exactly what slice 2's quiescence gate must compare to know that re-running the rules cannot change the answer. Hysteresis, the per-pane memory and the publish seam are deliberately absent and belong to the caller. The slice ships one measured MISS, asserted as a test rather than left to be discovered from a bug report: a first-run trust dialog arrives before the agent has set any title and with its footer replaced, so no fingerprint claims the pane and it reads Unknown.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect: a new crate, sited beside sprag-grid and pure for the same reason -- a verdict about somebody else's UI is only honest if a CAPTURED screen can be replayed against it, and purity is what makes that possible without a daemon, a pty or an agent. `AgentState { Unknown, Working, Blocked, Idle }` with `wire_str` returning `None` for Unknown, so the eventual pane-list key is additive by construction rather than by a serializer remembering to omit it.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `detect(screen, title, manifests)` takes the screen and the title as SEPARATE parameters. That is not a style choice: they are exactly the two inputs slice 2's quiescence gate must compare to prove that re-running the rules cannot change the answer, and bundling them into a pane would hide the property the gate rests on. The first manifest whose fingerprints match claims the pane, so ordering is meaningful and belongs to whoever assembles the list -- which is how a user manifest layers over a built-in one in slice 4 without this function ever learning about files.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Rule.all` (every match must hold) beside `Manifest.any` (any fingerprint is enough), named for their semantics so the difference is visible at the use site rather than in a doc. The asymmetry is derived: a rule wants specificity by conjunction instead of one unreadable regex, while IDENTIFICATION wants independent evidence, because a pane mid-dialog shows none of what a pane at rest shows and requiring every fingerprint would recognise the agent only in the state that happens to show all of them.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Rule.priority`, with declaration order as the tie-break. This exists because of one measurement and the code says so: on a blocked pane the blocked rule and the idle rule both match, since the glyph is identical in the two states. `max_by_key` returns the LAST maximum, so the iterator is reversed to make the tie fall to the FIRST rule -- a reader should not have to know which end of an iterator a tie falls off.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Verdict` carries the manifest name and the RULE ID that fired. A manifest that claims a pane but matches no rule yields Unknown WITH the agent named, because "I know what this is and not what it is doing" and "I do not know what this is" are different facts and a person debugging a manifest needs to tell them apart. The id riding the verdict is what keeps a future `explain` from becoming a second code path that can disagree with the first.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Region::BottomLines(n)` counts NON-EMPTY rows, so the window does not depend on how tall the pane is or on how much blank an agent's box drawing leaves behind; `Region::Title` yields the empty string for an absent title, which is the safe direction because a prefix test and a caret-anchored regex both fail on it. R250.publishable_decision_summary: R250: H3 slice 1 -- sprag-detect, the pure rule engine that reads what an agent pane is DOING from its screen and its OSC title. The round opened by taking the measurement R249 had recorded as slice 1's blocker rather than as an assumption: the title shown during a MID-SESSION PERMISSION DIALOG. Two probes answered it, and the free one answered it first -- a slash-command picker is a modal choice list that costs no model tokens at all, and its title was byte-identical to the idle title, which is already the whole finding. The paid probe then confirmed it on the real thing: a genuine tool-permission dialog was driven up on a live claude in a live sprag pane, and the title read the IDLE glyph beside a summary of a task that had already finished several turns earlier. So the answer is the one the design named as the branch that changes rule priority: the title cannot separate Blocked from Idle, the bottom-region rule carries that distinction alone, and the blocked rule must outrank the idle rule because on a blocked pane BOTH of them match. That measurement is now a test, and the test asserts the non-vacuity explicitly -- it checks that the idle rule really does match the same screen, because otherwise the priority assertion would be proving nothing. Hysteresis, the per-pane memory and the publish seam are deliberately absent and belong to the caller. The slice ships one measured MISS, asserted as a test rather than left to be discovered from a bug report: a first-run trust dialog arrives before the agent has set any title and with its footer replaced, so no fingerprint claims the pane and it reads Unknown.

R251.decision_summary: R251: the second-agent debt, paid. R249 and R250 both recorded that one agent is a sample rather than a vocabulary and that a second was owed before sprag-detect's regions and tests froze; both recorded it as a provisioning obstacle. The round re-verified that obstacle from the machine rather than from the note, found it still true, cleared it by installing codex -- an independently implemented agent, Rust and ratatui against claude's TypeScript and Ink -- and drove it in a real sprag pane the same way R249 drove claude. Every measurement cost zero model tokens on the subject, by the ordering R250 established: the sign-in picker and the trust dialog are the first screens codex shows, the model picker is a mid-session modal opened by a slash command, and the working spinner turns just as well on a request that is about to fail. Three things moved. The dialog marker is not a constant and not even a per-agent constant: three glyphs were measured across the two agents and two of them are inside codex alone, so the pattern now matches the measured class. A fingerprint needs conjunction: claude is identified by one string in a fixed footer while codex has no constant string at any width, so Manifest.any became a disjunction of conjunctions and Fingerprint exists to carry that. And the braille spinner generalised where the resting glyph did not: codex's working title is a braille frame exactly as claude's is, and the range R250 wrote for the animation rather than for its two observed frames matched four frames from another program in another language, while codex has no resting glyph at all and its idle rule is a priority fallback instead. What survived untouched is the larger half of the answer -- both Region variants, all three Test variants, Rule.priority, and the twelve-row window, which codex's dialogs landed inside without adjustment. The round also produced a finding the design did not anticipate and could not have reached with one agent: a modal covers the two things codex's fingerprint is made of, so a blocked codex pane is not recognised as codex at all, in the one state this front exists to report. That is not fixable by a better fingerprint, and it moves agent IDENTITY into the per-pane memory slice 2 was scoped to build for hysteresis alone.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: a new Fingerprint type, and Manifest.any becomes a list of them rather than a list of single matches -- a disjunction of CONJUNCTIONS. The extra level is a measurement rather than a symmetry with Rule.all. claude is identified by one string in a fixed footer, "? for shortcuts", and one condition is all it needs. codex has no constant string anywhere on its screen at any width: its footer is model, effort, a middle dot and the working directory, every part of which is configurable or the user's, and the one line naming the product scrolls out of the transcript with the rest of the conversation. It is identifiable only as its composer line AND the shape of its footer together, and flattening that back into Manifest.any would have put the conjunction inside a regex spanning rows -- the exact thing Rule.all's own doc comment says the design refuses.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: dialog_pattern's selection marker becomes a CLASS of three measured glyphs instead of the single literal it was written from. claude marks with U+276F, codex marks its sign-in picker with plain ASCII 0x3E and its directory-trust dialog with U+203A. Two different markers inside ONE agent is the part that settles it: the marker is not a per-agent constant either, so a manifest keyed on the glyph one probe happened to show is a manifest about that probe. Everything else about the shape survived unchanged across both agents -- a marker, then a digit and a period at the start of a line, then at least one more numbered option below.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: a codex manifest, built-in beside claude's. Its rules are structurally claude's -- the same dialog rule through the widened marker, the same braille spinner rule, the same priority ordering for the same measured reason -- and its FINGERPRINT is the only place the two agents genuinely differ. That similarity is the point of shipping it: a vocabulary that needed a second set of concepts for a second agent would not have been a vocabulary.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: codex_composer_pattern and codex_footer_pattern match SHAPES rather than words. The footer is read as two tokens, a middle dot and an absolute path, because the model name and the reasoning effort are both configurable and the path is the user's; nothing in it is a constant to test for. It was captured at 80 and again at 160 columns, so the shape is the footer itself rather than a truncation artefact of one probe width.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: painted_title_pattern, which asks only that the pane has painted a title at all, replaces the negation this rule was first written as. codex has no resting glyph -- at rest its title is the bare working-directory name, exactly what a shell puts there -- so the idle rule was first written as "a title that does not begin with a spinner frame". That is a second spelling of what Rule.priority already decides, and the crate now says so and takes its specificity from the ordering instead.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: five codex screens captured verbatim from a real pane and replayed through the real emulator in the tests -- the sign-in picker, the directory-trust dialog, the mid-session model picker, the composer at rest, and the working title. Seven new tests, including one that asserts the two built-in manifests do not claim each other's panes, which is the property slice 4's user-layered manifests will rest on and which no single-manifest test could have shown.
verification_bullets: THE INHERITED OBSTACLE WAS RE-VERIFIED BEFORE IT WAS ACTED ON, WHICH IS THE RULE R249 PAID FOR. "Only claude is on this box" was a not-built sentence carried forward from two rounds, and the round that would act on it re-read it from the machine rather than from the note: fifteen candidate agent CLIs probed on PATH, one hit, and the one apparent second hit was a shell builtin rather than a tool. The obstacle was real and still real, so the round cleared it instead of re-promoting it. Cost of the check: one command.

THE FREE-PROBE ORDERING FROM R250 WAS USED AGAIN AND ANSWERED EVERYTHING BUT ONE THING. Every measurement in this round cost zero model tokens on the subject agent. The sign-in picker and the directory-trust dialog are the first two screens codex ever shows; the model picker is a mid-session modal that opens on a slash command with no model call; and the working state was read from a turn that failed on a deliberately invalid API key, because a request that is in flight spins the same spinner as one that will succeed. What that does NOT cover is stated rather than left implied: codex's tool-APPROVAL dialog was never seen, because producing one needs a working credential, and the dialog rule's application to it is therefore an inference from three other codex dialogs rather than a measurement of that one.

FIVE REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL FIVE RED, WITH THE MUTATED LINE PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN. The Fingerprint conjunction weakened to a disjunction (1 test red); the dialog marker narrowed back to claude's lone glyph (2 red); the painted-title pattern widened to accept the empty title (1 red); the composer window narrowed from three bottom rows to one (4 red); and the footer shape stripped of its separator and path (1 red). Printing the mutated line is R250's rule applied without having to be reminded, since the failure it guards against -- a mutation harness that fails to mutate -- is indistinguishable from a passing proof. Restoration was verified by diff against a byte copy taken before the first proof, not by git checkout.

THE THIRD REVERT-PROOF CAME BACK GREEN, AND THAT IS A FINDING ABOUT THIS ROUND'S OWN CODE RATHER THAN ABOUT THE HARNESS. codex's idle rule was written as a negation -- a title not beginning with a braille frame -- with a paragraph of reasoning attached. Widening that pattern to match anything at all turned no test red, and it could not: the spinner rule outranks the idle rule, so on a working pane priority decides the answer no matter what the idle pattern says, and on a resting pane both readings agree. The negation was a second statement of a fact Rule.priority already carries, which is a mechanism that can silently disagree with spinner_pattern the day either is edited. It was replaced by what the rule actually needs -- that a title exists at all -- and the proof then went red on the one input that distinguishes them, a claimed pane that has painted no title. Twice now a revert-proof has caught the instrument; this is the first time it has caught the design.

THE CENTRAL FINDING OF R250 WAS INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED BY AN AGENT THAT SHARES NO CODE WITH THE FIRST. On codex's mid-session model picker the title reads the resting form, with no spinner, exactly as claude's title reads the idle glyph during a permission dialog. The rule is now asserted by a test that drives them.

Every measurement cost zero model tokens on the subject, by the ordering R250 established: the sign-in picker and the trust dialog are the first screens codex shows, the model picker is a mid-session modal opened by a slash command, and the working spinner turns just as well on a request that is about to fail. publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: a new Fingerprint type, and Manifest.any becomes a list of them rather than a list of single matches -- a disjunction of CONJUNCTIONS. crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: dialog_pattern's selection marker becomes a CLASS of three measured glyphs instead of the single literal it was written from. claude marks with U+276F, codex marks its sign-in picker with plain ASCII 0x3E and its directory-trust dialog with U+203A. crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: a codex manifest, built-in beside claude's. FIVE REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL FIVE RED, WITH THE MUTATED LINE PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN. Restoration was verified by diff against a byte copy taken before the first proof, not by git checkout.

THE THIRD REVERT-PROOF CAME BACK GREEN, AND THAT IS A FINDING ABOUT THIS ROUND'S OWN CODE RATHER THAN ABOUT THE HARNESS. codex's idle rule was written as a negation -- a title not beginning with a braille frame -- with a paragraph of reasoning attached. R252.decision_summary: R252: H3 slice 2 -- the per-pane memory, which is where everything a single frame cannot know had to go. Slice 1 shipped a rule engine that answers from one screen and one title; three of the measurements this front rests on are about a pane over time and none of them could be honoured without somewhere to remember. The slice ships `sprag_detect::Tracker`: the quiescence gate with its pending exception, the settle window that keeps an animated signal from publishing a flicker, and -- scope grown by R251 -- the agent IDENTITY carried across the states in which a modal covers the fingerprint. Three things were found, and two of them changed what shipped. FIRST, the design asked for two hysteresis parameters, "N consecutive evaluations with a wall-clock cap", and the count is not a second mechanism: a pending candidate is REPLACED by any observation that disagrees with it, so "this has been the answer since t" already means "nothing has disagreed since t", and the count adds no evidence to that. Under the OR the design's own sentence implies -- the cap exists precisely because a quiet pane never reaches N -- the count can only publish EARLIER than the window, so on a pane that repaints quickly, which is what an agent printing output IS, N observations arrive in milliseconds and the guard collapses to nothing; under an AND it is worse, because a pane that goes quiet after one observation never reaches N and freezes in its previous state forever, which is the failure the pending exception exists to prevent, arriving by the other door. The parameter was deleted rather than tested into place, which is R251's own lesson (when specificity could come from two places only one is doing the work) applied to a pair of knobs instead of a pair of rules. SECOND, the identity memory needs a BOUND, and the bound comes from the same measurement that made the memory necessary: `codex` at rest is a bare working-directory title over a prompt line, which is what a SHELL looks like too, so without the fingerprint there is nothing left to tell an agent at rest from the shell that outlived it. So memory may carry identity only while the pane is showing something ACTIVE -- a dialog or a spinner, evidence a rule SAW -- and the identity is let go the moment the published answer is that nobody claims the pane. Without that bound `codex`'s idle rule, which fires on a title merely existing, would report a plain shell as a resting agent forever. THIRD, and read from the code rather than assumed: the quiescence key needs the screen WIDTH. `Screen::resized`, the resize path an alternate screen takes, copies every row's damage stamp verbatim while truncating the cells to the new width, so a narrowing resize is a content change that no stamp records. The screen KIND, by the same reading, is NOT needed -- the two buffers are separate `Screen` objects with per-buffer stamps and a fresh buffer is blank with all-zero stamps, so the only reading where stamps could coincide across a switch is one where the text is identical as well -- and that term was left out rather than added for safety, because a term no test could turn red is a claim rather than a mechanism. One further consequence was taken deliberately: the settle window applies to a FIRST publication too, and that is what absorbs the second miss R251 pinned, `codex`'s transient hint window, instead of publishing a three-second Unknown blip on the wire.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker`, one per pane, holding the published verdict, a monotonic `seq` that moves only on a published CHANGE, the pending candidate with the instant it was first seen, the last reading of the inputs, and the remembered agent. It owns no clock and no manifests: `now` and the manifest list arrive on every `observe` call, so a workspace keeps one manifest list and a test writes arithmetic instead of a sleep -- the shape `Keymap::route` already uses (R248). `observe` is meant to be called on EVERY tick including the empty ones, and the quiescence gate lives inside it rather than at the call site so no caller can hold a pane's pending transition open by deciding for itself that nothing was worth asking about.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Hysteresis` carries ONE window, where the design named a count and a cap. The doc comment states why the count is not a second mechanism rather than leaving a reader to wonder which of the two is load-bearing, and `DEFAULT_SETTLE` is two seconds because the artifact the window exists to absorb is one frame of an animation measured at about 1 Hz -- a window shorter than the period it guards against publishes exactly the flicker it was added for. A test holds the default to that reason, the treatment `history-limit` and `repeat-time` get against the emulator and the keymap.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the quiescence key is the per-row damage stamps AND the screen width AND the title, and each of the three is there because the rules can read it. The stamps are the same comparison the projection gate and the wire client already make against the same values (R218, R220). The width is there because `Screen::resized` copies stamps verbatim across a width change while truncating the cells, so `row_text` moves where no stamp does. An absent title is stored as the empty string exactly as `detect` reads it, so two titles this cannot tell apart are two the rules cannot tell apart either. Nothing else is in the key, and the screen kind's absence is argued in the same place rather than left as an oversight.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the publication policy is one asymmetry, derived rather than asserted. A verdict resting on evidence PRESENT on the screen is published on sight; one resting on an ABSENCE has to hold for the window. That is why a dialog reaches a person immediately while a return to rest does not, and it is the same predicate that bounds the identity memory -- one property named once (`AgentState::is_active`), read twice.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the identity memory. When no manifest claims the pane, the remembered manifest is asked directly, by NAME rather than by position in the list, because slice 4 reloads that list from a file and a name survives a reload. The verdict is accepted only if it is active, and the identity is dropped the moment a verdict with no agent is published. Both halves are asserted by tests, in both directions.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `AgentState::is_active`, and arbitration extracted from `detect` into `Manifest::verdict` so identification and arbitration are separable without becoming two code paths that can disagree -- the argument `Rule::id` already makes one level down. `detect` is now the composition of the two halves and its behaviour is unchanged, which slice 1's twenty-two tests still assert.
verification_bullets: THE GATE THE DESIGN NAMED FOR THIS SLICE IS MET, AND IT ASSERTS ITS OWN NON-VACUITY. Six braille frames replayed at the measured 1 Hz produce ONE publication, not six. That assertion would pass unchanged in a world where the tracker froze after the first frame, so the test goes on to drive a dialog into the same pane and assert the publication count moves to two -- a frozen tracker fails there. The same discipline R250 paid for on arbitration, applied to a claim about counting.

THE QUIESCENCE SKIP IS PROVEN BY CHANGING THE RULES UNDERNEATH IT, WHICH IS THE ONLY WAY TO SEE A SKIP WITHOUT ADDING A COUNTER FOR TESTS TO READ. A pane is published as idle, then the same inputs are offered again with a manifest whose idle rule has been rewritten to say Working: only an evaluation could notice the rewrite, so a verdict that does not move is the skip. The test then moves one row and asserts the rewritten manifest lands at once -- so what was measured is a skip and not a stop.

THE RESIZE TEST ASSERTS ITS OWN PREMISE RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. It reads every row's damage stamp before and after the resize and asserts they are IDENTICAL, so the test is demonstrably about the width term. If `sprag-vt` ever begins stamping rows on resize, that assertion fails and says the premise died, instead of the test quietly becoming vacuous while still passing.

ELEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL ELEVEN RED, WITH THE MUTATED TEXT PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN AND THE FAILING TEST NAMES CAPTURED. The pending exception removed (6 red); the quiescence gate forced never to skip (1); the width term dropped from the key (1); the title term dropped (2); publish-on-sight removed so everything waits (7); the window removed so everything publishes at once (6); the identity memory replaced by the unclaimed verdict (1); the active-evidence bound on that memory dropped (2); the identity never let go (1); the window re-started on every re-observation instead of measured from first sight (1); the default window lowered below the measured spinner period (3). The harness refuses to run a proof whose edit did not land, and the file was compared byte-for-byte against a copy taken before the first proof rather than restored with `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice.

THE PROOF MATRIX CAUGHT A TEST THAT WAS PASSING FOR A WEAKER REASON THAN ITS NAME CLAIMED. Lowering the default window below the spinner period left `a_pause_in_the_animation_does_not_publish_a_return_to_rest` green, because the test never ticked DURING the pause: it would have passed with a window of one nanosecond. A tick inside the pause was added, and the proof then went red on it. Reading which test each mutation kills is what exposed this; a proof matrix scored only as red-or-green would have hidden it.

A PROPERTY NO TEST COVERED WAS FOUND BY ASKING WHAT A MUTATION WOULD NOT CATCH, BEFORE RUNNING IT. Re-starting a pending candidate's window on every re-observation is a real defect -- a pane that repaints faster than the window would never settle -- and nothing in the suite would have noticed. `a_pane_that_keeps_repainting_settles_when_the_candidate_has_held_long_enough` was written first and the mutation then had somewhere to land.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates; the workspace suite 1488 to 1500 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus twelve is exactly this slice's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved. The PTY suite and the live GUI pixel smoke were NOT run: `sprag-detect` still has no dependents, so neither harness can reach it, and running them would be provenance for a claim this round does not make.
carry_forward_bullets: TWO KNOBS WHERE ONE IS DOING THE WORK IS THE SAME DEFECT AS TWO RULES WHERE ONE IS, AND IT ARRIVES WITH REASONING ATTACHED. R251 found a rule whose specificity could come either from its pattern or from its position in a priority order, and the honest fix was to delete the claim rather than test it into place. This round found the parameter version: a count of consecutive confirmations beside a wall-clock window, where the count is inert under the OR that makes the pair work at all and a freeze under the AND that would give it teeth. The general test is worth keeping and is cheap: state the two mechanisms' semantics precisely, then ask what input separates them. If none does, one of them is a second spelling. What makes this class hard to see is that a design sentence naming two parameters reads as MORE careful than one naming a single window, so the redundancy is disguised as rigour.

AN IDENTITY MEMORY NEEDS A BOUND, AND THE BOUND CAME FROM THE SAME MEASUREMENT THAT MADE THE MEMORY NECESSARY. "A pane that was an agent a moment ago is still that agent" is true and is not enough: `codex` at rest is measurably indistinguishable from a shell except by the fingerprint the modal covers, so memory carried without a bound would report the shell that outlives an agent as a resting agent forever -- and its idle rule fires on a title merely existing, so this is not hypothetical. The bound is that memory may only carry an ACTIVE verdict, and that is the SAME asymmetry the settle window rests on, so one named property does both jobs instead of two knobs drifting apart. Generalises: when a memory papers over missing evidence, the question to answer is not how long it lasts but what evidence it is allowed to substitute for.

A DAMAGE STAMP IS NOT THE WHOLE OF WHAT A READER READS, AND THE ONLY WAY TO KNOW IS TO READ THE PRODUCER. The quiescence skip is exact only if the key covers every input the rules touch. Row generations cover a row's CELLS; `row_text` is the cells AND the width, and `Screen::resized` -- the resize path an alternate screen takes -- copies each stamp verbatim while truncating cells to the new width. So the key needs the width, and that is a fact read out of `sprag-vt`, not a precaution. The same reading settled the term that was NOT added: the two screen buffers are separate objects with per-buffer stamps and a fresh one is blank with all-zero stamps, so no stale-identical reading with different text is reachable. A term that no test could turn red is a claim, and this one was argued in the doc comment instead of being added for safety.

SLICE 3 is next: the additive `agent` key on the pane list (the tracker already counts the `seq` it needs), the evaluation site inside the pane list's existing lock, `explain`, and the settle window as a `sprag-host` OPTION -- which lands there rather than here because `show-options` walks the option table and prints every option whether the user set it or not, so declaring one before an evaluation site reads it ships a control the user can set and nothing obeys. SLICE 4 is manifests in `config.toml`, layered over the built-ins on H2's keymap precedent. SLICE 5 is the surfaces. Two measured misses are still pinned by slice 1's tests and want fixing rather than rediscovering: an onboarding dialog arrives before any title and with the footer replaced, measured in BOTH agents, which is what a title-free fingerprint would buy; and one measurement remains unbought, `codex`'s tool-approval dialog, which needs a working credential, so the dialog rule's fit to that screen is still an inference from three other `codex` dialogs. R252.publishable_decision_summary: R252: H3 slice 2 -- the per-pane memory, which is where everything a single frame cannot know had to go. Slice 1 shipped a rule engine that answers from one screen and one title; three of the measurements this front rests on are about a pane over time and none of them could be honoured without somewhere to remember. The slice ships `sprag_detect::Tracker`: the quiescence gate with its pending exception, the settle window that keeps an animated signal from publishing a flicker, and -- scope grown by R251 -- the agent IDENTITY carried across the states in which a modal covers the fingerprint. Three things were found, and two of them changed what shipped. FIRST, the design asked for two hysteresis parameters, "N consecutive evaluations with a wall-clock cap", and the count is not a second mechanism: a pending candidate is REPLACED by any observation that disagrees with it, so "this has been the answer since t" already means "nothing has disagreed since t", and the count adds no evidence to that. Under the OR the design's own sentence implies -- the cap exists precisely because a quiet pane never reaches N -- the count can only publish EARLIER than the window, so on a pane that repaints quickly, which is what an agent printing output IS, N observations arrive in milliseconds and the guard collapses to nothing; under an AND it is worse, because a pane that goes quiet after one observation never reaches N and freezes in its previous state forever, which is the failure the pending exception exists to prevent, arriving by the other door. The parameter was deleted rather than tested into place, which is R251's own lesson (when specificity could come from two places only one is doing the work) applied to a pair of knobs instead of a pair of rules. SECOND, the identity memory needs a BOUND, and the bound comes from the same measurement that made the memory necessary: `codex` at rest is a bare working-directory title over a prompt line, which is what a SHELL looks like too, so without the fingerprint there is nothing left to tell an agent at rest from the shell that outlived it. So memory may carry identity only while the pane is showing something ACTIVE -- a dialog or a spinner, evidence a rule SAW -- and the identity is let go the moment the published answer is that nobody claims the pane. Without that bound `codex`'s idle rule, which fires on a title merely existing, would report a plain shell as a resting agent forever. THIRD, and read from the code rather than assumed: the quiescence key needs the screen WIDTH. `Screen::resized`, the resize path an alternate screen takes, copies every row's damage stamp verbatim while truncating the cells to the new width, so a narrowing resize is a content change that no stamp records. The screen KIND, by the same reading, is NOT needed -- the two buffers are separate `Screen` objects with per-buffer stamps and a fresh buffer is blank with all-zero stamps, so the only reading where stamps could coincide across a switch is one where the text is identical as well -- and that term was left out rather than added for safety, because a term no test could turn red is a claim rather than a mechanism. One further consequence was taken deliberately: the settle window applies to a FIRST publication too, and that is what absorbs the second miss R251 pinned, `codex`'s transient hint window, instead of publishing a three-second Unknown blip on the wire.
publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker`, one per pane, holding the published verdict, a monotonic `seq` that moves only on a published CHANGE, the pending candidate with the instant it was first seen, the last reading of the inputs, and the remembered agent. It owns no clock and no manifests: `now` and the manifest list arrive on every `observe` call, so a workspace keeps one manifest list and a test writes arithmetic instead of a sleep -- the shape `Keymap::route` already uses (R248). `observe` is meant to be called on EVERY tick including the empty ones, and the quiescence gate lives inside it rather than at the call site so no caller can hold a pane's pending transition open by deciding for itself that nothing was worth asking about.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Hysteresis` carries ONE window, where the design named a count and a cap. The doc comment states why the count is not a second mechanism rather than leaving a reader to wonder which of the two is load-bearing, and `DEFAULT_SETTLE` is two seconds because the artifact the window exists to absorb is one frame of an animation measured at about 1 Hz -- a window shorter than the period it guards against publishes exactly the flicker it was added for. A test holds the default to that reason, the treatment `history-limit` and `repeat-time` get against the emulator and the keymap.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the quiescence key is the per-row damage stamps AND the screen width AND the title, and each of the three is there because the rules can read it. The stamps are the same comparison the projection gate and the wire client already make against the same values (R218, R220). The width is there because `Screen::resized` copies stamps verbatim across a width change while truncating the cells, so `row_text` moves where no stamp does. An absent title is stored as the empty string exactly as `detect` reads it, so two titles this cannot tell apart are two the rules cannot tell apart either. Nothing else is in the key, and the screen kind's absence is argued in the same place rather than left as an oversight.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the publication policy is one asymmetry, derived rather than asserted. A verdict resting on evidence PRESENT on the screen is published on sight; one resting on an ABSENCE has to hold for the window. That is why a dialog reaches a person immediately while a return to rest does not, and it is the same predicate that bounds the identity memory -- one property named once (`AgentState::is_active`), read twice.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the identity memory. When no manifest claims the pane, the remembered manifest is asked directly, by NAME rather than by position in the list, because slice 4 reloads that list from a file and a name survives a reload. The verdict is accepted only if it is active, and the identity is dropped the moment a verdict with no agent is published. Both halves are asserted by tests, in both directions.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `AgentState::is_active`, and arbitration extracted from `detect` into `Manifest::verdict` so identification and arbitration are separable without becoming two code paths that can disagree -- the argument `Rule::id` already makes one level down. `detect` is now the composition of the two halves and its behaviour is unchanged, which slice 1's twenty-two tests still assert.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE GATE THE DESIGN NAMED FOR THIS SLICE IS MET, AND IT ASSERTS ITS OWN NON-VACUITY. Six braille frames replayed at the measured 1 Hz produce ONE publication, not six. That assertion would pass unchanged in a world where the tracker froze after the first frame, so the test goes on to drive a dialog into the same pane and assert the publication count moves to two -- a frozen tracker fails there. The same discipline R250 paid for on arbitration, applied to a claim about counting.

THE QUIESCENCE SKIP IS PROVEN BY CHANGING THE RULES UNDERNEATH IT, WHICH IS THE ONLY WAY TO SEE A SKIP WITHOUT ADDING A COUNTER FOR TESTS TO READ. A pane is published as idle, then the same inputs are offered again with a manifest whose idle rule has been rewritten to say Working: only an evaluation could notice the rewrite, so a verdict that does not move is the skip. The test then moves one row and asserts the rewritten manifest lands at once -- so what was measured is a skip and not a stop.

THE RESIZE TEST ASSERTS ITS OWN PREMISE RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. It reads every row's damage stamp before and after the resize and asserts they are IDENTICAL, so the test is demonstrably about the width term. If `sprag-vt` ever begins stamping rows on resize, that assertion fails and says the premise died, instead of the test quietly becoming vacuous while still passing.

ELEVEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL ELEVEN RED, WITH THE MUTATED TEXT PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN AND THE FAILING TEST NAMES CAPTURED. The pending exception removed (6 red); the quiescence gate forced never to skip (1); the width term dropped from the key (1); the title term dropped (2); publish-on-sight removed so everything waits (7); the window removed so everything publishes at once (6); the identity memory replaced by the unclaimed verdict (1); the active-evidence bound on that memory dropped (2); the identity never let go (1); the window re-started on every re-observation instead of measured from first sight (1); the default window lowered below the measured spinner period (3). The harness refuses to run a proof whose edit did not land, and the file was compared byte-for-byte against a copy taken before the first proof rather than restored with `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice.

THE PROOF MATRIX CAUGHT A TEST THAT WAS PASSING FOR A WEAKER REASON THAN ITS NAME CLAIMED. Lowering the default window below the spinner period left `a_pause_in_the_animation_does_not_publish_a_return_to_rest` green, because the test never ticked DURING the pause: it would have passed with a window of one nanosecond. A tick inside the pause was added, and the proof then went red on it. Reading which test each mutation kills is what exposed this; a proof matrix scored only as red-or-green would have hidden it.

A PROPERTY NO TEST COVERED WAS FOUND BY ASKING WHAT A MUTATION WOULD NOT CATCH, BEFORE RUNNING IT. Re-starting a pending candidate's window on every re-observation is a real defect -- a pane that repaints faster than the window would never settle -- and nothing in the suite would have noticed. `a_pane_that_keeps_repainting_settles_when_the_candidate_has_held_long_enough` was written first and the mutation then had somewhere to land.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates; the workspace suite 1488 to 1500 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus twelve is exactly this slice's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved. The PTY suite and the live GUI pixel smoke were NOT run: `sprag-detect` still has no dependents, so neither harness can reach it, and running them would be provenance for a claim this round does not make.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: TWO KNOBS WHERE ONE IS DOING THE WORK IS THE SAME DEFECT AS TWO RULES WHERE ONE IS, AND IT ARRIVES WITH REASONING ATTACHED. R251 found a rule whose specificity could come either from its pattern or from its position in a priority order, and the honest fix was to delete the claim rather than test it into place. This round found the parameter version: a count of consecutive confirmations beside a wall-clock window, where the count is inert under the OR that makes the pair work at all and a freeze under the AND that would give it teeth. The general test is worth keeping and is cheap: state the two mechanisms' semantics precisely, then ask what input separates them. If none does, one of them is a second spelling. What makes this class hard to see is that a design sentence naming two parameters reads as MORE careful than one naming a single window, so the redundancy is disguised as rigour.

AN IDENTITY MEMORY NEEDS A BOUND, AND THE BOUND CAME FROM THE SAME MEASUREMENT THAT MADE THE MEMORY NECESSARY. "A pane that was an agent a moment ago is still that agent" is true and is not enough: `codex` at rest is measurably indistinguishable from a shell except by the fingerprint the modal covers, so memory carried without a bound would report the shell that outlives an agent as a resting agent forever -- and its idle rule fires on a title merely existing, so this is not hypothetical. The bound is that memory may only carry an ACTIVE verdict, and that is the SAME asymmetry the settle window rests on, so one named property does both jobs instead of two knobs drifting apart. Generalises: when a memory papers over missing evidence, the question to answer is not how long it lasts but what evidence it is allowed to substitute for.

A DAMAGE STAMP IS NOT THE WHOLE OF WHAT A READER READS, AND THE ONLY WAY TO KNOW IS TO READ THE PRODUCER. The quiescence skip is exact only if the key covers every input the rules touch. Row generations cover a row's CELLS; `row_text` is the cells AND the width, and `Screen::resized` -- the resize path an alternate screen takes -- copies each stamp verbatim while truncating cells to the new width. So the key needs the width, and that is a fact read out of `sprag-vt`, not a precaution. The same reading settled the term that was NOT added: the two screen buffers are separate objects with per-buffer stamps and a fresh one is blank with all-zero stamps, so no stale-identical reading with different text is reachable. A term that no test could turn red is a claim, and this one was argued in the doc comment instead of being added for safety.

SLICE 3 is next: the additive `agent` key on the pane list (the tracker already counts the `seq` it needs), the evaluation site inside the pane list's existing lock, `explain`, and the settle window as a `sprag-host` OPTION -- which lands there rather than here because `show-options` walks the option table and prints every option whether the user set it or not, so declaring one before an evaluation site reads it ships a control the user can set and nothing obeys. SLICE 4 is manifests in `config.toml`, layered over the built-ins on H2's keymap precedent. SLICE 5 is the surfaces. Two measured misses are still pinned by slice 1's tests and want fixing rather than rediscovering: an onboarding dialog arrives before any title and with the footer replaced, measured in BOTH agents, which is what a title-free fingerprint would buy; and one measurement remains unbought, `codex`'s tool-approval dialog, which needs a working credential, so the dialog rule's fit to that screen is still an inference from three other `codex` dialogs. The evaluation's COST in this project's units is unmeasured and now measurable: the quiescence gate it depends on exists, and `sprag-latency` is the instrument.

R253.decision_summary: R253: H3 slice 3 -- the wire and the daemon, and a slice that could not be written as specified. The design sited the evaluation inside the pane list's existing lock and published an additive `agent` key, and both of those are right and shipped. What the design did not say is who makes anybody look again. Reading the client before writing any code: the poll connection parks on `scene/waitFor` with no timer, and the session revision is advanced by pane OUTPUT and by user actions -- so the evaluation is output-driven. Cross that with slice 2's publication policy and the two halves have different driving requirements. A verdict resting on PRESENT evidence is driven by the very output that produced the evidence, so `Blocked` reaches a person on sight. A verdict resting on an ABSENCE needs an observation one window later, and the last thing to move the revision was the output that STOPPED. `Idle` -- the state the design calls the one this front exists for -- could not confirm itself, and it would have failed data-dependently: several busy agent panes supply each other's wakes, so it works in exactly the scenario the front is pitched for and freezes in the quiet one. Worse, D8 makes `Unknown` the absent key, so the symptom would have been "an agent is waiting for you" indistinguishable on the wire from "this is not an agent" -- the one distinction D3 declares mandatory. The project's existing deadline precedent does not cover it and reading why named the mechanism: `Routed::again` needs no timer because the deadline is only ever compared against the next keystroke's arrival, and the settle window is the first deadline here whose EXPIRY is itself the event. So slice 3 grew a settle waker, and the waker was written wrong twice in the same shape as the thing it was fixing. First it computed the nearest deadline and slept, which publishes nothing because at start-up nothing is pending and a candidate created afterwards has no way to reach a sleeping thread -- unit-green, inert in the binary, found only by driving the shipped daemon over its socket. Then, once the appearance of a candidate became a condvar event, a probe showed a first-ever one-shot read still answering nothing: a candidate is created by an OBSERVATION and the pane list was the only observer, so a first read WAS the pane's first observation. The waker now also DISCOVERS panes, at one screen read per pane for the life of the daemon, and the one-shot contract is stated as a latency rather than an absolute. The memory itself moved crates for reasons read out of the code: the design's diagram put it on `sprag_terminal::Pane`, but the producer crate deliberately depends on the emulator and the PTY alone and the pure-read precedent the design cites is consumed host-side, and a `WorkspaceExternal` is rebuilt per request so a map held there would leave the hysteresis silently inert while every individual verdict still looked right.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: a new module, and the answer to a question the design got wrong. `AgentRegistry` holds one `Tracker` per pane plus the one manifest list they share, and `AgentClock` pairs that registry's mutex with the condvar that says a deadline now exists. The design's own shape diagram put this memory on `sprag_terminal::Pane`; the producer crate depends on the emulator and the PTY and nothing else on purpose, and `sprag-grid` -- the pure-read crate the design cites as its exact precedent -- is likewise consumed on the host side and never by the producer, so a detector belongs here. Two harder constraints came from the code rather than from taste: a `WorkspaceExternal` is rebuilt for every JSON-RPC request, so a map held as one of its fields would be born empty per poll with the hysteresis silently inert while every individual verdict still looked right; and `Workspace` exposes its panes immutably, so keeping the memory host-side means slice 3 adds no mutable accessor to the producer at all.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the evaluation site, inside the workspace lock the pane list already takes -- the screen is only reachable there. The verdicts leave that critical section as a map keyed by pane id, exactly as the projection tokens already do ten lines above, so `PaneInfo` grows no field and no `sprag_detect` type enters `sprag-terminal`. The additive `agent` key is `{state, name, rule, seq}`, and its ABSENCE is carried by `AgentRegistry::observe` returning nothing for an unclaimed pane rather than by this site remembering to check, so a workspace of shells cannot drift away from the pre-H3 wire shape.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: `spawn_agent_waker`, the thread that exists because the pane list is served only when a client asks and a client asks only when the scene revision moves. It parks on the clock's condvar, wakes for exactly three reasons -- a deadline came due, a candidate appeared, or the sweep interval elapsed -- observes the panes that are due or unknown, bumps only the sessions whose published answer MOVED, and prunes trackers against a daemon-wide census. A `debug_assert` states the invariant its liveness rests on: an observation must resolve a due candidate, or `park_until_due` returns instantly forever.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs + config.rs: `agent-settle-time`, the settle window as a user option, with `config::agent_settle` reading it from the file on every call like every other option reader here. WHERE it is read is the cost decision: `config::window_size` prices its own file read as one per window change, a rare-event justification, and the pane list is served on every client wake -- so the read happens only for a pane that will actually consult the window, and a workspace of settled panes reads the file zero times. Zero is a decision rather than an absence (hysteresis off), the third option to draw `history-limit`'s distinction, and `the_agent_settle_default_is_the_detectors_own` holds the default to `sprag_detect::DEFAULT_SETTLE`.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker::pending_deadline` (derived from `since + settle` rather than stored, so a policy that changes while a candidate waits moves the deadline it is already waiting on) and `set_policy`. Also the correction of a durable comment that said slice 3 would put this type on a pane.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `built_ins`, named as a list rather than spelled at each use because a manifest owns compiled regexes -- a caller that wrote `vec![claude(), codex()]` per evaluation would recompile every pattern on a path served once per client wake.

crates/sprag-host/src/lib.rs: `DaemonShared`, the three things a daemon shares into a scene assembly and an in-process host does not. Grouped rather than passed positionally because they share the property that is easy to get wrong separately -- each is `None` off a daemon, and a surface wired with some and not others answers plausibly while behaving differently from the daemon it stands in for.
verification_bullets: THE SLICE COULD NOT BE WRITTEN AS SPECIFIED, AND READING THE CODE BEFORE WRITING ANY IS WHAT FOUND IT. The design sited the evaluation inside the pane list's existing lock, which is correct and is not sufficient. The client poll thread parks on `scene/waitFor` with no timer at all -- `sprag-client/src/wire.rs` says the long poll is emphatically not given one and the GUI's module doc says event-driven, no polling -- while the session revision is advanced by pane OUTPUT and by user actions. So the evaluation is output-driven. Cross that with the publication policy and the two halves have different driving requirements: a verdict resting on PRESENT evidence is driven by the very output that produced the evidence, and a verdict resting on an ABSENCE needs an observation one window LATER, when the last thing to move the revision was the output that STOPPED. `Idle` -- the state the design calls the one the front exists for -- could not confirm itself, and the failure was data-dependent rather than deterministic: six busy agent panes supply each other's wakes, so it would have worked in exactly the scenario the front is pitched for and frozen in the quiet one.

THE PROJECT'S EXISTING DEADLINE PRECEDENT DOES NOT COVER THIS, AND READING WHY IS WHAT NAMED THE MECHANISM. `Routed::again` hands a repeat deadline back to its caller and needs no timer anywhere, because -- as the keymap says in as many words -- the deadline is simply compared against the next keystroke's arrival. A repeat window only ever matters when an event arrives. The settle window is the first deadline in this project whose EXPIRY is itself the event, so it is the first that cannot be carried passively. That is the whole argument for the waker existing, and it is an argument about this codebase rather than about detectors in general.

THE FIX HAD D9'S OWN DEFECT ONE LEVEL UP, AND ONLY DRIVING THE BINARY FOUND IT. The first waker computed the nearest deadline and slept until it. At start-up nothing is pending, so the nearest deadline is `None`, so it slept for its whole interval -- and the pane-list query that then created a two-second candidate had no way to tell it. Every unit test passed; the shipped daemon published nothing. A live drive over the real socket showed the pane list answering `idle` when polled and a parked `waitFor` timing out at eight seconds, which separates "the detector works" from "the daemon confirms". The mechanism written to serve a deadline nothing else would serve was itself waiting for an event nothing produced. The fix is not a shorter sleep -- waking a few times a second to ask whether anything is pending yet would take every workspace lock several times a second on an idle daemon -- so the appearance of a candidate became an event, and the condvar lives in one type with the memory's mutex so no caller can create a candidate and forget to signal.

A CLAIM WAS WRITTEN INTO THE DESIGN BEFORE IT WAS TRUE, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT CAUGHT IT COST ONE PROBE. The decision said a one-shot reader gets a settled answer. Measured on a daemon nobody had queried, a first-ever read of an agent pane answered nothing -- and so did an immediate second read. A candidate is created by an OBSERVATION, and the pane-list query was the only observer, so a first-ever read WAS that pane's first observation and a resting verdict has to hold. The claim was false for exactly the caller slice 5 is for: an MCP or CLI peer with no frontend attached. The correct target rather than the cheap one: the waker now also DISCOVERS panes, observing a pane while it is UNKNOWN, which costs one screen read per pane for the life of the daemon because a pane is unknown once. The walk that recurs is one `spawn_durability_saver` already performs at the same interval and then does strictly more work than, so the marginal cost on an idle daemon is a second cheap lock acquisition every five seconds. The contract is now stated as a latency: a pane's state is known within one sweep plus one settle window of its birth, with nobody asking.

NINE REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL NINE RED, WITH THE MUTATED TEXT PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN AND THE FAILING TEST NAMES CAPTURED. The candidate-appeared signal removed; park ignoring the deadline; the window never re-read for a pane already pending; the agent key emitted for every pane; a dead pane's tracker never forgotten; the sweep never discovering an unknown pane; the waker never observing; the waker BUMPING without observing; and the pending deadline stored rather than derived. Restoration was verified by byte comparison against a copy taken before the first proof, never `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice. The harness refused one proof for not landing -- correctly, and for the wrong reason: its "did the edit land" test counted occurrences of the replacement text, which a nearby `debug_assert` reading the same expression made two. Counting the replacement is the wrong test; the right one is that the anchor is GONE and the replacement is present.

THE PROOF MATRIX CAUGHT A TEST WHOSE DOCSTRING CLAIMED MORE THAN ITS ASSERTIONS DID, WHICH IS THE SECOND ROUND RUNNING THAT THIS HAS PAID. `an_idle_agent_pane_settles_with_no_client_activity_and_no_output` PASSED under a waker that bumped the session without observing: the wake arrives, the woken client re-queries, and that query publishes. So the test pinned "the daemon wakes a reader on its own clock" and not "the daemon confirms the verdict itself". Two things followed. The docstring now says which test pins which half. And the revision-stability check added to catch the same mutation ALSO passed at first, because it ran after a pane-list read -- and a pane-list read publishes the verdict, curing the pane of being due. Reordered to measure the revision before any pane list is read, the mutation went red and reported something sharper than expected: the revision had climbed from 264 to 6,178,283 in twelve seconds, because a due candidate that nothing resolves makes `park_until_due` return instantly forever. That spin is now stated as the invariant the loop rests on, in a `debug_assert`.

A `pgrep -f` PATTERN MATCHED THE SHELL RUNNING IT AND KILLED THE PROBE MID-RUN. The project already records that `pkill -f` is unsafe here and that `pkill -x` is the form to use. This is a second face of it: the pattern was text from the probe's own command line, so `pgrep -f` returned the bash process executing the very command that was searching. Probes now own a pid file and a private socket and never match on text. The rule generalises past process names -- a search whose pattern appears in the searcher's own state can find itself.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates, after it caught a public doc comment linking to a private item (a LIB gate doing its job, unlike the structural false positive it is on a bin); the workspace suite 1500 to 1519 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus nineteen is exactly this slice's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved. The wire_client PTY suite is REACHABLE for the first time in this front -- `sprag-detect` now has a dependent -- and its three new tests drive the shipped `sprag-term` binary end to end.
carry_forward_bullets: A MECHANISM'S TRIGGER IS PART OF THE MECHANISM, AND THIS ROUND GOT IT WRONG TWICE IN THE SAME SHAPE. First in the design: the evaluation had a site and no driver, so a verdict resting on an absence could never be confirmed. Then in the fix: the waker had a deadline and no way to hear about a deadline created after it went to sleep. Both read as complete while being written, because in both cases the thing that was missing is invisible in the code that is present -- there is no line where a driver ought to be. The question that finds it is cheap and should be asked of every new deadline, window, or pending state: WHAT EVENT MAKES SOMEBODY LOOK AGAIN, and does that event still happen when the thing being waited for is the absence of activity? A deadline whose expiry is itself the event needs a mechanism; a deadline that only matters when the next event arrives does not, which is why `Routed::again` needed nothing and this needed a thread.

A UNIT-GREEN SUBSYSTEM CAN BE INERT IN THE BINARY, AND ONLY THE BINARY SAYS SO. The waker's every component was tested and correct: the deadline accessor, the due test, the seq comparison, the prune. The composition published nothing. What exposed it was driving the shipped daemon over its real socket and reading two different observations -- the pane list answering correctly when polled, and a parked `waitFor` timing out -- because the first is satisfied by the client's own query and only the second is about the daemon. The general rule for this project's front: when a subsystem's whole purpose is to act WITHOUT being asked, no test that asks can confirm it. Find the observable that only the unasked path can produce (here a revision bump on a workspace with no output) and assert on that.

WRITING A CLAIM INTO A DESIGN IS WRITING IT DOWN, AND THE RULE APPLIES TO ONE'S OWN DECISIONS. "A one-shot reader gets a settled answer" was recorded as a consequence of the new mechanism, in the same document that argues for measuring before asserting, and it was false when written -- the mechanism confirmed candidates and did not discover panes. One probe (a daemon left alone for five seconds, then asked once) settled it. The correction was not to soften the sentence but to make it true, and then to state it as a LATENCY rather than an absolute, because that is what it actually is: known within one sweep plus one window of a pane's birth. A claim that cannot be stated without a bound was not ready to be stated.

STILL NOT BUILT, each re-read against the code as it stands. SLICE 4 is manifests in `config.toml`, layered over the built-ins on H2's keymap precedent -- `AgentRegistry::new` already takes the list rather than calling `built_ins` itself, so the layering has a seam and no type in this slice learns about files. SLICE 5 is the surfaces: MCP `agent_state` / `agent_explain`, a CLI verb, and the state in both frontends' pane lists. `explain` is NOT owed by slice 3 and is not a verb here: D7 puts the rule's identity in every verdict and the wire already carries it, so what remains is a surface, and saying so in one place stops the item reading as the other slice's job from both sides.
