R253.publishable_decision_summary: R253: H3 slice 3 -- the wire and the daemon, and a slice that could not be written as specified. The design sited the evaluation inside the pane list's existing lock and published an additive `agent` key, and both of those are right and shipped. What the design did not say is who makes anybody look again. Reading the client before writing any code: the poll connection parks on `scene/waitFor` with no timer, and the session revision is advanced by pane OUTPUT and by user actions -- so the evaluation is output-driven. Cross that with slice 2's publication policy and the two halves have different driving requirements. A verdict resting on PRESENT evidence is driven by the very output that produced the evidence, so `Blocked` reaches a person on sight. A verdict resting on an ABSENCE needs an observation one window later, and the last thing to move the revision was the output that STOPPED. `Idle` -- the state the design calls the one this front exists for -- could not confirm itself, and it would have failed data-dependently: several busy agent panes supply each other's wakes, so it works in exactly the scenario the front is pitched for and freezes in the quiet one. Worse, D8 makes `Unknown` the absent key, so the symptom would have been "an agent is waiting for you" indistinguishable on the wire from "this is not an agent" -- the one distinction D3 declares mandatory. The project's existing deadline precedent does not cover it and reading why named the mechanism: `Routed::again` needs no timer because the deadline is only ever compared against the next keystroke's arrival, and the settle window is the first deadline here whose EXPIRY is itself the event. So slice 3 grew a settle waker, and the waker was written wrong twice in the same shape as the thing it was fixing. First it computed the nearest deadline and slept, which publishes nothing because at start-up nothing is pending and a candidate created afterwards has no way to reach a sleeping thread -- unit-green, inert in the binary, found only by driving the shipped daemon over its socket. Then, once the appearance of a candidate became a condvar event, a probe showed a first-ever one-shot read still answering nothing: a candidate is created by an OBSERVATION and the pane list was the only observer, so a first read WAS the pane's first observation. The waker now also DISCOVERS panes, at one screen read per pane for the life of the daemon, and the one-shot contract is stated as a latency rather than an absolute. The memory itself moved crates for reasons read out of the code: the design's diagram put it on `sprag_terminal::Pane`, but the producer crate deliberately depends on the emulator and the PTY alone and the pure-read precedent the design cites is consumed host-side, and a `WorkspaceExternal` is rebuilt per request so a map held there would leave the hysteresis silently inert while every individual verdict still looked right.
publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: a new module, and the answer to a question the design got wrong. `AgentRegistry` holds one `Tracker` per pane plus the one manifest list they share, and `AgentClock` pairs that registry's mutex with the condvar that says a deadline now exists. The design's own shape diagram put this memory on `sprag_terminal::Pane`; the producer crate depends on the emulator and the PTY and nothing else on purpose, and `sprag-grid` -- the pure-read crate the design cites as its exact precedent -- is likewise consumed on the host side and never by the producer, so a detector belongs here. Two harder constraints came from the code rather than from taste: a `WorkspaceExternal` is rebuilt for every JSON-RPC request, so a map held as one of its fields would be born empty per poll with the hysteresis silently inert while every individual verdict still looked right; and `Workspace` exposes its panes immutably, so keeping the memory host-side means slice 3 adds no mutable accessor to the producer at all.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the evaluation site, inside the workspace lock the pane list already takes -- the screen is only reachable there. The verdicts leave that critical section as a map keyed by pane id, exactly as the projection tokens already do ten lines above, so `PaneInfo` grows no field and no `sprag_detect` type enters `sprag-terminal`. The additive `agent` key is `{state, name, rule, seq}`, and its ABSENCE is carried by `AgentRegistry::observe` returning nothing for an unclaimed pane rather than by this site remembering to check, so a workspace of shells cannot drift away from the pre-H3 wire shape.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: `spawn_agent_waker`, the thread that exists because the pane list is served only when a client asks and a client asks only when the scene revision moves. It parks on the clock's condvar, wakes for exactly three reasons -- a deadline came due, a candidate appeared, or the sweep interval elapsed -- observes the panes that are due or unknown, bumps only the sessions whose published answer MOVED, and prunes trackers against a daemon-wide census. A `debug_assert` states the invariant its liveness rests on: an observation must resolve a due candidate, or `park_until_due` returns instantly forever.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs + config.rs: `agent-settle-time`, the settle window as a user option, with `config::agent_settle` reading it from the file on every call like every other option reader here. WHERE it is read is the cost decision: `config::window_size` prices its own file read as one per window change, a rare-event justification, and the pane list is served on every client wake -- so the read happens only for a pane that will actually consult the window, and a workspace of settled panes reads the file zero times. Zero is a decision rather than an absence (hysteresis off), the third option to draw `history-limit`'s distinction, and `the_agent_settle_default_is_the_detectors_own` holds the default to `sprag_detect::DEFAULT_SETTLE`.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker::pending_deadline` (derived from `since + settle` rather than stored, so a policy that changes while a candidate waits moves the deadline it is already waiting on) and `set_policy`. Also the correction of a durable comment that said slice 3 would put this type on a pane.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `built_ins`, named as a list rather than spelled at each use because a manifest owns compiled regexes -- a caller that wrote `vec![claude(), codex()]` per evaluation would recompile every pattern on a path served once per client wake.

crates/sprag-host/src/lib.rs: `DaemonShared`, the three things a daemon shares into a scene assembly and an in-process host does not. Grouped rather than passed positionally because they share the property that is easy to get wrong separately -- each is `None` off a daemon, and a surface wired with some and not others answers plausibly while behaving differently from the daemon it stands in for.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE SLICE COULD NOT BE WRITTEN AS SPECIFIED, AND READING THE CODE BEFORE WRITING ANY IS WHAT FOUND IT. The design sited the evaluation inside the pane list's existing lock, which is correct and is not sufficient. The client poll thread parks on `scene/waitFor` with no timer at all -- `sprag-client/src/wire.rs` says the long poll is emphatically not given one and the GUI's module doc says event-driven, no polling -- while the session revision is advanced by pane OUTPUT and by user actions. So the evaluation is output-driven. Cross that with the publication policy and the two halves have different driving requirements: a verdict resting on PRESENT evidence is driven by the very output that produced the evidence, and a verdict resting on an ABSENCE needs an observation one window LATER, when the last thing to move the revision was the output that STOPPED. `Idle` -- the state the design calls the one the front exists for -- could not confirm itself, and the failure was data-dependent rather than deterministic: six busy agent panes supply each other's wakes, so it would have worked in exactly the scenario the front is pitched for and frozen in the quiet one.

THE PROJECT'S EXISTING DEADLINE PRECEDENT DOES NOT COVER THIS, AND READING WHY IS WHAT NAMED THE MECHANISM. `Routed::again` hands a repeat deadline back to its caller and needs no timer anywhere, because -- as the keymap says in as many words -- the deadline is simply compared against the next keystroke's arrival. A repeat window only ever matters when an event arrives. The settle window is the first deadline in this project whose EXPIRY is itself the event, so it is the first that cannot be carried passively. That is the whole argument for the waker existing, and it is an argument about this codebase rather than about detectors in general.

THE FIX HAD D9'S OWN DEFECT ONE LEVEL UP, AND ONLY DRIVING THE BINARY FOUND IT. The first waker computed the nearest deadline and slept until it. At start-up nothing is pending, so the nearest deadline is `None`, so it slept for its whole interval -- and the pane-list query that then created a two-second candidate had no way to tell it. Every unit test passed; the shipped daemon published nothing. A live drive over the real socket showed the pane list answering `idle` when polled and a parked `waitFor` timing out at eight seconds, which separates "the detector works" from "the daemon confirms". The mechanism written to serve a deadline nothing else would serve was itself waiting for an event nothing produced. The fix is not a shorter sleep -- waking a few times a second to ask whether anything is pending yet would take every workspace lock several times a second on an idle daemon -- so the appearance of a candidate became an event, and the condvar lives in one type with the memory's mutex so no caller can create a candidate and forget to signal.

A CLAIM WAS WRITTEN INTO THE DESIGN BEFORE IT WAS TRUE, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT CAUGHT IT COST ONE PROBE. The decision said a one-shot reader gets a settled answer. Measured on a daemon nobody had queried, a first-ever read of an agent pane answered nothing -- and so did an immediate second read. A candidate is created by an OBSERVATION, and the pane-list query was the only observer, so a first-ever read WAS that pane's first observation and a resting verdict has to hold. The claim was false for exactly the caller slice 5 is for: an MCP or CLI peer with no frontend attached. The correct target rather than the cheap one: the waker now also DISCOVERS panes, observing a pane while it is UNKNOWN, which costs one screen read per pane for the life of the daemon because a pane is unknown once. The walk that recurs is one `spawn_durability_saver` already performs at the same interval and then does strictly more work than, so the marginal cost on an idle daemon is a second cheap lock acquisition every five seconds. The contract is now stated as a latency: a pane's state is known within one sweep plus one settle window of its birth, with nobody asking.

NINE REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL NINE RED, WITH THE MUTATED TEXT PRINTED BEFORE EACH RUN AND THE FAILING TEST NAMES CAPTURED. The candidate-appeared signal removed; park ignoring the deadline; the window never re-read for a pane already pending; the agent key emitted for every pane; a dead pane's tracker never forgotten; the sweep never discovering an unknown pane; the waker never observing; the waker BUMPING without observing; and the pending deadline stored rather than derived. Restoration was verified by byte comparison against a copy taken before the first proof, never `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice. The harness refused one proof for not landing -- correctly, and for the wrong reason: its "did the edit land" test counted occurrences of the replacement text, which a nearby `debug_assert` reading the same expression made two. Counting the replacement is the wrong test; the right one is that the anchor is GONE and the replacement is present.

THE PROOF MATRIX CAUGHT A TEST WHOSE DOCSTRING CLAIMED MORE THAN ITS ASSERTIONS DID, WHICH IS THE SECOND ROUND RUNNING THAT THIS HAS PAID. `an_idle_agent_pane_settles_with_no_client_activity_and_no_output` PASSED under a waker that bumped the session without observing: the wake arrives, the woken client re-queries, and that query publishes. So the test pinned "the daemon wakes a reader on its own clock" and not "the daemon confirms the verdict itself". Two things followed. The docstring now says which test pins which half. And the revision-stability check added to catch the same mutation ALSO passed at first, because it ran after a pane-list read -- and a pane-list read publishes the verdict, curing the pane of being due. Reordered to measure the revision before any pane list is read, the mutation went red and reported something sharper than expected: the revision had climbed from 264 to 6,178,283 in twelve seconds, because a due candidate that nothing resolves makes `park_until_due` return instantly forever. That spin is now stated as the invariant the loop rests on, in a `debug_assert`.

A `pgrep -f` PATTERN MATCHED THE SHELL RUNNING IT AND KILLED THE PROBE MID-RUN. The project already records that `pkill -f` is unsafe here and that `pkill -x` is the form to use. This is a second face of it: the pattern was text from the probe's own command line, so `pgrep -f` returned the bash process executing the very command that was searching. Probes now own a pid file and a private socket and never match on text. The rule generalises past process names -- a search whose pattern appears in the searcher's own state can find itself.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates, after it caught a public doc comment linking to a private item (a LIB gate doing its job, unlike the structural false positive it is on a bin); the workspace suite 1500 to 1519 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus nineteen is exactly this slice's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved. The wire_client PTY suite is REACHABLE for the first time in this front -- `sprag-detect` now has a dependent -- and its three new tests drive the shipped `sprag-term` binary end to end.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: A MECHANISM'S TRIGGER IS PART OF THE MECHANISM, AND THIS ROUND GOT IT WRONG TWICE IN THE SAME SHAPE. First in the design: the evaluation had a site and no driver, so a verdict resting on an absence could never be confirmed. Then in the fix: the waker had a deadline and no way to hear about a deadline created after it went to sleep. Both read as complete while being written, because in both cases the thing that was missing is invisible in the code that is present -- there is no line where a driver ought to be. The question that finds it is cheap and should be asked of every new deadline, window, or pending state: WHAT EVENT MAKES SOMEBODY LOOK AGAIN, and does that event still happen when the thing being waited for is the absence of activity? A deadline whose expiry is itself the event needs a mechanism; a deadline that only matters when the next event arrives does not, which is why `Routed::again` needed nothing and this needed a thread.

A UNIT-GREEN SUBSYSTEM CAN BE INERT IN THE BINARY, AND ONLY THE BINARY SAYS SO. The waker's every component was tested and correct: the deadline accessor, the due test, the seq comparison, the prune. The composition published nothing. What exposed it was driving the shipped daemon over its real socket and reading two different observations -- the pane list answering correctly when polled, and a parked `waitFor` timing out -- because the first is satisfied by the client's own query and only the second is about the daemon. The general rule for this project's front: when a subsystem's whole purpose is to act WITHOUT being asked, no test that asks can confirm it. Find the observable that only the unasked path can produce (here a revision bump on a workspace with no output) and assert on that.

WRITING A CLAIM INTO A DESIGN IS WRITING IT DOWN, AND THE RULE APPLIES TO ONE'S OWN DECISIONS. "A one-shot reader gets a settled answer" was recorded as a consequence of the new mechanism, in the same document that argues for measuring before asserting, and it was false when written -- the mechanism confirmed candidates and did not discover panes. One probe (a daemon left alone for five seconds, then asked once) settled it. The correction was not to soften the sentence but to make it true, and then to state it as a LATENCY rather than an absolute, because that is what it actually is: known within one sweep plus one window of a pane's birth. A claim that cannot be stated without a bound was not ready to be stated.

R254.decision_summary: R254: H3 slice 4 -- manifests in `config.toml`, layered, and the input the quiescence gate was not watching. The slice has three deliverables and each one turned out to be a claim that had to be read from the code rather than taken from the design's sentence. FIRST, the format: the readable TOML shape is a match table keyed by its region, and the built-ins refute it, because `codex`'s single fingerprint is a composer line in the bottom three rows AND a footer shape in the bottom one -- two matches on the SAME region with different windows, which a region-keyed table has nowhere to put. So a conjunction is an array, and the gate that keeps the vocabulary honest is that the format must be able to say what the built-ins say. SECOND, "runtime reload on the same terms as the keymap" is a claim about the keymap, and the keymap does two different things: `config::keymap` reads the file on every call, while the runtime RELOAD is `ClientConfig`, a holder that keeps the file's text and re-reads from a wake it already has. Only the second is a reload, and only the second is affordable here -- every other setting in that file costs a READ, and a manifest list costs a parse and a regex compile, on a path served on every client wake. So the daemon's equivalent of the keystroke is the agent waker's sweep, and the contract is a latency: an edit takes effect within one sweep. THIRD, and this is the finding: a reload is a THIRD INPUT to a gate that was watching two. D4 earns the quiescence skip by arguing the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title, so a pane where neither has moved cannot reach a different verdict -- which holds for exactly as long as the RULES do not move, and this slice is what makes them move. Unwatched, a manifest edit would never reach a settled pane, and the pane a user edits a manifest to correct is a quiet one, because a quiet pane is where a wrong verdict is visible and stuck. The edit would appear to do nothing while every individual verdict still looked right. The correction restores the exactness rather than qualifying it -- the list carries an identity and that identity is a term of the key -- and it cost R252's own instrument: the skip was proved by rewriting a rule underneath the tracker and asserting the verdict did not move, which is precisely this defect used as a measuring device, so with the rules in the key there is nothing left for a behavioural test to see. Making the daemon re-read the file was then still not enough to make an edit ARRIVE: the waker asks about a pane for two reasons, due or unknown, and the pane in question is neither, so `stale` is a third. That is the third time in one front that a mechanism has been written with work to do and no event to be woken by, which is why the reload's own tempting signal was deleted rather than shipped -- the only reloader is the waker, and a thread cannot notify itself.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Ruleset`, the manifest list carried together with the identity of that list. The type exists because the quiescence gate's exactness has a premise -- the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title -- and this slice is what falsifies it, since a user edits `config.toml` and the list is replaced underneath a workspace of settled panes. The identity sits BESIDE the list rather than in a parameter a caller can forget to pass, which is `AgentClock`'s argument one crate up, where the condvar lives in one type with the mutex so no caller can create a candidate and neglect to signal. The revision is drawn from a process-wide counter and compared for EQUALITY only: a per-ruleset counter would make two independently built lists interchangeable to the gate, which is the bug this field exists to prevent wearing the costume of the fix.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the rules are the quiescence key's fourth term, beside the row generations, the width and the title. `Tracker::observe` takes a `&Ruleset` where it took a manifest slice, so the arity does not change and the identity cannot be left behind; `Tracker::evaluated_under` reports which rules produced the published verdict, which is what the daemon's third reason to look at a pane is derived from.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: the `[[agent]]` file format and its layering, beside `DeclaredBind` and for the same reason -- `sprag-detect` is the pure crate and owns no serde. A conjunction is an ARRAY of matches (`all`), a match is one region spec plus exactly one of starts_with / contains / regex, and a region is `title` or `bottom:N` parsed at the edge in `KeySpec::parse`'s shape. The layering's grain is a RULE keyed on `Rule::id`: an entry naming a built-in replaces matching ids IN PLACE, appends new ones, appends fingerprints, and `disable = [ids]` removes one. An entry naming an unknown agent is a new manifest at the FRONT of the list. Refusals at the edge rather than silence later: an empty conjunction (it holds for every pane), a pattern that does not compile, a rule id both declared and disabled, a `disable` naming a rule that is not there, a new agent with no fingerprint, and a state the wire cannot carry -- the last read out of `AgentState::wire_str` rather than spelled again, so `unknown` falls out as unwritable without a second rule saying so.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `AgentManifests`, the DAEMON's holder for the file. Every other reader in this module reads per call on purpose, and a manifest list cannot be bought on those terms: `built_ins` says why in its own docs, since a manifest owns compiled regexes and the pane list is served on every client wake. So this holds the file's TEXT and re-reads from a wake that already exists, keeps the last good list across a broken edit, records the reason for a surface that can show it, and takes a path so a test can drive it without mutating the process-global environment its siblings read. `read_text` is now shared with `ClientConfig` so "a missing file is not an error" is one decision rather than two that can drift.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry` holds a `Ruleset`; `reload` swaps it while KEEPING every pane's memory, and `stale` reports a pane whose published verdict was reached under a list that has since been replaced. The memory survives for two different reasons, both asserted: `seq` must not restart or a manifest edit reads on the wire as a state change on every pane at once, and the remembered identity survives because R252 made it a manifest NAME rather than a position in the list, in as many words because slice 4 reloads that list from a file.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: the waker re-reads the file in its sweep and hands the new list over, and its `ask` predicate gains a third reason. `AgentClock` documents why a reload does NOT signal, which is the shape that was written first and deleted: the only reloader is the waker itself, and a thread cannot notify itself.

crates/sprag-host/Cargo.toml: `regex`, because a user's pattern is compiled where it is READ. It is `sprag-detect`'s own crate rather than a second engine in the tree, since `Test::Regex` already holds a compiled `Regex` in the public type.
verification_bullets: THE BUILT-INS DECIDED THE FILE FORMAT, AND THEY REFUTED THE READABLE ONE. The obvious TOML shape for a match set is a table keyed by its region -- `{ title = ..., bottom = ... }` -- and `codex` cannot be written in it: its single fingerprint is a composer line in `bottom:3` AND a footer shape in `bottom:1`, two matches on the SAME region with different windows, which a region-keyed table has nowhere to put. Reading the built-ins before choosing the format is what caught it, and the gate that keeps it caught is that the format must be able to say what the built-ins say. That is asserted BEHAVIOURALLY -- a declared agent and a built-in are run against one painted screen and must reach the same verdict -- because a field-by-field comparison would prove they have the same shape rather than the same meaning, and meaning is what a user redeclaring an agent needs.

"RUNTIME RELOAD ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE KEYMAP" IS A CLAIM ABOUT CODE, AND THE CODE SAYS SOMETHING OTHER THAN WHAT THE PHRASE SUGGESTS. `config::keymap` does read the file on every call, but the runtime RELOAD is `ClientConfig`: a holder that keeps the file's text and re-reads from a wake it already has -- the keystroke whose meaning the table decides -- adding, in its own words, no thread, no timer and no wake. Manifests cannot be read per evaluation at all, and for a sharper reason than the settle window's: every other setting in that file costs a READ, and this one costs a parse and a compile, on a path served on every client wake. So the daemon's equivalent of the keystroke is the agent waker's sweep, and the consequence is stated as a LATENCY rather than left to be discovered -- an edit takes effect within one sweep, the shape slice 3's discovery contract already has.

THE FINDING: A RELOAD IS A THIRD INPUT TO A GATE THAT WAS WATCHING TWO. D4 earns the quiescence skip by arguing the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title, so a pane where neither moved cannot reach a different verdict. That is true for exactly as long as the RULES do not move, and this slice makes them move. Left unwatched, a manifest edit would never reach a settled pane -- and the pane a user edits a manifest to correct is a QUIET one, because a quiet pane is where a wrong verdict is visible and stuck. The symptom would have been an edit that appears to do nothing while every individual verdict still looks right, which is R253's own signature failure. The fix restores the exactness rather than qualifying it: the list carries an identity and the identity is a term of the key.

THE FIX NEEDED A SECOND MECHANISM, WHICH IS THE SAME FINDING ONE LEVEL OUT. Making the daemon re-read the file does not make an edit ARRIVE. The waker asks about a pane for two reasons, due or unknown, and the pane in question is neither: it is settled, known, and quiet. So `AgentRegistry::stale` is a third reason. This is the third time in one front that a mechanism has been written with work to do and no event to be woken by, and it is why `AgentClock` now records why a reload does not signal: the only reloader is the waker itself, and a thread cannot notify itself.

THE SLICE'S OWN GATE, IN THE DESIGN'S WORDS -- a user manifest correcting a built-in rule -- ASSERTS BOTH HALVES OF "CORRECTING". The named rule is replaced, so the file's pattern decides and the built-in's no longer fires; and every other rule of that agent is still there in its original position, which is what "without redeclaring the rest" means and what a wholesale replacement would quietly lose. Asserted through `detect` rather than by reading the rule back, because what the user changed is what the pane SAYS.

AN END-TO-END TEST DRIVES THE SHIPPED DAEMON, BECAUSE SLICE 3 PAID FOR THAT LESSON. Every part of the reload is unit-tested and the COMPOSITION is what fails -- exactly the state slice 3's waker was in when the shipped daemon published nothing at all. So `an_edited_manifest_reaches_a_pane_that_is_not_moving` spawns a real `sprag-term` with its own `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, lets an agent-shaped pane settle under the built-ins, PARKS on `scene/waitFor`, and only then edits the file on disk. The parking is what makes the observation about the daemon: a pane-list read drives an evaluation, so "edit, then read the pane list" would pass with no reload at all, because the reading client would do the work.

THIRTEEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL THIRTEEN RED, with the mutated text printed before each run and the failing test names captured. The rules term dropped from the key; the revision never recorded; a reload rebuilding the per-pane memory; `stale` answering for a pane nobody has observed; a new agent appended instead of offered first; a corrected rule appended instead of replaced in place; an empty conjunction accepted; a rule both declared and disabled resolved instead of refused; the holder treating an unchanged file as an edit; a broken edit dropping the manifests that worked; the waker never re-reading the file; the waker re-reading but never handing the list over; and the sweep never asking about a stale pane. Restoration was by byte comparison against a copy taken before each proof, never `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice.

TWO PROOFS SCORED FOR REASONS THAT WERE NOT ABOUT THE CODE, AND BOTH FAULTS WERE THE MATRIX'S. One was REFUSED for not landing, correctly: its replacement CONTAINED its anchor, so "the anchor is gone" could never hold. R254.publishable_decision_summary: R254: H3 slice 4 -- manifests in `config.toml`, layered, and the input the quiescence gate was not watching. The slice has three deliverables and each one turned out to be a claim that had to be read from the code rather than taken from the design's sentence. FIRST, the format: the readable TOML shape is a match table keyed by its region, and the built-ins refute it, because `codex`'s single fingerprint is a composer line in the bottom three rows AND a footer shape in the bottom one -- two matches on the SAME region with different windows, which a region-keyed table has nowhere to put. So a conjunction is an array, and the gate that keeps the vocabulary honest is that the format must be able to say what the built-ins say. SECOND, "runtime reload on the same terms as the keymap" is a claim about the keymap, and the keymap does two different things: `config::keymap` reads the file on every call, while the runtime RELOAD is `ClientConfig`, a holder that keeps the file's text and re-reads from a wake it already has. Only the second is a reload, and only the second is affordable here -- every other setting in that file costs a READ, and a manifest list costs a parse and a regex compile, on a path served on every client wake. So the daemon's equivalent of the keystroke is the agent waker's sweep, and the contract is a latency: an edit takes effect within one sweep. THIRD, and this is the finding: a reload is a THIRD INPUT to a gate that was watching two. D4 earns the quiescence skip by arguing the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title, so a pane where neither has moved cannot reach a different verdict -- which holds for exactly as long as the RULES do not move, and this slice is what makes them move. Unwatched, a manifest edit would never reach a settled pane, and the pane a user edits a manifest to correct is a quiet one, because a quiet pane is where a wrong verdict is visible and stuck. The edit would appear to do nothing while every individual verdict still looked right. The correction restores the exactness rather than qualifying it -- the list carries an identity and that identity is a term of the key -- and it cost R252's own instrument: the skip was proved by rewriting a rule underneath the tracker and asserting the verdict did not move, which is precisely this defect used as a measuring device, so with the rules in the key there is nothing left for a behavioural test to see. Making the daemon re-read the file was then still not enough to make an edit ARRIVE: the waker asks about a pane for two reasons, due or unknown, and the pane in question is neither, so `stale` is a third. That is the third time in one front that a mechanism has been written with work to do and no event to be woken by, which is why the reload's own tempting signal was deleted rather than shipped -- the only reloader is the waker, and a thread cannot notify itself.
publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `Ruleset`, the manifest list carried together with the identity of that list. The type exists because the quiescence gate's exactness has a premise -- the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title -- and this slice is what falsifies it, since a user edits `config.toml` and the list is replaced underneath a workspace of settled panes. The identity sits BESIDE the list rather than in a parameter a caller can forget to pass, which is `AgentClock`'s argument one crate up, where the condvar lives in one type with the mutex so no caller can create a candidate and neglect to signal. The revision is drawn from a process-wide counter and compared for EQUALITY only: a per-ruleset counter would make two independently built lists interchangeable to the gate, which is the bug this field exists to prevent wearing the costume of the fix.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: the rules are the quiescence key's fourth term, beside the row generations, the width and the title. `Tracker::observe` takes a `&Ruleset` where it took a manifest slice, so the arity does not change and the identity cannot be left behind; `Tracker::evaluated_under` reports which rules produced the published verdict, which is what the daemon's third reason to look at a pane is derived from.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: the `[[agent]]` file format and its layering, beside `DeclaredBind` and for the same reason -- `sprag-detect` is the pure crate and owns no serde. A conjunction is an ARRAY of matches (`all`), a match is one region spec plus exactly one of starts_with / contains / regex, and a region is `title` or `bottom:N` parsed at the edge in `KeySpec::parse`'s shape. The layering's grain is a RULE keyed on `Rule::id`: an entry naming a built-in replaces matching ids IN PLACE, appends new ones, appends fingerprints, and `disable = [ids]` removes one. An entry naming an unknown agent is a new manifest at the FRONT of the list. Refusals at the edge rather than silence later: an empty conjunction (it holds for every pane), a pattern that does not compile, a rule id both declared and disabled, a `disable` naming a rule that is not there, a new agent with no fingerprint, and a state the wire cannot carry -- the last read out of `AgentState::wire_str` rather than spelled again, so `unknown` falls out as unwritable without a second rule saying so.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `AgentManifests`, the DAEMON's holder for the file. Every other reader in this module reads per call on purpose, and a manifest list cannot be bought on those terms: `built_ins` says why in its own docs, since a manifest owns compiled regexes and the pane list is served on every client wake. So this holds the file's TEXT and re-reads from a wake that already exists, keeps the last good list across a broken edit, records the reason for a surface that can show it, and takes a path so a test can drive it without mutating the process-global environment its siblings read. `read_text` is now shared with `ClientConfig` so "a missing file is not an error" is one decision rather than two that can drift.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry` holds a `Ruleset`; `reload` swaps it while KEEPING every pane's memory, and `stale` reports a pane whose published verdict was reached under a list that has since been replaced. The memory survives for two different reasons, both asserted: `seq` must not restart or a manifest edit reads on the wire as a state change on every pane at once, and the remembered identity survives because R252 made it a manifest NAME rather than a position in the list, in as many words because slice 4 reloads that list from a file.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: the waker re-reads the file in its sweep and hands the new list over, and its `ask` predicate gains a third reason. `AgentClock` documents why a reload does NOT signal, which is the shape that was written first and deleted: the only reloader is the waker itself, and a thread cannot notify itself.

crates/sprag-host/Cargo.toml: `regex`, because a user's pattern is compiled where it is READ. It is `sprag-detect`'s own crate rather than a second engine in the tree, since `Test::Regex` already holds a compiled `Regex` in the public type.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE BUILT-INS DECIDED THE FILE FORMAT, AND THEY REFUTED THE READABLE ONE. The obvious TOML shape for a match set is a table keyed by its region -- `{ title = ..., bottom = ... }` -- and `codex` cannot be written in it: its single fingerprint is a composer line in `bottom:3` AND a footer shape in `bottom:1`, two matches on the SAME region with different windows, which a region-keyed table has nowhere to put. Reading the built-ins before choosing the format is what caught it, and the gate that keeps it caught is that the format must be able to say what the built-ins say. That is asserted BEHAVIOURALLY -- a declared agent and a built-in are run against one painted screen and must reach the same verdict -- because a field-by-field comparison would prove they have the same shape rather than the same meaning, and meaning is what a user redeclaring an agent needs.

"RUNTIME RELOAD ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE KEYMAP" IS A CLAIM ABOUT CODE, AND THE CODE SAYS SOMETHING OTHER THAN WHAT THE PHRASE SUGGESTS. `config::keymap` does read the file on every call, but the runtime RELOAD is `ClientConfig`: a holder that keeps the file's text and re-reads from a wake it already has -- the keystroke whose meaning the table decides -- adding, in its own words, no thread, no timer and no wake. Manifests cannot be read per evaluation at all, and for a sharper reason than the settle window's: every other setting in that file costs a READ, and this one costs a parse and a compile, on a path served on every client wake. So the daemon's equivalent of the keystroke is the agent waker's sweep, and the consequence is stated as a LATENCY rather than left to be discovered -- an edit takes effect within one sweep, the shape slice 3's discovery contract already has.

THE FINDING: A RELOAD IS A THIRD INPUT TO A GATE THAT WAS WATCHING TWO. D4 earns the quiescence skip by arguing the rules are a pure function of the screen and the title, so a pane where neither moved cannot reach a different verdict. That is true for exactly as long as the RULES do not move, and this slice makes them move. Left unwatched, a manifest edit would never reach a settled pane -- and the pane a user edits a manifest to correct is a QUIET one, because a quiet pane is where a wrong verdict is visible and stuck. The symptom would have been an edit that appears to do nothing while every individual verdict still looks right, which is R253's own signature failure. The fix restores the exactness rather than qualifying it: the list carries an identity and the identity is a term of the key.

THE FIX NEEDED A SECOND MECHANISM, WHICH IS THE SAME FINDING ONE LEVEL OUT. Making the daemon re-read the file does not make an edit ARRIVE. The waker asks about a pane for two reasons, due or unknown, and the pane in question is neither: it is settled, known, and quiet. So `AgentRegistry::stale` is a third reason. This is the third time in one front that a mechanism has been written with work to do and no event to be woken by, and it is why `AgentClock` now records why a reload does not signal: the only reloader is the waker itself, and a thread cannot notify itself.

THE SLICE'S OWN GATE, IN THE DESIGN'S WORDS -- a user manifest correcting a built-in rule -- ASSERTS BOTH HALVES OF "CORRECTING". The named rule is replaced, so the file's pattern decides and the built-in's no longer fires; and every other rule of that agent is still there in its original position, which is what "without redeclaring the rest" means and what a wholesale replacement would quietly lose. Asserted through `detect` rather than by reading the rule back, because what the user changed is what the pane SAYS.

AN END-TO-END TEST DRIVES THE SHIPPED DAEMON, BECAUSE SLICE 3 PAID FOR THAT LESSON. Every part of the reload is unit-tested and the COMPOSITION is what fails -- exactly the state slice 3's waker was in when the shipped daemon published nothing at all. So `an_edited_manifest_reaches_a_pane_that_is_not_moving` spawns a real `sprag-term` with its own `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, lets an agent-shaped pane settle under the built-ins, PARKS on `scene/waitFor`, and only then edits the file on disk. The parking is what makes the observation about the daemon: a pane-list read drives an evaluation, so "edit, then read the pane list" would pass with no reload at all, because the reading client would do the work.

THIRTEEN REVERT-PROOFS MEASURED, ALL THIRTEEN RED, with the mutated text printed before each run and the failing test names captured. The rules term dropped from the key; the revision never recorded; a reload rebuilding the per-pane memory; `stale` answering for a pane nobody has observed; a new agent appended instead of offered first; a corrected rule appended instead of replaced in place; an empty conjunction accepted; a rule both declared and disabled resolved instead of refused; the holder treating an unchanged file as an edit; a broken edit dropping the manifests that worked; the waker never re-reading the file; the waker re-reading but never handing the list over; and the sweep never asking about a stale pane. Restoration was by byte comparison against a copy taken before each proof, never `git checkout`, which has eaten uncommitted work in this project twice.

R255.decision_summary: R255: the agent evaluation's cost -- and the instrument that had to be rebuilt before the number could mean anything. The debt was recorded twice: once because slice 3 put the evaluation on the pane list, and once because slice 4 put the rule list into the quiescence gate's key and thereby destroyed the only behavioural test the skip had. Paying the first half exactly as it was written turns out to be impossible, and finding that out is the round's methodological result. The comparison the debt names -- the same pane list with and without the evaluation -- was built the honest way, `HostState::with_agents` consuming and returning the very host already measured, so the two rows are the same three panes and the same request text with one difference. Ten runs put the difference at +0.07 to +4.22 us on a request costing 7.4 to 8.7 us. Every run is positive, so the SIGN is settled; the magnitude spans sixty-fold, so the SIZE is not, and an earlier battery of five runs -- differing only in which rows preceded these two -- produced two NEGATIVE differences. Those are precisely the rows R221 already recorded as the noisiest in this instrument, the only ones served while three live PTY panes and their reader threads share the process, which is interference a 64 KiB copy cannot see and therefore cannot cancel. So the question had to be asked one level down, from a row with no PTY in it: one `AgentClock::observe` on a settled pane costs 0.056 to 0.086 us. The second half is the more durable one. A duration cannot restore a lost test -- R221 measured why, and this project has answered the same question twice before in counts (R217's projection meter, R219's allocation counter) -- so the skip's proof comes back as `sprag_detect::work`, two process-wide counters read as a delta by `sprag-detect/tests/meter.rs`. Deleting the quiescence gate outright, which R254 recorded as turning no test red, now turns two red. And making that meter honest forced a change to production code for R217's own stated reason: the cost must not be payable without being counted. `Tracker::evaluate` walked the manifest list itself while `detect` -- the crate's public matcher -- had NO production caller at all, so a counter in the obvious place would have counted nothing the daemon does. The tracker now identifies through `detect`, which is the same argument `Rule::id` already makes one level down: a second matcher is a matcher that can disagree.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `DetectWork` and `work()`, two monotonic process-wide counters read as a delta. `evaluations_total` is one per `detect` call and so one per look the quiescence gate did NOT skip -- the number the gate exists to hold down. `manifests_total` is the VOLUME, and it is deliberately not `evaluations * len`: identification stops at the first manifest that CLAIMS the pane, so it is counted inside the `find` predicate rather than added as a length. That distinction is the price of slice 4's layering rule, which puts a user's new agent at the FRONT of the list, and it is charged to every ordinary shell pane in the workspace -- the population that never claims and therefore always pays for all of it.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `detect` is now the ONE place the rules run, which is what makes the counters a meter rather than an estimate. The doc says so at the function, because the property a reader has to be able to trust is not that the number is incremented but that no path reaches an evaluation without passing here.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker::evaluate` delegates its identification to `detect` instead of walking the manifest list a second time. Two reasons, and neither is the counter: the crate already argues at `Rule::id` that a second arbitration path is a path that can disagree, and the two loops were textually the same `find`. `Manifest::verdict` always names its own manifest on the verdict, so `agent.is_some()` is exactly `the list claimed this pane` and the identity memory reads it from there. The fallback for a pane whose modal covers its fingerprint (R251) is untouched and is part of the same one evaluation, so it adds no second count.

crates/sprag-detect/tests/meter.rs: a new test binary, on `sprag-grid/tests/meter.rs`'s pattern and for the same stated reason -- the counters are process-wide, so a delta taken in the unit module would be measuring whichever of a dozen parallel tests happened to be evaluating at the time. Five tests: a settled pane observed 64 times costs ZERO evaluations; a pane that repaints costs exactly one per look; a reload costs exactly one and then goes quiet again; the tracker's delegation is metered once and not twice; and an unclaimed pane is offered the whole list where a claimed one stops at its position.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: six new rows and three derived blocks. `detect` on a claimed and on an unclaimed screen; `Tracker::observe` with the gate hitting and with it missing; the pane list with and without the detector; and `AgentClock::observe` against registries of 1, 8 and 64 remembered panes. The gate-miss row alternates between two rulesets that say the SAME thing, so every look is a full evaluation and every look reaches the verdict already published -- pricing the skip against a like-for-like alternative rather than against a different answer, which a changed screen would have been.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the two `Tracker` rows and the pane-list row read `sprag_detect::work` across themselves and print the counts. A row claiming to skip must have skipped and a row claiming to evaluate must have evaluated, and without that the pair could be measuring one code path twice and reporting the difference as a saving. It reports 124 evaluations over 125 calls on the gate-miss row, not 125, and the missing one is explicable: the alternation's first call lands on the ruleset the tracker was already settled under.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the module docs carry the ten-run ranges with the machine and the build profile beside them, and the pane-list row prints DO NOT QUOTE THIS ROW with the reason -- it bounds the cost and does not resolve it.
verification_bullets: THE DEBT COULD NOT BE PAID AT THE LEVEL IT WAS WRITTEN AT, AND ONE RUN WOULD HAVE HIDDEN THAT. The first single run of the finished instrument reported the detector at +16.5% of the pane list and 0.481 us per pane, and that number was very nearly written down. Five runs of that same battery gave -8.6%, -7.4%, +1.9%, +3.9% and +12.9% -- two of them NEGATIVE. The battery was then extended and ten runs of the final one gave +0.07 to +4.22 us, all positive, a sixty-fold spread on the size. The sign is a result; the magnitude is not, and the difference between the two batteries is only which rows ran before these two. R221 had already recorded why: the whole-request rows are the only ones served while three live PTY panes and their reader threads share the process, and that is interference the control does not share and so cannot cancel.

SO THE NUMBER CAME FROM A ROW WITH NO PTY IN IT, AND IT IS STATED AS A LOWER BOUND RATHER THAN AS THE ANSWER. One `AgentClock::observe` on a settled pane costs 0.056 to 0.086 us with 1 to 8 panes remembered. That is the DETECTOR's part of a pane's entry and not the whole per-pane cost -- the title clone and the screen lock the pane list also performs are not in the row, and this instrument has not separated them. Saying which part was measured is the difference between a bound and a claim.

THE GATE IS WORTH 3040x TO 3605x WHAT IT SKIPS, and the ratio is the half that repeats: it held to within 8% across ten runs while its two absolutes moved by more than 20%, which is R221's rule about ratios taken inside one run arriving again. A look at a quiet pane costs 0.014 to 0.023 us; the evaluation it declines to run costs 42.6 to 52.0 us. The shape is the finding: ONE EVALUATION IS 11.1x TO 12.8x THE WHOLE PANE-LIST REQUEST THAT WOULD CARRY IT, where R221 found the projection at half a percent of the fetch it is named for. The gate is not an optimisation on this path; it is what keeps the pane list the cost of a pane list. An unclaimed screen costs 1.93x to 2.05x a claimed one, which is the whole list against one manifest.

THE SKIP HAS A RED TEST AGAIN, WHICH IS WHAT R254 SAID IT HAD LOST. Five revert-proofs, all five RED, with the mutated text printed before each run and the failing test names captured, restoration by byte comparison against a copy taken before each proof and never `git checkout`. The evaluation counter never incrementing (3 red); manifests counted as the list LENGTH instead of as those consulted (1 red); the tracker walking the list itself instead of delegating (3 red); THE QUIESCENCE GATE ITSELF never firing (2 red); and the RULES term dropped from the gate's key (2 red, one of them R254's own behavioural test). Deleting the gate is the one that matters: R254 recorded in as many words that it turned no test red, and it now turns two.

THE MATRIX'S OWN FILTER WAS WRONG AGAIN, AND THIS TIME IT UNDER-REPORTED RATHER THAN FALSE-GREENED. `cargo test -p sprag-detect` stops after the FIRST failing test binary, so a mutation that kills a lib unit test never reaches `tests/meter.rs` at all. M5 was scored as one failing test; run with `--no-fail-fast` it is two, and the second is the one this round wrote. It was caught by disbelieving a prediction that did not come true rather than by any gate -- the mutation was expected to kill the new reload test and appeared not to. THE FILTER IS PART OF THE PROOF, one round after the same lesson cost a false green.

A SCALING TERM NOBODY HAD PRICED, MEASURED WITH A CONTROL RATHER THAN REASONED ABOUT. A single look grows LINEARLY with the number of panes the registry remembers, at 2.70 to 3.35 ns each. `AgentClock::observe` reads the nearest deadline before and after every look and each read walks every tracker, so a pane list over N panes performs 2N^2 tracker visits. R255.publishable_decision_summary: R255: the agent evaluation's cost -- and the instrument that had to be rebuilt before the number could mean anything. The debt was recorded twice: once because slice 3 put the evaluation on the pane list, and once because slice 4 put the rule list into the quiescence gate's key and thereby destroyed the only behavioural test the skip had. Paying the first half exactly as it was written turns out to be impossible, and finding that out is the round's methodological result. The comparison the debt names -- the same pane list with and without the evaluation -- was built the honest way, `HostState::with_agents` consuming and returning the very host already measured, so the two rows are the same three panes and the same request text with one difference. Ten runs put the difference at +0.07 to +4.22 us on a request costing 7.4 to 8.7 us. Every run is positive, so the SIGN is settled; the magnitude spans sixty-fold, so the SIZE is not, and an earlier battery of five runs -- differing only in which rows preceded these two -- produced two NEGATIVE differences. Those are precisely the rows R221 already recorded as the noisiest in this instrument, the only ones served while three live PTY panes and their reader threads share the process, which is interference a 64 KiB copy cannot see and therefore cannot cancel. So the question had to be asked one level down, from a row with no PTY in it: one `AgentClock::observe` on a settled pane costs 0.056 to 0.086 us. The second half is the more durable one. A duration cannot restore a lost test -- R221 measured why, and this project has answered the same question twice before in counts (R217's projection meter, R219's allocation counter) -- so the skip's proof comes back as `sprag_detect::work`, two process-wide counters read as a delta by `sprag-detect/tests/meter.rs`. Deleting the quiescence gate outright, which R254 recorded as turning no test red, now turns two red. And making that meter honest forced a change to production code for R217's own stated reason: the cost must not be payable without being counted. `Tracker::evaluate` walked the manifest list itself while `detect` -- the crate's public matcher -- had NO production caller at all, so a counter in the obvious place would have counted nothing the daemon does. The tracker now identifies through `detect`, which is the same argument `Rule::id` already makes one level down: a second matcher is a matcher that can disagree.
publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `DetectWork` and `work()`, two monotonic process-wide counters read as a delta. `evaluations_total` is one per `detect` call and so one per look the quiescence gate did NOT skip -- the number the gate exists to hold down. `manifests_total` is the VOLUME, and it is deliberately not `evaluations * len`: identification stops at the first manifest that CLAIMS the pane, so it is counted inside the `find` predicate rather than added as a length. That distinction is the price of slice 4's layering rule, which puts a user's new agent at the FRONT of the list, and it is charged to every ordinary shell pane in the workspace -- the population that never claims and therefore always pays for all of it.

crates/sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `detect` is now the ONE place the rules run, which is what makes the counters a meter rather than an estimate. The doc says so at the function, because the property a reader has to be able to trust is not that the number is incremented but that no path reaches an evaluation without passing here.

crates/sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker::evaluate` delegates its identification to `detect` instead of walking the manifest list a second time. Two reasons, and neither is the counter: the crate already argues at `Rule::id` that a second arbitration path is a path that can disagree, and the two loops were textually the same `find`. `Manifest::verdict` always names its own manifest on the verdict, so `agent.is_some()` is exactly `the list claimed this pane` and the identity memory reads it from there. The fallback for a pane whose modal covers its fingerprint (R251) is untouched and is part of the same one evaluation, so it adds no second count.

crates/sprag-detect/tests/meter.rs: a new test binary, on `sprag-grid/tests/meter.rs`'s pattern and for the same stated reason -- the counters are process-wide, so a delta taken in the unit module would be measuring whichever of a dozen parallel tests happened to be evaluating at the time. Five tests: a settled pane observed 64 times costs ZERO evaluations; a pane that repaints costs exactly one per look; a reload costs exactly one and then goes quiet again; the tracker's delegation is metered once and not twice; and an unclaimed pane is offered the whole list where a claimed one stops at its position.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: six new rows and three derived blocks. `detect` on a claimed and on an unclaimed screen; `Tracker::observe` with the gate hitting and with it missing; the pane list with and without the detector; and `AgentClock::observe` against registries of 1, 8 and 64 remembered panes. The gate-miss row alternates between two rulesets that say the SAME thing, so every look is a full evaluation and every look reaches the verdict already published -- pricing the skip against a like-for-like alternative rather than against a different answer, which a changed screen would have been.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the two `Tracker` rows and the pane-list row read `sprag_detect::work` across themselves and print the counts. A row claiming to skip must have skipped and a row claiming to evaluate must have evaluated, and without that the pair could be measuring one code path twice and reporting the difference as a saving. It reports 124 evaluations over 125 calls on the gate-miss row, not 125, and the missing one is explicable: the alternation's first call lands on the ruleset the tracker was already settled under.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the module docs carry the ten-run ranges with the machine and the build profile beside them, and the pane-list row prints DO NOT QUOTE THIS ROW with the reason -- it bounds the cost and does not resolve it.

R256.decision_summary: R256: the quadratic term R255 measured and deferred, removed -- and the deferral's stated reason turned out to be true in a way that only a test could show. R255 found a per-look cost growing linearly with the number of panes the agent registry remembers, 2.70 to 3.35 ns each, because `AgentClock::observe` read the registry's NEAREST DEADLINE before and after every look to decide whether the settle waker needed telling, and the pane list calls that once per pane -- 2N^2 tracker visits per client wake. It was recorded as measured-not-fixed on the grounds that the cheap alternative is a change to a WAKE POLICY rather than a refactor, needing its own argument and its own proof. Both now exist. The argument is about what `observe` can touch: it mutates exactly ONE tracker, so every other pane's deadline is identical after, so the registry's minimum can only have moved if THIS pane's deadline moved -- which makes "this pane's deadline changed and is now Some" a strict SUPERSET of "the minimum moved and is now Some". Nothing the whole-registry comparison would have signalled is lost; what the superset adds is a wake when the new deadline is not the nearest one, and the waker's own docs already record a spurious wake as harmless. The proof is that the OBVIOUS cheap version is wrong, and it is wrong in a way no reasoning in R255 had reached: a `None` -> `Some` edge misses a pane whose candidate is ALREADY waiting when the user shortens `agent-settle-time`, because `Tracker::pending_deadline` is derived from `since + settle` rather than stored -- deliberately, so a shortened window moves the wait it is already serving -- and a waker parked on the old deadline would sleep straight through the new one. That is a fourth instance of this front's recurring defect (a mechanism with work to do and no event to wake it), and it was caught by writing the test before trusting the shape. Measured after: 0.85x to 1.16x across a 64-fold registry span where it was 3.98x to 4.32x, a slope straddling zero, and a look at sixty-four remembered panes down from 0.226-0.275 us to 0.079-0.092 us. The trade is stated rather than hidden: two hash lookups cost about 20 ns more than two walks of a one-entry registry, so a workspace below about eight panes pays a bounded constant for a term that was otherwise unbounded, and the eight-pane rows are indistinguishable before and after, which is what a crossover there predicts.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry::pending_deadline(id)` -- one hash lookup for the question `AgentClock::observe` actually has, where `next_deadline` answers a question about the whole registry and visits every tracker to do it. `is_due` now delegates to it rather than repeating the lookup-and-compare, so there is one definition of `this pane's deadline`. `next_deadline` keeps its walk and gains a doc saying who it is FOR: the waker, once per wake, never once per pane.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentClock::observe` compares that pane's deadline across the look instead of the registry's minimum. The condition is unchanged in form -- `after != before && after.is_some()` -- and changed in quantity, which is the smallest diff that removes the term. The doc carries the soundness argument (only one tracker is mutated, so only its deadline can move the minimum), the superset it produces, and the 20 ns constant it costs at one pane.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentWork` / `agent::work()`, a process-wide count of trackers visited by a nearest-deadline scan. It exists because the change moves no verdict, wakes no different client and alters no wire byte -- exactly the class R255 recorded as needing a count rather than a behaviour, since an exact optimisation has no behavioural observable and the tidier-looking whole-registry read would come back the first time somebody simplified the function. `sprag_grid::work` and `sprag_detect::work` are the same instrument for the same reason.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `a_shortened_window_wakes_a_waker_parked_on_the_old_one`, the case that decides what the edge is compared ON. A candidate is already waiting, the user shortens the window, nothing APPEARS, and the deadline moves into the past. A parked waker must be told. This is the test the obvious cheap version fails, and it is why the comparison is on deadlines rather than on presence.

crates/sprag-host/tests/agent_cost.rs: the count gate, in its own binary because the counter is process-wide and this crate's unit tests park wakers in parallel -- a delta taken there would be measuring whichever test happened to be parking. Two tests: eight looks at one pane in a registry of sixty-four visit ZERO trackers; and the waker's own park still visits all sixty-four exactly once. The second exists so that a meter reading zero cannot be mistaken for a meter that was never wired up, which is how this kind of gate rots.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the scaling rows and their prose re-aimed. They were the instrument that FOUND the term; they are now the regression check that says it stays gone, and the middle registry size stays because it is what tells a reappearance (a walk climbs with the entry count) from noise. The module docs carry both ten-run ranges, before and after, with the machine and the build profile beside them.
verification_bullets: THE DEFERRAL'S REASON WAS TRUE, AND THE TEST IS WHAT SHOWED IT. R255 declined to make this change on the grounds that it is a wake-policy question needing its own proof. The obvious cheap version -- signal when the pane goes from having no deadline to having one -- reads as exactly equivalent and is not: `Tracker::pending_deadline` is DERIVED from `since + settle`, deliberately, so that shortening `agent-settle-time` moves a wait already being served. A pane pending before and pending after can therefore have a deadline that just moved into the past, and a `None` -> `Some` edge is blind to it. Written as `a_shortened_window_wakes_a_waker_parked_on_the_old_one` and measured as a revert-proof: with the presence edge in place the test hangs to its timeout. Fourth instance in this front of a mechanism with work to do and no event to wake it.

THE SOUNDNESS ARGUMENT IS ABOUT WHAT THE FUNCTION CAN TOUCH, not about the sizes involved. `observe` mutates one tracker; every other pane's deadline is identical after; therefore the registry's minimum can only have moved if this pane's deadline moved. `this pane's deadline changed and is now Some` is a strict superset of `the minimum moved and is now Some`, so nothing the old comparison signalled is lost. The extra wakes are the case where the new deadline is not the nearest, and the waker's docs already record a spurious wake as harmless -- it re-reads `any_due` and parks again.

MEASURED, TEN RUNS BEFORE AND TEN AFTER, SAME BOX AND SAME BUILD PROFILE. The 64-versus-1 ratio went from 3.98x-4.32x to 0.85x-1.16x, and the slope from 2.70-3.35 ns per remembered pane to -0.222..+0.175 ns -- flat, straddling zero. A look at a registry of sixty-four went from 0.226-0.275 us to 0.079-0.092 us, 2.5x to 3.5x faster. The middle registry size remains the control that distinguishes a walk from a cache effect, and it now lands within about 1% of the flat line rather than on the climbing one.

THE TRADE IS MEASURED AND STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. Two hash lookups cost about 20 ns more than two walks of a ONE-entry registry, so the single-pane row moved from 0.056-0.065 us to 0.068-0.095 us -- ten runs each, ranges that do not overlap, so it is real rather than drift. Crossover is near eight panes and the eight-pane rows are indistinguishable before and after, which is what a crossover there predicts. A bounded constant against an unbounded term. The version with NO lookups exists -- `AgentRegistry::observe` holds the tracker already and could hand its deadline back -- and is deliberately not taken: the registry's docs make a point of knowing nothing about the signal, so asking the memory about the MEMORY and leaving the clock to decide about WAKING is the seam, and 20 ns is what it costs.

FOUR REVERT-PROOFS, ALL FOUR RED, with the mutated text printed, the anchor asserted GONE rather than the replacement counted, restoration by byte comparison and never `git checkout`, and `--no-fail-fast` from the start because R255 measured what happens without it. The whole-registry read restored (the count gate dies); the presence edge instead of the deadline (the shortened-window test dies); the visit counter never incrementing (the waker-park test dies, which is the one that proves the meter is wired at all); and the signal removed altogether (two tests die).

What it is not worth is a round: the fix and both its proofs came to a few dozen lines, and the reason for not doing it was never a cost. Read every deferral of one's own as an omission in an exclusion's clothes until the sentence describing it is longer than the change would have been.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentClock::observe` compares that pane's deadline across the look instead of the registry's minimum. crates/sprag-host/tests/agent_cost.rs: the count gate, in its own binary because the counter is process-wide and this crate's unit tests park wakers in parallel -- a delta taken there would be measuring whichever test happened to be parking. crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the scaling rows and their prose re-aimed. publishable_verification_bullets: THE DEFERRAL'S REASON WAS TRUE, AND THE TEST IS WHAT SHOWED IT.
