R257.decision_summary: R257: H3 slice 5, the surfaces -- and the slice's one sentence turned out to be a claim about code that the code refutes for one of the two frontends it names. Slice 5 read "MCP agent_state / agent_explain, a CLI verb, and the state in both frontends' pane lists", and sprag-tui has no pane list: 1297 lines with ZERO occurrences of title, label, status or bar, and its own paint docs record the chrome-lessness as a decision rather than a gap ("what makes the focused pane identifiable without a coloured border"). So that surface was DERIVED, and the two candidates are not equal. A status ROW must come out of the window, so this client would report a smaller area, which re-arbitrates window-size and reflows every pane in the session -- each time an agent starts or exits; it is also permanent chrome whose contents are a front of their own (tmux's status-left / status-right / formats). The outer terminal's WINDOW TITLE costs no row, no reflow and no arbitration, it is visible while the window is NOT focused (for "come back to me" the more useful half), and it is where this project ALREADY publishes the same fact for the other frontend: sprag-gui writes the focused pane's display title -- the very string that now carries the agent marker -- into its OS window title, which is also what tmux's set-titles does. The second derivation is the WORDING. The GUI puts the phrase beside a pane's title and the terminal client puts it in a digest: different PLACES, which is exactly why the words became one function in sprag-client. Two match blocks over "blocked" are how a user comes to read "blocked" in one client and "needs an answer" in the other, about one pane, in one session -- the drift the GUI's own exit marker is a single function to prevent, one level out. "blocked" renders as "needs an answer" because AgentState::Blocked is "the agent has ASKED something and cannot continue until it is answered": a request, not a fault, which is dead_marker's editorial rule ("exited" rather than tmux's "dead") applied a second time. Three further decisions were forced by reading the code rather than the design. The state crosses the wire as a STRING and not as the enum, because a client parses it from a daemon that may be newer than itself, so an unknown token must survive as itself and reach a surface. HostClient::pane_agent defaults to None and that default is the IN-PROCESS arm's real answer rather than a courtesy to an older impl: D2 puts the detector daemon-side because three consumers computing one fact are three authorities, so giving the in-process Host a registry would BE the second evaluation site D2 refuses. And a DEAD pane's marker is suppressed, because the detector reads a screen and a dead pane's final screen still shows what the agent last painted -- "(claude working) (exited)" contradicts itself.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs: `PaneAgent` {state, name, rule, seq} beside `PaneNotification`, and `HostClient::pane_agent` defaulted to `None`. `state` is a `String` and the doc says which side of the wire that is for: an unrecognised token from a newer daemon reaches a surface instead of collapsing into an enum's fallback. The default is documented as the in-process arm's honest answer (D2), not as a courtesy.

crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: the `agent` key parsed onto the poll cache (`parse_agent`, `WirePane::agent`, `PaneSeed::agent`) and served by `pane_agent`. `state` is REQUIRED -- a missing key, a null, a non-object and an object without a state all read as `None`, because a defaulted `idle` would tell a user an agent was waiting for them in a pane holding a shell. Re-adopted every wake INCLUDING back to `None` (an agent that exits leaves a shell behind), and KEPT across a transient query miss (a hiccup must not blank a `blocked` title).

crates/sprag-client/src/agent.rs: NEW module -- `agent_phrase` and `agent_urgency`, the vocabulary both frontends render through. The membership argument is stated at the top: the subject is a host fact and the alternative is two clients describing one pane differently. `agent_urgency` exists because a terminal truncates a title from the RIGHT, so blocked-before-idle-before-working is not cosmetic; an unknown token sorts LAST rather than first, so a future daemon's routine state cannot displace a blocked pane.

crates/sprag-gui/src/view.rs + a11y.rs + slotview.rs: `agent_marker` frames the shared phrase and owns the dead-pane rule; `pane_display_title` carries it BETWEEN the child's own title and the exit marker (increasing order of finality), so it reaches the dock header, the tab label, a floater's OS title and the main window's OS title at once; `terminal_a11y_node` pushes the SAME string, so the sighted title and the spoken name cannot drift. `SlotView::pane_agent` is the slot-to-id adapter.

crates/sprag-tui/src/paint.rs: `agent_window_title` -- `sprag: SESSION` alone for a workspace of shells (D8's additive rule at this surface), else `sprag: SESSION -- claude needs an answer (pane 9), claude working (pane 4)`, urgency-ordered with a STABLE sort so equal urgencies keep host order and the title does not reshuffle between wakes. The pane id is named because it is the only handle this client's panes have and it is the id `sprag panes`, `sprag agent` and the MCP tools all take. `title_change` is the equality skip, EXTRACTED so a test can hold it: `Surface::add_change` records every title it is handed, so a title re-sent per frame is one OSC per keystroke on the path R246 measured.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: `retitle` at the top of `paint`, which is the one function that writes the terminal at all -- so every path that repaints also re-titles and no future caller can add a repaint that forgets to. `Painted` bundles the paint cache and the last title, because they are one concept (what the terminal was last told, so telling it again can be skipped) and because `paint` reaching eight arguments was a NEW clippy warning this round created rather than silenced.

crates/sprag-mcp/src/main.rs: `agent_state` (the `pane` argument OPTIONAL -- "which pane needs a human" is a question about the SET, and a pane with no verdict is reported EXPLICITLY because D3 forbids that collapse) and `agent_explain` (the rule id plus the REMEDY: the id is what an `[[agent]]` block redefines or disables, which is what makes a mis-detection fixable without a release). Plus the additive `agent:` line on `list_panes`, `AgentInfo` / `parse_agent_info`, and the roster doc stops COUNTING its tools -- the count in prose said seven while there were nine.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `sprag agent [-t SESSION] [PANE]`. One line per pane an agent manifest claims and nothing for a shell; naming a PANE turns the same reading into a DIAGNOSIS (the rule that fired, and what to edit), answers a shell pane explicitly, and refuses an absent pane -- `require_pane`'s rule, because the caller named that pane.

crates/sprag-gui/src/bin/sprag-smoke.rs: the slice's own live gate, `check_an_agents_state_reaches_the_painted_pane_title`, plus the a11y half of the same claim. Placed beside the one-pane check whose daemon-to-client pane correspondence it needs, and it leaves the pane set as it found it.
verification_bullets: THE SLICE'S OWN SENTENCE WAS FALSE FOR ONE FRONTEND, AND IT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `grep -c ""` on sprag-tui's binary is 1297 lines and a case-insensitive grep for title|label|status|bar returns NOTHING -- so "the state in both frontends' pane lists" names a surface that does not exist in one of them. This is the fourth time in this front that a plan sentence had to be read from the code before it could be acted on, and the reason it matters here is that the honest alternative (a status row) is not a smaller version of the same thing: it changes every pane's size through window-size arbitration.

TEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL TEN RED, on the discipline this project has paid for: the anchor asserted PRESENT before and GONE after, the mutated line PRINTED, `--no-fail-fast` from the start (R255), and restoration by byte comparison against a copy taken first, never `git checkout` (R244). The GUI title dropping the marker (1 red); the marker no longer yielding to a dead child (3 red); `blocked` rendered as its wire token (4 red, across THREE crates -- which is the shared-vocabulary claim proving itself); a survivor keeping a verdict the host stopped sending (1 red); a state defaulted to `idle` in the client parse (1 red) and in the MCP parse (1 red); the title losing its urgency order (2 red); the title re-sent every frame (1 red); the paint path no longer re-titling (1 red -- the composition proof); and the CLI listing every pane rather than the claimed ones (1 red).

THE LIVE GUI PIXEL SMOKE: 124 checks passed, 0 failed, including both new ones. The painted string observed was `coin@...: ~ (claude needs an answer)` and the accessible name `Terminal: /bin/bash (claude needs an answer)`. That first string carries an unplanned proof: the pane's shell had already rewritten the OSC title, so the title-shaped fingerprint was GONE and the pane stayed CLAIMED through the footer fingerprint alone -- which is why the probe paints the footer, and it is the case a title-only probe would have passed while proving less. The check also asserts the phrase is ABSENT before the drive, so it cannot pass on a state that was already there.

THE TERMINAL CLIENT'S GATE IS THE SHIPPED BINARY'S OWN OSC, READ THROUGH SPRAG'S EMULATOR. `a_blocked_agent_pane_reaches_the_terminals_window_title` boots a daemon, paints an agent-shaped screen from a real child, attaches the real `sprag-tui` on a real pseudoterminal, and asserts the window title the emulator consumed. Four joints have to hold and each is green on its own if any one is broken: publish, parse, ask, emit. `Blocked` is used because it rests on evidence PRESENT on the screen and publishes on sight, so the gate needs no sleep and cannot flake on one.

THE CLI'S TEST IS WHAT PINS THE WIRE KEY'S SPELLING. `the_cli_reports_which_pane_an_agent_is_waiting_in` drives the shipped daemon and reads `state`, `name` and `rule` out of the `agent` key that a different crate writes -- the R253 seam, where a unit test over hand-written JSON agrees with itself about all four names. It also holds the additive rule (a shell pane contributes no line), the named-pane diagnosis, and the refusal for an absent pane.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0, after the eight-argument warning this round created was fixed by bundling the two paint records rather than allowed; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates (two `sprag_detect` intra-doc links had to become prose in sprag-client, which does not depend on the detector -- the gate caught a link that would have shipped broken); the workspace suite 1551 to 1567 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus SIXTEEN is exactly this round's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved; the citation gate 112 of 112 sources scanned, the new one included.

WHAT IS NOT PROVED, NAMED RATHER THAN IMPLIED. The two MCP tools are unit-proved only: `sprag-mcp` has no integration harness at all and never has, so nothing runs its bridge against a live daemon. The risk that a unit fixture disagrees with the real wire is retired for the KEY they read (the CLI test above proves the same four names live) and the tool bodies use the same `query_panes` bridge every existing tool uses -- but the composition itself is unwitnessed, and that is a pre-existing gap this round did not widen and did not close.
carry_forward_bullets: H3'S SLICE LIST IS NOW COMPLETE (1 through 5), and one item R254 pointed AT slice 5 is still owed -- the pointer was mis-aimed, which is worth recording rather than quietly inheriting. R254 said the broken-manifest report path "needs slice 5's surface". It does not: `config::AgentManifests::unusable()` already keeps the reason for a surface and today it reaches only a `tracing::warn`, and the error is GLOBAL while every surface this slice built reads a PER-PANE key. The manifests are the daemon's (the detector runs daemon-side, D2), so a client re-parsing the file to report on it would be a second authority answering about a file the daemon may not have re-read. What it needs is a new global wire fact plus a surface for it in each client -- a different mechanism from this slice's, so it is named here with its shape rather than left as "slice 5 will do it".

STILL NOT MEASURED, unchanged since R255: the settle waker's own sweep, which takes a screen read per pane daemon-wide once every five seconds and which no row prices; and the socket, since every latency row is served in-process. Slice 5 adds one more unpriced path of its own: the terminal client now walks its pane cache and formats a digest on every paint, equality-skipped at the OSC but NOT at the walk. It is `pane_ids` plus one hash-free scan per frame against a paint this project measures in milliseconds, so it is expected to be invisible -- which is a prediction, not a measurement, and this sentence is the record that nobody has taken one.

REJECTED WITH ITS COST, so a later round does not re-open it as an oversight: a STATUS ROW for the terminal client. It is the surface tmux has and it would show every agent pane on screen rather than in a title, but the row must come out of the window, so its appearance and disappearance travel through `window-size` arbitration and reflow every pane in the session -- twice per agent lifetime, and on every client attached to it. The title has no such coupling. If the row is ever built it should be built as a status-line FRONT (formats, left/right, the option that turns it off), not as a corner of an agent feature.

SLICE 4'S REMAINING UNCOVERED PROPERTIES ARE UNCHANGED and neither is a surface question: the reload's LATENCY, and a reload landing on a PENDING candidate. Slice 1's two measured misses also stand: the title-free fingerprint (an onboarding dialog that arrives before any title, measured in both agents), and `codex`'s tool-approval dialog, still unbought because it needs a working credential.

TEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL TEN RED, on the discipline this project has paid for: the anchor asserted PRESENT before and GONE after, the mutated line PRINTED, `--no-fail-fast` from the start (R255), and restoration by byte comparison against a copy taken first, never `git checkout` (R244). The GUI title dropping the marker (1 red); the marker no longer yielding to a dead child (3 red); `blocked` rendered as its wire token (4 red, across THREE crates -- which is the shared-vocabulary claim proving itself); a survivor keeping a verdict the host stopped sending (1 red); a state defaulted to `idle` in the client parse (1 red) and in the MCP parse (1 red); the title losing its urgency order (2 red); the title re-sent every frame (1 red); the paint path no longer re-titling (1 red -- the composition proof); and the CLI listing every pane rather than the claimed ones (1 red).

THE LIVE GUI PIXEL SMOKE: 124 checks passed, 0 failed, including both new ones. The painted string observed was `coin@...: ~ (claude needs an answer)` and the accessible name `Terminal: /bin/bash (claude needs an answer)`. That first string carries an unplanned proof: the pane's shell had already rewritten the OSC title, so the title-shaped fingerprint was GONE and the pane stayed CLAIMED through the footer fingerprint alone -- which is why the probe paints the footer, and it is the case a title-only probe would have passed while proving less. The check also asserts the phrase is ABSENT before the drive, so it cannot pass on a state that was already there.

THE TERMINAL CLIENT'S GATE IS THE SHIPPED BINARY'S OWN OSC, READ THROUGH SPRAG'S EMULATOR. `a_blocked_agent_pane_reaches_the_terminals_window_title` boots a daemon, paints an agent-shaped screen from a real child, attaches the real `sprag-tui` on a real pseudoterminal, and asserts the window title the emulator consumed. Four joints have to hold and each is green on its own if any one is broken: publish, parse, ask, emit. `Blocked` is used because it rests on evidence PRESENT on the screen and publishes on sight, so the gate needs no sleep and cannot flake on one.

THE CLI'S TEST IS WHAT PINS THE WIRE KEY'S SPELLING. `the_cli_reports_which_pane_an_agent_is_waiting_in` drives the shipped daemon and reads `state`, `name` and `rule` out of the `agent` key that a different crate writes -- the R253 seam, where a unit test over hand-written JSON agrees with itself about all four names. It also holds the additive rule (a shell pane contributes no line), the named-pane diagnosis, and the refusal for an absent pane.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0, after the eight-argument warning this round created was fixed by bundling the two paint records rather than allowed; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates (two `sprag_detect` intra-doc links had to become prose in sprag-client, which does not depend on the detector -- the gate caught a link that would have shipped broken); the workspace suite 1551 to 1567 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus SIXTEEN is exactly this round's test count, so nothing elsewhere moved; the citation gate 112 of 112 sources scanned, the new one included.

WHAT IS NOT PROVED, NAMED RATHER THAN IMPLIED. The two MCP tools are unit-proved only: `sprag-mcp` has no integration harness at all and never has, so nothing runs its bridge against a live daemon. The risk that a unit fixture disagrees with the real wire is retired for the KEY they read (the CLI test above proves the same four names live) and the tool bodies use the same `query_panes` bridge every existing tool uses -- but the composition itself is unwitnessed, and that is a pre-existing gap this round did not widen and did not close.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: H3'S SLICE LIST IS NOW COMPLETE (1 through 5), and one item R254 pointed AT slice 5 is still owed -- the pointer was mis-aimed, which is worth recording rather than quietly inheriting. R254 said the broken-manifest report path "needs slice 5's surface". It does not: `config::AgentManifests::unusable()` already keeps the reason for a surface and today it reaches only a `tracing::warn`, and the error is GLOBAL while every surface this slice built reads a PER-PANE key. The manifests are the daemon's (the detector runs daemon-side, D2), so a client re-parsing the file to report on it would be a second authority answering about a file the daemon may not have re-read. What it needs is a new global wire fact plus a surface for it in each client -- a different mechanism from this slice's, so it is named here with its shape rather than left as "slice 5 will do it".

STILL NOT MEASURED, unchanged since R255: the settle waker's own sweep, which takes a screen read per pane daemon-wide once every five seconds and which no row prices; and the socket, since every latency row is served in-process. Slice 5 adds one more unpriced path of its own: the terminal client now walks its pane cache and formats a digest on every paint, equality-skipped at the OSC but NOT at the walk. It is `pane_ids` plus one hash-free scan per frame against a paint this project measures in milliseconds, so it is expected to be invisible -- which is a prediction, not a measurement, and this sentence is the record that nobody has taken one.

REJECTED WITH ITS COST, so a later round does not re-open it as an oversight: a STATUS ROW for the terminal client. It is the surface tmux has and it would show every agent pane on screen rather than in a title, but the row must come out of the window, so its appearance and disappearance travel through `window-size` arbitration and reflow every pane in the session -- twice per agent lifetime, and on every client attached to it. The title has no such coupling. If the row is ever built it should be built as a status-line FRONT (formats, left/right, the option that turns it off), not as a corner of an agent feature.

SLICE 4'S REMAINING UNCOVERED PROPERTIES ARE UNCHANGED and neither is a surface question: the reload's LATENCY, and a reload landing on a PENDING candidate. Slice 1's two measured misses also stand: the title-free fingerprint (an onboarding dialog that arrives before any title, measured in both agents), and `codex`'s tool-approval dialog, still unbought because it needs a working credential.

R258.decision_summary: R258: `sprag-mcp` gets the integration harness R257 recorded it had never had -- and the harness's first job turned out to be defending against its own subject. The crate is the agent-facing MCP surface: an AI inside a pane reads and drives its siblings through eleven tools that bridge to the daemon's wire. Every test it had called a handler function directly, which left three layers unobserved. The protocol loop had no test of ANY kind: `serve` and `dispatch` decide whether a real `initialize` line is answered, whether a NOTIFICATION correctly is not, and whether one stray byte on the pipe ends the session -- and a server that answers a notification is broken for every client while every unit test stays green. stdout as a protocol channel is a property of the PROCESS, unreachable from inside it, and its failure mode is total: one log line desynchronises the client, which then fails on the NEXT message rather than on the bad one. And every tool spells a path with the wire SSOT and hands it to a daemon in another crate, which is the seam R253 was bitten at -- a unit test over hand-written JSON agrees with itself about all of those names. Then the socket resolve forced the harness's shape. The crate's signature robustness is that it self-configures in any pane: its own SPRAG_HOST_RPC_SOCK, else the first /proc ancestor carrying one. That second layer is a HAZARD FOR A TEST SUITE, because sprag's own developers run the suite inside a sprag pane, where the walk resolves their LIVE terminal -- so a test that merely forgot to set the variable would not fail, it would type into the panes the author is working in. The precedence is therefore the safety property rather than a layering detail, and it is asserted rather than assumed: an ancestor advertising a DIFFERENT daemon is set up deliberately and the answer must come from the socket the child was given. The same hazard makes the crate's most user-visible message ("not inside a sprag terminal") unassertable by the naive test, which would pass on CI and fail on the author's machine; the construction that makes it deterministic is `setsid --fork`, which re-parents the server out of the suite's whole ancestor chain onto init or the login sub-reaper, neither of which can carry a per-instance socket because both predate any daemon. Two /proc premises were measured before they were written down: a shell's `/proc/<pid>/environ` is the EXEC-time snapshot, so an ancestor that has since `unset` the variable still advertises it -- which is also WHY the production feature works, a pane shell having been exec'd with the daemon's socket exported -- and /bin/sh here forks its last command rather than exec'ing into it. The second is not portable, so it became an assertion instead of a premise.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: NEW, and the crate's first integration test of any kind. The shipped `sprag-mcp` binary is spawned with its three streams piped and spoken to as an MCP client speaks to it -- one newline-delimited JSON-RPC message at a time -- against a real `sprag-term` daemon with real panes. Eight tests over four claims: the protocol loop, stdout's purity, the wire vocabulary, and the two-layer socket resolve.

crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: `McpServer`, the client side. Reading is done by a thread into a channel rather than inline, for two reasons that are both failure modes rather than preferences: a response that never comes has to become a failed assertion instead of a hung suite, and stderr has to be drained CONCURRENTLY or a chatty log run fills its pipe and blocks the server mid-reply. `request` asserts the response echoes the id, which is what makes every negative in the file work -- an unsolicited line arrives THERE and fails on the id rather than being silently consumed.

crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: `spawn_behind_ancestor` and `assert_forked`. The intermediate is /bin/sh, which forks its last command here rather than exec'ing into it; because that is a property of dash and not of shells, `assert_forked` reads the kernel's own process-children list and fails loudly if the shell tail-exec'd, and reads the shell's environ to confirm the ancestor really advertises what the walk is supposed to find. A premise that decides how much a test proves is held as an assertion, not as a comment.

crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: `spawn_orphaned`, and it waits for the shim to exit BEFORE any request goes out. Without that wait the shim is briefly still the parent, so the walk would climb through the test binary into the ambient environment -- the exact data-dependent flake the construction exists to remove.

crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: `wait_for_tool_count`, because ONE occurrence of typed text in a pane running `cat` is the pane's own echo and proves only that the bytes reached that PTY. The second is `cat` writing the line back, so the CHILD PROCESS received a completed line. The count is what makes the Enter load-bearing, and waiting on it rather than asserting after a first sighting is what keeps the two from racing.

crates/sprag-mcp/src/main.rs: one durable comment corrected against a measurement rather than left standing. The unit test's revert-proof claimed that defaulting `state` fails all THREE rejection assertions; measured, it fails TWO -- the missing-key case is held by `entry.get("agent")?` one line earlier. Worth naming because that third case is the only one a real daemon produces, which is why the live harness cannot hold that guard at all.
verification_bullets: FOURTEEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL FOURTEEN RED, on this project's discipline: the anchor asserted GONE in the same pass that applied the mutation (a check `grep` cannot do -- these anchors span lines, and the first version of the driver reported a false ANCHOR STILL PRESENT for exactly that reason), the mutated line PRINTED, `--no-fail-fast`, and restoration by byte comparison against a copy taken first. Answering a notification; dying on a malformed line; answering an unknown method with a success result; the log subscriber writing to stdout; the 1-based number used as the host id; a misspelled links slot; `agent_state` omitting the pane with no verdict; the rule field not read off the wire; `agent_explain` dropping the remedy; the ancestor walk tried first; the ancestor fallback deleted; a hard-coded default socket; write_pane's Enter suppressed two different ways.

THREE OF THOSE FAILED WITH THE DAEMON'S OWN REFUSAL, which is the whole reason the file exists: the misspelled slot dies on `UnknownIntrospectPath` and the number-as-id dies on `NoExternalAtPath`, both from the daemon rather than from an assertion about a fixture. That is the class of defect a unit test over hand-written JSON cannot produce, because it agrees with itself about every name.

ONE REVERT-PROOF CAME BACK GREEN AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN PROPPED UP. Defaulting the parsed `state` to `idle` changes nothing this harness can see: a real daemon OMITS the `agent` key entirely for a pane no manifest claims, so the parse returns None before a state is read, and the defensive default is unreachable from here. The population that would expose it -- a daemon sending `agent: null`, or an object with no state -- does not exist on this wire. So the doc comment that claimed it was corrected in both places, and the honest generalisation is written down: an integration harness does not subsume the tests beneath it.

THE ORPHAN CONSTRUCTION WAS PROVED LOAD-BEARING BY A CONTROL PAIR, not by argument. This box has no ambient socket in its ancestor chain (measured), so a naive version of that test would pass here and fail for anyone running the suite inside a sprag pane. The hazard was therefore created artificially -- the test binary given an ambient SPRAG_HOST_RPC_SOCK -- and measured both ways: orphaned it still PASSES, and with the orphaning removed and everything else identical it FAILS. That is the flake the construction removes, demonstrated rather than asserted.

TEN CONSECUTIVE RUNS OF THE FILE, 10 passed / 0 failed, one green run being no evidence about a harness whose every wait crosses three processes and two sockets. Every wait polls the CONDITION the assertion reads; the one negative that could have wanted a quiet window (a notification produces no line) is held by ORDERING instead -- the next request's response must be the FIRST line to arrive.

R259.decision_summary: R259: the omission R258 named and priced in the same breath, built -- because pricing it was the argument for building it. R258's carry-forward said three of the eleven MCP read tools were gated only on their EMPTY branch (`read_last_command` on its no-shell-integration fallback, `read_pane_links` and `read_pane_images` on "this pane shows none"), because the pane those tests run is `cat` and `cat` emits no OSC 133, no OSC 8 and no graphics. It then said the gap was "cheap to add with the right child program and not in this round's claim". That sentence is this project's own recorded failure mode: an item costing LESS than the paragraph excluding it is an omission wearing an exclusion's clothes, and the owner asked the one-word question that exposes it. The cost was one child process. What the empty-branch tests could not see is the whole rendering half: each of those three tools formats a slot value into the text an agent reads, and a tool that got its non-empty case wrong passed every assertion, because the assertion was about the empty case. So one child now emits all three artifacts in the exact forms this workspace already drives through its own emulator -- an OSC 8 hyperlink with an id, a 2x2 Kitty RGBA transmit, and a full OSC 133 cycle (prompt, command, input end, output start, one output line, exit 0) -- and each tool has to turn a real slot value into a real answer. The cycle also lights the pane list's shell-integration line, which no test in that file reached at all for the same structural reason: a resting pane has no such line, so it is observable only on a pane that emitted marks. Two harness lessons came out of the proofs rather than out of the design. A wait whose needle IS the claim converts a rendering regression into a thirty-second timeout instead of an immediate failure, so the wait was moved onto the link's EXISTENCE and the rendering left to the assertion. And the pane had to be made taller than every other pane in the file: at six rows the link scrolls off while the command cycle is still printing, so the artifacts must still be on screen when the tools ask.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-mcp/tests/mcp_stdio.rs: `the_list_read_tools_render_what_a_pane_actually_shows`, the other half of `the_query_slots_every_read_tool_names_are_the_daemons_own`. One `sh -c` child emits an OSC 8 hyperlink with an id, a Kitty `a=T,f=32,s=2,v=2,i=7` transmit whose 16-byte RGBA payload is base64, and a full OSC 133 A/B/C/D cycle with exit 0, then `cat` so the pane stays alive and quiet. Every escape form is copied from a fixture this workspace already drives through the same emulator, so a failure is about the TOOL rather than about whether the sequence was well-formed.

R260.decision_summary: R260: the settle waker's sweep, priced -- and the paragraph that priced it by ARGUMENT named the small term and omitted the large one. The sweep is the one loop in this daemon that runs whether or not anybody asks: every five seconds, for the life of the process, it discovers panes nobody has queried, carries a manifest edit to the panes it invalidates, and forgets the panes that are gone. Three rounds recorded its cost as never measured; what it had instead was a paragraph of reasoning. That paragraph said the evaluation happens once per pane for the life of the daemon rather than once per interval, which is true and is the part that matters; then it said what recurs is the walk -- the registry lock, then each workspace lock, and a pane-id read each -- and that since spawn_durability_saver already takes exactly those locks at exactly this interval and then does strictly more, this thread's marginal cost is a second cheap lock acquisition every five seconds. Measured, two things are wrong with it. It omits the clock lock the walk takes ONCE PER PANE, which is the real per-pane cost rather than a pane-id read. And it omits entirely the config-file read that R254 put on this same loop one slice later: at ONE pane, 94% of a sweep is that read, and at sixty-four it is still 26%. R254's own justification was followed to its file and is not at fault -- it priced the SCHEDULING (this wake already exists, so the reload adds no thread, no timer and no wake), which is true and is a different claim from what the work costs. The two claims live in two files and only one was updated when the code moved. The comparator was read rather than assumed: the durability saver does take the same locks at the same period and does strictly more per pane, so the shared half of the argument is right; it also reads no file at all, writing only when the shape moved, so nothing in it corresponds to the term that dominates. Nothing here asks for a code change -- a sweep is 7.0 to 8.4 us at sixty-four panes against a five-second period, 0.00014% of one core -- which is a result rather than a reason the measurement was unnecessary, because the shape it exposes is the thing a future slice would reason from.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry::owes_evaluation(id, now, sweep)`, the waker's whole test for "ask about this one". It was a closure inline in a `thread::spawn` in a binary for three slices, which is reachable by nothing -- no unit test could witness the composition of its three questions (each was tested alone) and no instrument could price the one piece of the sweep that runs once per pane per interval. Measuring it is what required it to be callable.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `SWEEP_INTERVAL` moved here from `sprag-term`'s private constant, because a second binary now needs the same five seconds to say what fraction of a period the work occupies -- and one bin cannot see another's private item, so the alternative was a second spelling with a comment asking the next person not to let them drift.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: fourteen rows pricing every term that recurs per sweep, PTY-free for R255's reason -- the per-pane question at three registry sizes, `any_due` at three, `retain_live` at three, the census build at three, and the manifest re-read at both of its operating points (a file that exists and is unchanged, and a config path with no file behind it). Measured through `AgentClock::with`, because the sweep takes that lock once per PANE and a row over the bare registry method would be measuring something the daemon never calls.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: the cost paragraph rewritten from the measurement, with the two corrections named as corrections rather than quietly replaced, and the one term still unmeasured (what the locks cost) stated with WHY it is unmeasured -- a single-threaded instrument measures a lock uncontended, and uncontended is not what a lock costs.

crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: two more durable claims corrected against the same run. `retain_live`'s "the census is a by-product of work it is doing anyway" is true about the WALK and false about the cost -- building the set is 2.9x to 3.0x the prune it serves. `AgentWork`'s "the waker's own park, which asks once per wake" undercounted by half: a wake reads the whole registry TWICE, once to choose a sleep and once on waking, and the second cannot be dropped because a candidate appearing is what cuts the sleep short.

crates/sprag-host/tests/agent_cost.rs: two count gates for the two claims a duration cannot hold -- the sweep's per-pane question visits ZERO other trackers, and one turn of the waker's loop visits every tracker exactly twice.
verification_bullets: SEVEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL SEVEN RED, on this project's discipline: literal string replacement rather than a regex, the anchor asserted GONE in the same pass that applied the mutation, the mutated line PRINTED, `--no-fail-fast`, and restoration verified by BYTE COMPARISON against a copy taken first. Four on the extracted predicate (the sweep gate dropped, and each of `is_due`, `stale`, `knows` in turn), one on the property beneath the steady-state test (`publish` keeping its candidate), and two on the count gates.

THE TWO COUNT-GATE MUTATIONS ARE BEHAVIOUR-IDENTICAL, WHICH IS THE POINT, and each turned exactly ONE test red out of the entire `sprag-host` package. Giving `owes_evaluation` a whole-registry read it does not need changes no verdict, no wake and no wire byte; computing `any_due`'s minimum without going through the metered reader gives the same answer. Nothing behavioural could see either. The counter saw both, which is the difference between a gate and an illustration.

THE STEADY-STATE TEST IS RECORDED AS A RESTATEMENT RATHER THAN PROPPED UP. `a_settled_pane_under_unchanged_rules_owes_nothing_on_either_wake` survives all four mutations of the function it tests, and the fifth mutation that does turn it red turns four OLDER tests red as well. So it is not independently load-bearing: it states, at the level the cost claim is made, an answer the tracker tests already hold. Kept for that reason and labelled as that, not counted as a fifth guard.

FIVE RUNS OF `sprag-latency --release` ON THIS BOX (i9-14900HX, powersave governor), minima, quoting the RANGE because one run of this tool is not a measurement. One sweep: 1.96-2.33 us at one pane, 2.50-2.95 us at eight, 7.01-8.38 us at sixty-four. Per pane 0.039-0.043 us, flat at -0.02 to +0.06 ns per remembered pane across a 64x span. `any_due` 0.021-0.024 us at one pane and 0.082-0.094 us at sixty-four, about 1.0 ns per tracker visited -- the same order as the 1.35-1.68 ns per visit R255 inferred from a different row, which is an independent corroboration rather than a restatement. The manifest read 1.84-2.20 us with a file and 0.58-0.66 us with none, the same as asking 47 to 51 panes whether they owe an evaluation.

THE METER AGREED EXACTLY IN ALL FIVE RUNS. Every `deadline_visits_total` in the sweep block is accounted for by `any_due`'s call count times its registry size, with nothing left over for the per-pane question, the prune or the census -- so the tool checks its own claim each run and prints MISMATCH if it ever stops holding, rather than printing two raw numbers a reader has to divide.

The `sprag-host` binaries were rebuilt before the suite.
carry_forward_bullets: THE SHAPE OF THIS FAILURE IS WORTH MORE THAN THE NUMBER. A cost paragraph is a claim about code, and it decays the way any other claim about code decays -- except that nothing recomputes it. R254 added a file read to a loop whose cost paragraph lived in a different file and never mentioned files; both texts were true when written, and the pair became false without either being edited. The generalisation: WHEN A ROUND ADDS WORK TO AN EXISTING LOOP, THE THING TO RE-READ IS NOT THE CODE IT TOUCHED BUT WHATEVER PRICES THAT LOOP -- and if the price is an argument rather than a number, that is the round to make it a number.

"X already does strictly more at the same interval" was half right, and the half it got wrong was not in X -- it was a term this side had grown that X had no counterpart for. Reading the comparator is necessary and is not sufficient; the enumeration on one's OWN side has to be re-derived from the code too.

STILL OWED, unchanged: the broken-manifest report path needs a new GLOBAL wire fact plus a surface in each client; slice 4's reload latency and a reload landing on a PENDING candidate; slice 1's two measured misses (the title-free fingerprint, codex's tool-approval dialog which needs a credential).

R261.decision_summary: R261: the term R260 refused to claim, measured -- and the round is mostly a record of how many plausible answers it had first. R260 priced every recurring term of the settle waker's sweep and named one it would not: what the locks cost, on the grounds that a single-threaded instrument acquires a lock uncontended and uncontended is not what a lock costs. What a lock costs is the WAIT it inflicts, so the subject is not the sweep at all -- it is a pane-list READER's latency while the sweep runs. Three answers came out of that harness in order, and the first two were wrong. ONE: a single condition against a control with no second thread said the sweep costs a reader ten times its median. Most of that was not a lock. A pass only does real work when panes owe an evaluation, forcing that means churning the ruleset, and the pane list runs the SAME detector under the SAME clock -- so the reader's own request started evaluating every pane too. TWO: pairing each sweeping condition with a control that sweeps a PRIVATE registry at the same rate said +160 to +237 us. The pair was not matched: one background loop reloaded one clock and the other reloaded two, so they churned at different rates, and the difference measured churn rather than sharing. What caught it was not care -- it was printing the sweeper's own pass and evaluation COUNTS beside the latencies, at which point a condition claiming every pane owed an evaluation was visibly evaluating three panes across two thousand passes. THREE, and the answer: for the pass that actually recurs, sharing the registry costs a reader -1.4 to +5.9 us on the median and -1.6 to +6.4 us at p99, measured at seven to twelve MILLION times the daemon's real duty cycle. The recurring pass is free. The churning pass cannot be answered the same way at all, and that is a property of the system rather than of the instrument: sharing the registry changes WHO evaluates, not only who waits, so the two conditions cannot be matched -- R255's shape again. It is bounded directly instead, by the pass's own duration, 64 to 87 us for three panes against 0.58 to 1.04 us quiet.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/sweep.rs: NEW. `sweep_once(registry, agents, channels, now, discover) -> SweepReport`, which is the pass the waker thread used to hold as a closure. Every input it reads was already a library type, so the binary held host logic the library owned every piece of -- and the consequence was the usual one: the pass could not be called, so it could not be tested and could not be measured. What stays in `sprag-term` is the scheduling: the thread, the park, the `last_sweep` clock, and the manifest re-read that must precede a pass.

crates/sprag-host/src/sweep.rs: `SweepReport {visited, evaluated, moved}`, returned rather than left as side effects. It is what lets a test assert the pass's behaviour instead of inferring it, and what lets the harness put a CONTROL ON ITS OWN PROBE -- the evaluation count is what exposed a churning condition that was not churning.

crates/sprag-host/src/sweep.rs: five tests, of which two close items the arc debt register lists as DELIBERATELY UNCOVERED. `a_pass_forgets_the_tracker_of_a_pane_that_is_gone` -- the register's reason was that a leaked tracker is unobservable through any surface, true only while the pass lived in a binary; the registry's own length is the observable. `only_the_session_whose_answer_moved_is_woken` -- the register's reason was that it needs a two-session harness, which needed a callable pass.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the contention section. A reader thread timed over six conditions, each sweeping condition paired with a control that does the SAME work on a private registry; a tail estimator rather than the minimum, because for a contention question the minimum is by definition the sample that did not collide; and the sweeper's own pass and evaluation counts printed beside every row.
crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: the cost paragraph's last open term filled in, and `spawn_agent_waker` reduced to the loop it always should have been.
verification_bullets: FOUR REVERT-PROOFS ON THE EXTRACTED PASS, ALL FOUR RED, same discipline as R260's seven: the per-pane gate dropped (three tests red at once), the prune dropped, every session woken rather than only those that moved, and discovery on every wake rather than only on a sweep. Eleven red across the pair of rounds.

THE PROBE'S OWN CONTROL IS THE ROUND'S BEST INSTRUMENT AND IT CAUGHT A DEFECT IN MY HARNESS. Printing the sweeper's pass and evaluation counts beside the latencies showed a condition that claimed every pane owed an evaluation evaluating THREE panes over two thousand passes: one toggle was shared between two clocks, so each clock was handed the same ruleset every iteration and nothing ever went stale. Without that column both churning conditions would have reported a lock cost of zero, and the zero would have been the harness rather than the daemon.

THE SAME COLUMN THEN SHOWED SOMETHING THAT IS NOT A DEFECT. With the churn fixed, the private control's sweeper evaluated three panes on every pass while the shared one evaluated a fraction -- because the reader had done the rest. That is the structural reason the churning pair cannot be matched, and it is visible only as a count.

FIVE RUNS, and the box is DISCLOSED rather than assumed: another project was building throughout, load average 10 to 13, and the tool's own control spread read 29% to 240% against the 19% a quiet run gives. That inflates every absolute here by roughly two to two and a half times -- `detect (shell)` read 126 us against the 42.6 to 52.0 R255 recorded, and `request panes slot` 18.7 us against 7.4 to 8.7, the same factor on rows this round did not touch. The PAIRED differences are what the design exists to keep, and they are what is quoted.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates; the workspace suite 1580 to 1585 tests passed, 0 failed, and the plus FIVE is exactly this round's test count. The `sprag-host` binaries were rebuilt before the suite.
carry_forward_bullets: THE RULE THIS ROUND EARNED: A PROBE NEEDS A CONTROL ON THE PROBE. This project already holds that a measurement needs a control for its subject, and that a control cancels only the noise it shares. Neither would have caught this: the harness was well controlled and was measuring a background thread that was not doing the thing its name said. The check is cheap and mechanical -- have the thing under test COUNT what it did, and print the count beside the latency. A condition that claims to evaluate every pane must show them evaluated. Same family as the meter that gates the pane list's zero, aimed at the instrument instead of at the code.

AND: TWO PLAUSIBLE WRONG ANSWERS ARRIVED BEFORE THE RIGHT ONE, both large, both with a story. The first had no control at all; the second had a control that was not matched. The tell in both cases was that the number was interesting -- 10x, then +237 us -- and the discipline that saved it was not scepticism but instrumentation. Do not trust a concurrency difference until the background thread can prove what it did.

THE CHURNING COMPARISON IS UNRESOLVABLE BY THIS DESIGN AND THAT IS RECORDED AS A PROPERTY, NOT A GAP. Sharing a registry changes who evaluates, not only who waits, so no pairing can hold the reader's own work constant while varying the sharing. Anyone wanting a true contention number for that regime needs a different instrument -- a reader that does NOT run the detector, which means a request other than the pane list, or an instrumented lock. Neither was bought, and the direct bound (the pass's own duration) answers what the round owed.

STILL NOT MEASURED, now two: the SOCKET, since every latency row is served in-process; and the terminal client's per-paint pane-cache walk for the title digest. R260's lock term is CLOSED. A third item is worth naming rather than discovering: every absolute number in `sprag-latency`'s module doc was taken on a quiet box, and a reader who runs it on a loaded one will find them all two to three times larger. The control spread is printed for exactly that reason and should be read FIRST -- this round nearly wrote a stale-detector finding out of a busy box before checking it.

R262.decision_summary: R262: the socket, priced -- and it is the largest term in this tool by a wide margin. `sprag-latency` has served every request IN-PROCESS through `handle_request` since it was written, and its module doc has stated the wire's cost as an unpriced bound for four rounds. A real `sprag-term` is now spawned beside this binary with the same panes, geometry and boot command, driven over its Unix socket with the same request texts, and a client's wall clock is decomposed into the three things it actually is: the daemon's own work (already measured in-process), the client's PARSE of the reply, and the transport left over after both. Four runs: a round trip is 22 to 35 us of FIXED cost, for a `scene/revision` whose entire answer is fourteen bytes and whose in-process cost is about ONE microsecond -- so the wire is roughly THIRTY TIMES the daemon's work for a small request. A 912-byte pane list costs 43 to 74 us of transport, putting the size term at 15 to 45 ns per byte, some fifty times slower than this box copies memory: the part that scales is per-MESSAGE handling on both ends rather than bandwidth. What that does to the rest of the tool is the point rather than a footnote. The projection at 0.18% of a frame, the agent gate at three thousand times what it skips, the sweep at microseconds per five seconds -- every one is a change to a term that is a fraction of the round trip carrying it. Read the other way it is the retrospective argument for what this project already built: the fetch gate (R220) and `waitFor` over polling both cut the NUMBER of round trips, and neither could have cut the cost of one.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: `socket_host` locates `sprag-term` BESIDE this binary rather than taking a path from the environment (a tool given a path measures whatever was there), and refuses the rows with a build hint when it is absent. `CARGO_BIN_EXE_*` exists only for tests, so a bin finds its sibling itself.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: `SocketHost`, a Drop guard that kills the daemon and unlinks its socket, kill first because the host holds the socket open until it exits. The spawned daemon is topped up to `PANE_COUNT` through the same mux SPAWN action a client uses and then WAITED for -- a pane list taken mid-boot is a shorter answer, and the byte check would read that as the two hosts disagreeing.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: `result_bytes`, because the equivalence check has to compare like with like. `HostConn::call` hands back the RESULT and `handle_request` returns the whole JSON-RPC response; the first version compared a payload against an envelope and flagged BOTH rows as answering different questions, on 34 bytes of wrapper.
crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-latency.rs: the module doc's socket exclusion rewritten from a disclaimer into a section, with the figures, the machine and the profile.
verification_bullets: THE EQUIVALENCE BETWEEN THE TWO HOSTS IS PRINTED ON EVERY ROW, not argued once. `scene/revision` matches to the BYTE, 14 against 14. The pane list does not -- 912 against 1024, because the hosts' pane LABELS differ -- and that residue is priced with the tool's OWN size slope rather than waved off: 112 bytes at 15-45 ns each is one to five us against a transport of 43 to 74, inside the run-to-run band. A row comparing two different answers says so in its own output.

THE MIDDLE TERM IS A SUBTRACTION and says so: the transport is what is left after the daemon's work and the client's parse come out of the wall clock, so it carries both of their errors. It is also the only one of the three no measurement in this repository could reach directly.

THE SIZE TERM IS CHECKED AGAINST A PHYSICAL BOUND rather than reported as a rate: 15-45 ns per byte is about fifty times slower than this box copies memory, so calling it bandwidth would be wrong. A number that would have been quoted as a throughput is quoted as what it is.
NO RESOURCE LEAK, checked after a full run rather than reasoned about: no `sprag-latency-*.sock` under the temp dir, no `sprag-term` left alive.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates; the workspace suite 1585 passed / 0 failed, UNCHANGED -- this round adds an instrument and no test, and the count saying so is the check that it added nothing else.
carry_forward_bullets: THE NUMBER RE-PROPORTIONS EVERY OTHER NUMBER THIS PROJECT HAS MEASURED. R218's projection gate, R220's fetch gate, R255's detector cost, R256's quadratic removal, R260's sweep were all measured against each other and against a frame; against the WIRE they are all small. That makes none of them wrong -- a quadratic term is still unbounded and the fetch gate is worth MORE now, not less -- but the next optimisation proposed on the daemon side should be asked how many ROUND TRIPS it removes before it is asked how many microseconds.

SECOND TIME IN THREE ROUNDS THAT A COMPARISON'S TWO SIDES DID NOT MATCH. R261 paired a sweeper against a control churning at a different rate; here the size check compared a payload against an envelope. Both were caught by an output the harness prints about ITSELF, not by review. Printing what the instrument did -- counts, sizes, rates -- beside what it measured is three-for-three in this arc.

STILL NOT MEASURED, now ONE, and registered with its obstacle: the terminal client's per-paint pane-cache walk. `retitle` walks `pane_ids()` then calls `pane_agent(id)` per id, each taking the cache lock again and LINEARLY SCANNING for the id -- N+1 lock acquisitions and N-squared compares per paint, plus up to three String clones per agent pane, on the per-keystroke path R246 measured. Reading it is not measuring it. It needs a live `WireHost`, which is on the far side of the dependency edge from `sprag-latency` (sprag-client depends on sprag-host, not the reverse), so it needs a harness in sprag-tui or sprag-client rather than a row here.

STILL OWED, unchanged: the broken-manifest report path needs a GLOBAL wire fact plus a surface in each client; slice 4's reload latency and a reload on a PENDING candidate; slice 1's two measured misses.

R263.decision_summary: R263: the last unmeasured path, measured -- and building the harness found a hard ceiling nobody knew was there. The terminal client rebuilds its window title on every PAINT, which for this client is every KEYSTROKE (R246), and throws the answer away: the equality skip is at the OSC and not at the walk. R262 registered it with its obstacle -- it needs a live `WireHost`, on the far side of `sprag-host`'s dependency edge from `sprag-latency` -- so the measurement lives where its subject does, as an example in `sprag-tui` that spawns its own daemon. Three things came out and only the first was the one being looked for. ONE, the number: the walk, the title build and the discarded comparison together are 0.9 us over 62 panes no manifest claims and 15 to 17 us when every one is an agent -- a third of a percent of a 5 ms paint, at a pane count that cannot be exceeded, so documented rather than restructured. TWO: THE EMPTY BRANCH UNDERSTATES IT NINETEENFOLD. A workspace of `cat` panes is claimed by nothing, so no string is cloned and the title never leaves its baseline; the first version of the harness measured exactly that and would have reported the plumbing. R259's shape at a different surface, caught by a guard that refuses to report a populated row it could not populate. THREE: THE QUADRATIC WALK IS NOT THE LARGER HALF, the opposite of what reading the code said. `pane_ids()` then `pane_agent(id)` per id really is N+1 cache locks and N^2 comparisons, and on a populated workspace the digest STRING BUILD is comparable to or larger than the walk feeding it -- so a fix aimed at the term the code makes obvious would have been aimed at the smaller one.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-tui/src/paint.rs: `session_agents`, the walk lifted out of the binary's `retitle` so something can call it. Same move as R260's predicate and R261's sweep pass, for the same reason and now for the third time: a thing composed inside a binary is reachable by no test and no instrument.

crates/sprag-tui/examples/title-cost.rs: NEW. Spawns a real daemon, brings up a real `WireHost` at 1, 8 and 62 panes, and times the walk, the title build and the whole of what a paint pays -- in BOTH branches, a workspace no manifest claims and one where every pane is an agent. An example rather than a bin because it needs the crate's own lib and a daemon binary it locates beside itself.

crates/sprag-tui/examples/title-cost.rs: the populated fixture paints BOTH halves of a real `claude` pane. The footer alone fingerprints a pane and fires no RULE -- every rule reads the title's resting glyph -- so `pane_agent` answers `None` and the walk quietly measures the empty branch again. That was the first version, and the guard that refuses a row it could not populate is what caught it.

crates/sprag-tui/src/paint.rs: `session_agents`'s doc carries the two corrections rather than only the number, because both are things the next reader would otherwise re-derive wrongly from the same code.
verification_bullets: A HARD CEILING FOUND WHILE BUILDING THE HARNESS, AND MEASURED RATHER THAN GUESSED. 64 panes would not boot: `WireHost::spawn_or_attach` fails with serde_json's `recursion limit exceeded`. The cause was probed directly -- the daemon's layout slot is a nested binary tree whose JSON depth is exactly `2N + 3`, confirmed at 4/8/16 panes (11/19/35) and at the boundary: 62 panes serialise to depth 127 and 63 to 129, across serde_json's default limit of 128. So a session is capped at 62 panes for every client that shares `WireHost`, which is both of them, and the 63rd does not degrade a client -- it stops it attaching at all. Bracketed to the exact pane count rather than reported as a range.

THE GUARD ON THE POPULATED BRANCH IS THE REASON THE NUMBER IS RIGHT. A row that claims every pane is an agent waits until `session_agents` actually returns one per pane and SKIPS ITSELF otherwise, with a message. It fired twice while the fixture was wrong, both times printing `only 0 of N panes were claimed`, which is what sent me to the manifest instead of to the report.

TWO RUNS OF THE FULL BATTERY plus several partial ones, minima quoted, release only (the harness refuses a debug build -- R246 is why this project knows the difference matters here). At 62 panes: empty branch 0.93 to 1.26 us, populated 15.7 to 17.6 us. At 8 panes: 0.12 to 0.14 against 1.83 to 2.02.

NO RESOURCE LEAK, checked rather than reasoned: `WireHost` deliberately does not own its daemon's lifetime, so the harness reaps one the way `sprag kill-server` does -- kill every session, and a daemon with nothing left to serve exits. After a full run, no socket under the temp dir and no `sprag-term` alive.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0; the rustdoc gate at 16 crates (importing `HostClient` into `paint.rs` made two pre-existing fully-qualified links redundant, which the gate caught and which are now plain); the workspace suite 1585 passed / 0 failed, unchanged -- an instrument and an extraction, no test.
carry_forward_bullets: THE 62-PANE CEILING IS THE ROUND'S REAL FINDING AND IT IS OPEN. The repair is a decision, not a measurement: raise the client's limit with a configured `serde_json` deserializer, or flatten the layout's wire shape so depth stops tracking the pane count. The second removes the class rather than moving the number, and it touches the wire, so it wants a design. Nothing in the project reaches 62 panes today, which is exactly why it went unnoticed -- and why it will be found by a user rather than by a test unless a gate is put at the boundary.

THIRD ROUND RUNNING, THE THING THAT CAUGHT THE ERROR WAS THE HARNESS REPORTING ON ITSELF. R261: the sweeper's evaluation count exposed a condition that was not churning. R262: the reply-size check exposed a payload compared against an envelope. R263: a guard on the populated branch exposed a fixture that fingerprinted a pane without giving it a state. None of the three was caught by reading the harness.

AND READING CODE PREDICTS THE WRONG HALF. The N+1 locks and the N^2 scan are what `retitle` makes obvious, and they are the smaller term on a populated workspace; the string build is the larger. Every measurement in this arc has been worth more than the argument it replaced, but this is the first where the argument pointed at the wrong SUBJECT rather than at the wrong size.

NOTHING IS LEFT ON THE UNMEASURED LIST. The socket (R262), the sweep and its locks (R260, R261) and this walk are all priced. The next number this project wants is not on that list -- it is a gate at the 62-pane boundary, and a decision about the layout's wire shape.

STILL OWED, unchanged: the broken-manifest report path needs a GLOBAL wire fact plus a surface in each client; slice 4's reload latency and a reload on a PENDING candidate; slice 1's two measured misses.

R264.decision_summary: R264: the 62-pane ceiling, removed -- and the repair was not the choice R263 registered, because the two options were not independent. R263 found that a client cannot attach to a session of more than 62 panes and left the fix as a decision: configure the deserializer, or flatten the layout's wire shape. Reading the code first turned that into one option. The scope was larger than attach -- the same depth bites a client's layout WRITE and, worst, `load_snapshot`, which answers `None` on a parse error and turns a saved session into a silent empty boot, so a 63-pane session saved fine and restored as nothing. And `layout.rs` documented serde_json's recursion limit as the thing that kept `validate`/`adopt` from overflowing a stack, so raising the limit would not have moved a number, it would have deleted a stated safety property. That comment was also wrong in a second way it had never been read for: the in-process arm reaches the same code through `serde_json::from_value`, which has no recursion limit at all, so the protection was never universal. So: flatten the shape, and give the bound a name and a number instead of inheriting one from a parser. `LayoutWire` now serialises to an ARENA -- nodes naming their children by index -- at a constant depth of four whatever the pane count, and `LayoutNodeWire` LOST its serde derives so the nested spelling is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Flattening is not free and the price is paid in the same commit: an arena can express three things the nested form made impossible -- a dangling index, a node reached twice (a cycle, on which `adopt` loops forever, or a shared sub-tree, which duplicates panes), and an unreachable node whose panes would silently vanish -- and each is refused by name, by an ITERATIVE walk that runs before anything recursive touches the tree.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-terminal/src/layout.rs: hand-written `Serialize`/`Deserialize` for `LayoutWire` over a flat `{nodes, root}` arena; `LayoutNodeWire` loses its derives, so nothing can emit the nested shape by accident -- a structural bar rather than a convention, because one forgotten derive is all it takes to put the ceiling back. The in-memory type is unchanged, so no construction site in the GUI, the host or the tests churned.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/layout.rs: `MAX_LAYOUT_DEPTH` = 1024, enforced in the deserialiser -- the type's own gate, which every wire value passes and `from_value` no longer bypasses. `build_arena` walks ITERATIVELY to bound the depth and to reject a dangling index, a node reached twice and an unreachable node; only then does `nest` recurse, on a tree already proved shallow enough to walk.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/snapshot.rs + registry.rs: `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` 1 -> 2 with a new `MIN_READABLE_SNAPSHOT_VERSION`, and `from_snapshot` tests a RANGE rather than equality. A bump alone would have cost every user their saved sessions once; the legacy nested arrangement is still READ (`LegacyNode`), so a snapshot migrates by being loaded, while an older build still refuses a version-2 file loudly instead of parsing the header and dying on the layout.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: six tests pinned the wire shape LITERALLY and failed, which is what they are for. Read assertions now resolve through `root_node`/`child` helpers and the client-authored gestures are written flat -- so the host's accept-a-flat-write path is exercised by the tests that were already there.
crates/sprag-tui/examples/title-cost.rs + src/paint.rs: the ceiling was documented in R263 as live, in a doc comment, a constant's doc AND a line the harness PRINTS. All three corrected.
verification_bullets: THE GATE WENT RED FIRST AND IT REPRODUCED THE RECORDED BOUNDARY WITH NO DAEMON. Two tests: depth must not track the pane count (8 panes measured 18 against a 2-pane 6), and a client's own `serde_json::from_str` must parse the served reply at any count (63 panes: `recursion limit exceeded`). Both green after the flatten. The measured formula is `2N + 2` where R263 recorded `2N + 3`; the 62/63 boundary is identical, so the difference is one level of counting convention, not a disagreement -- recorded rather than quietly adopted.

THE DEPTH BOUND IS PROVED FROM BOTH SIDES, because a bound tested only from the rejecting side is indistinguishable from one set far too low. An arrangement at exactly `MAX_LAYOUT_DEPTH` is walked AND recursively built on an ordinary test thread; one level past it is refused with a message naming the bound. The accepting half is the evidence the constant was chosen with rather than asserted.

END-TO-END AGAINST A REAL DAEMON, not only in unit tests: `title-cost` at 63 and 100 panes -- 63 being the exact count that would not boot -- spawns a real `sprag-term`, attaches a real `WireHost` and reports every row. This is the same harness whose failure to boot at 64 found the ceiling in R263.

THE MALFORMED-ARENA REFUSALS ARE TESTED BY NAME, one case each, plus the fourth that fell out of writing them: nodes carried under a null root would have been silently dropped by the empty-arrangement arm, which is the same vanishing the unreachable-node check exists to prevent -- refusing it there but not here would have been a hole in that argument.

GATES GREEN. fmt clean; clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0; rustdoc gate at 16 crates; workspace suite 1585 -> 1591 passed / 0 failed, the six being this round's proofs. Two commits, `e2f2376` and `9e4b92f`, both through the pre-commit gates.
carry_forward_bullets: REMOVING THE CEILING RE-OPENED A VERDICT THAT RESTED ON IT. R263 concluded the per-paint title walk was worth documenting rather than fixing on TWO premises: the cost is small, and 62 was a count the wire could not exceed. The second is now gone, and the term is the one that GROWS -- re-measured here, the empty-branch walk goes 1.9 us at 63 panes to 3.8 us at 100, and the whole path 31.7 to 35.6 us. Still under one percent of a paint, so still not worth fixing, but the argument now has one leg instead of two and must be RE-TAKEN, not requoted, at a much larger count. A fix that removes a bound should be asked which conclusions were leaning on it.

THE REGISTERED CHOICE WAS NOT THE REAL ONE, and reading the code is what showed it. R263 left `configure the deserializer, or flatten the wire` as two options; the first would have deleted a documented stack-overflow bound that three recursive functions rely on, so there was one option and a hazard wearing the costume of the other. The same read found the scope was three sites rather than one, and that the worst of them SWALLOWS its error. A registered decision is a claim about the alternatives, and it gets read from the code like any other.

A PROTECTION NOBODY CHOSE IS A PROTECTION NOBODY CHECKED. `serde_json`'s recursion limit was load-bearing by accident, was documented as if deliberate, capped a user at 62 panes, and did not even cover the in-process path it claimed to. The class is worth watching for: a durable comment that names an EXTERNAL mechanism as a safety property, with no test that would fail if the mechanism stopped applying.

NOTHING REACHES 62 PANES TODAY, WHICH IS WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED FOR SO LONG, and the gates added here are unit-level for the same reason -- a boundary test that spawns 63 PTYs does not belong in a suite that runs on every commit. The end-to-end confirmation is an example run by hand. That is a deliberate split, not an omission, and it means a future regression would be caught by the depth test rather than by an attach.

STILL OWED, unchanged: the broken-manifest report path needs a GLOBAL wire fact plus a surface in each client; slice 4's reload latency and a reload on a PENDING candidate; slice 1's two measured misses.

R265.decision_summary: R265: the carry-forward R264 wrote was the wrong shape, and the owner's question -- "why defer it? ignoring cost, what is long-term correct?" -- is what turned it up. R264 measured the per-paint title walk, found it under a percent of a paint, and inherited R263's "documented, not fixed" with one premise repaired. Reading the code instead of the number found something else. The walk was `pane_ids()` then `pane_agent(id)` per id against a cache whose OWN DOC justified its addressing with "a linear scan over the small pane set" -- the premise R264 had removed one round earlier when it lifted the wire's 62-pane ceiling. So this was not a separate optimisation to schedule; it was the same expired bound one layer up. And the defect it hides is not cost: that cache is `Arc<Mutex<Vec<WirePane>>>` shared with the POLL THREAD, which replaces it wholesale, so a walk taking the lock N+1 times could pair one generation's pane list with another's verdicts -- a pane that closed drops silently out of the answer and one that opened is never asked about. The trait had already named this exact class three hundred lines above, in `pane_cells_and_token`: "One call rather than two, and that is the whole reason it exists", about a client that read the cells and then the token. The fix is that precedent applied where it was missed, plus the addressing repair the ceiling's removal made overdue: `PaneCache` owns the panes AND the index derived from them, both private behind one constructor, so an index that disagrees with its panes is not a bug to test for but a value that cannot be built.

R266.decision_summary: R266: the owner asked the same question twice, and the second time it was about a promise I had made and dropped inside the same conversation. R265's own plan said the third step was to key the title on a token and check the key's completeness in the code FIRST; R265 shipped the first two steps and closed the third by declaring the leftover string clone "the right cost", which is a scope cut wearing a decision's clothes. It was also a false dichotomy: owned clone versus a caller's closure under the lock are not the only options, and neither is the right question, because the correct answer is not to make the work cheaper but to STOP DOING IT when nothing it reads has moved. The title is derived from the pane verdicts and the session name, both of which the client already mirrors. So `HostClient::pane_agents_token` -- an `Option<u64>` whose `None` means "ask again", which is the treatment `WirePane::projection` already gives a frame's token in this same crate, and which makes the safe direction the default rather than a thing each impl must remember. AND THE FIRST VERSION OF IT WAS INERT, which is the round's real content: a token counting every cache REPLACEMENT is complete and useless, because `refresh_to_set` replaces the contents on every wake and a wake is what a pane echoing a keystroke causes -- so during the typing this was built to make cheap, the token would have moved on every single paint. Unit-green, dead in the binary, the exact failure this project has recorded three times. The token now tracks the AGENT PROJECTION its reader reads, and the test that would have caught the first version exists and was proved to catch it.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs: `HostClient::pane_agents_token() -> Option<u64>`, defaulting to `None`. An `Option` rather than a counter every impl fakes, because `None` means recompute: an impl that says nothing costs a caller work, and only one that actively claims a token can make a caller skip. The contract is stated in the direction a mistake has to fall.

crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: `PaneCache::replace` is now the ONE way contents change, and it moves `agents_generation` only when `same_agents` says the agent projection actually moved -- the ids in order and each verdict, which is exactly what `pane_agents` returns, so the two are defined together and cannot drift apart quietly.

crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: `get_mut` is GONE, replaced by `set_dims`. Handing out `&mut WirePane` would let a caller write `agent` and make the token a promise instead of a property; narrowing the write to the field it was always for makes that unrepresentable rather than forbidden. Same move as R264's derive removal and R265's private cache fields.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: `Painted::title_from` holds the token and the session the current title was derived from, and `retitle` returns before walking anything when neither moved. The doc names the two skips as different: `title_change` keeps an unchanged title off the WIRE and is downstream of building it; this one skips BUILDING it.
verification_bullets: THE FALSIFIER FOR THE INERT VERSION EXISTS AND WAS PROVED TO CATCH IT. `typing_into_a_pane_does_not_move_the_agent_token` feeds a wake in which the projection token and the frame move and the verdict does not; restoring the unconditional bump -- the version I first wrote -- fails exactly that test and nothing else. The mutated line was printed both ways.

AND THE OTHER DIRECTION IS PINNED TOO: `the_generation_moves_when_only_a_verdict_moved` changes a state with the pane SET identical, which is the change a key built from the pane list could not see and would have shown `working` for a pane that is now `blocked`, for ever, invisibly. Removing the bump from `replace` reddens both new tests and nothing else.

THE GATE'S OWN ARITHMETIC WAS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE MORE IMPORTANT FINDING. The summed total read one LOW twice. The cause is not flakiness: parallel test binaries interleave stdout, an anchored `grep '^test result'` drops a line that got a prefix, and the same drop would hide a FAILED target while the sum still reported zero failures. Counted unanchored, this round is 1596, not 1595. Every total this project has recorded that way is a lower bound.

SO THE SUITE WAS RE-RUN FOR ITS EXIT CODE rather than for a number scraped out of its output: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1596 passed / 0 failed. `cargo test` already answers this question and the pipeline was throwing the answer away.
GATES GREEN: fmt clean, clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features at 0, rustdoc gate 16 crates (it caught a public doc linking to a private item, twice).
carry_forward_bullets: A COMPLETE KEY AND A USEFUL KEY ARE DIFFERENT PROPERTIES, and R254's rule only asks for the first. "Every input is in the cache, so count the cache" is airtight against staleness and worthless against cost, because the cache also holds the frames -- the very thing that changes on the keystroke the skip was for. Ask a new cache key BOTH questions: what can make it stale, and what makes it move that its reader does not care about.

THE ANCHORED TEST-COUNT GREP IS A REAL HAZARD AND IS NOT FIXED IN ANY SCRIPT YET. `cargo test | grep '^test result'` can silently drop a target's line under parallel output, which means it can report zero failures for a run that had one. Read the EXIT CODE. Worth a pass over anything in `.githooks` or the round ritual that counts this way.

THE INHERITED "STILL OWED" LIST WAS CARRIED FOUR ROUNDS VERBATIM (R262 through R265, each saying "unchanged") and was re-derived from the code this round for the first time. The broken-manifest item is REAL and now priced exactly: `AgentFile::unusable()` captures the reason, `report_manifests` sends it to a `tracing::warn` nobody reads, a test at `config.rs:3231` says the reason is "kept for a surface", and there is no surface -- the only `unusable()` a client reads is the KEYMAP file's, in `sprag-gui/src/keys.rs`. The daemon silently falls back to built-in manifests. The shape is `global_commands`'s: render host-side, cross as a sentence, paint in each client.
STILL OWED, and re-derived rather than copied: the manifest report path above; slice 4's reload LATENCY and a reload on a PENDING candidate; slice 1's two measured misses.
