R267.decision_summary: R267: the broken-manifest report path, which R266 priced exactly and R257 had already re-aimed once. The defect is not that a report was missing but that the surface which sends a user to fix the file is the same surface that cannot tell them the file was refused: `sprag agent PANE` prints "no agent (no manifest claims this pane)" and then instructs the reader to write an `[[agent]]` block in config.toml -- which is exactly what a reader HAS written when the daemon refused their file and fell back to the last list that worked. `agent_explain` carries the same instruction to an agent. So the fact had to reach those surfaces, not merely exist. THE DESIGN QUESTION was where the answer comes from, and the neighbouring slot answers it the wrong way for this fact: `global_commands` re-reads its file on every call, and a manifest slot doing the same would be a SECOND AUTHORITY reporting on a first -- after a broken edit the rules in force are neither the built-ins nor the file's but the last ones that PARSED, and only the waker that did the re-read knows that. So the report is published by the daemon's own holder into the clock every client already reaches, and the slot is a lock and a clone rather than a disk read. AND THE PUBLISH SITE IS THE WHOLE OF IT: a broken edit REPLACES NOTHING, so `AgentManifests::refresh` answers `false`, so the natural place to publish -- beside the `reload`, inside `if replaced` -- would have covered every case except the one the report exists for. That version was written, mutated back in, and measured red. ALSO RE-DERIVED rather than inherited: R266 recorded the shape as "paint in each client", and the TUI has no surface to paint on and never had one -- `global_commands` does not reach it either.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry` holds the RENDERED sentence beside the ruleset it explains, and `set_manifest_report` is deliberately NOT folded into `reload`. The two move on different events -- a broken edit moves the report and leaves the ruleset alone -- so one call taking both would be published in the branch the report is never in. The type still reads no file and holds no path: it is handed the sentence exactly as it is handed the Ruleset.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: `adopt_manifests` is the ONE publisher, called at boot synchronously (before the socket mounts, so a request cannot race a thread that has not been scheduled) and on every sweep. The reload stays inside `if replaced`; the report is published outside it, which is the whole content of the function and is written out as such.

crates/sprag-host/src/wire.rs + workspace.rs: `AGENT_MANIFESTS_SLOT`, a FIXED slot answering `{error}` or `null` -- the shape its two config neighbours use, so a client that meets all three parses one thing. Unscoped, because the ruleset is the daemon's: scoping it would name a session for a fact no session owns. `agent_manifests_value` reads the clock; a host with no detector answers `null`, which is the same instruction to a client as a healthy file.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs + sprag-client/src/wire.rs: `HostClient::agent_manifest_report() -> Option<String>`, defaulting to `None` -- and the default IS the in-process arm's real answer, `pane_agent`'s treatment: the manifests are read by the daemon's waker, so a host without one holds no verdict rather than withholding one. Not `Result`-shaped, because the ruleset never crosses this wire and there is no success value to carry.

The three surfaces, each already telling a reader to edit that file: `sprag agent` prints the refusal FIRST and on STDERR (the rows are a shape scripts slice); `agent_explain` prefixes every answer with `manifest_caveat`, whose wording is split into a pure function so it is testable without a host; the GUI palette collects it as the fourth member of `config_errors`, beside the project's, the user commands' and the keymap's.
verification_bullets: THE PUBLISH SITE'S REVERT-PROOF IS THE ROUND'S CENTRAL PROOF, and it was run against the SHIPPED DAEMON over a real socket. `a_broken_agent_manifest_is_reported_and_the_report_clears_when_it_is_fixed` boots a daemon on a good config (null), breaks the file, and requires the sentence to appear from a sweep the test never asks for -- then requires it to CLEAR when the file is fixed. Moving the publish inside `if replaced` fails it with the message the test predicts: the daemon detects with the last good list and says nothing. Mutated line printed both ways; byte-restored.

A DOCUMENTED REVERT-PROOF WAS WRONG AND WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. The CLI test claimed `println!` in place of `eprintln!` would fail the STDOUT assertion. It does not: the sentence leaves the stream the EARLIER assertion reads, so that one fails first and the stdout claim is never exercised. The mutation that isolates it is printing to BOTH streams -- measured red on that assertion, naming the row it polluted. The doc now says so instead.

FOUR MORE REVERT-PROOFS, all red with the mutated line printed and the file byte-restored: drop the GUI's `errors.extend` and both new palette tests fail; drop `manifest_caveat()` from `agent_explain` and the live MCP gate fails, printing the trap verbatim ('no agent manifest claims this pane... add an `[[agent]]` block'); have the slot stop asking the clock and the middle reading returns to `null`; drop the CLI's query and the stderr assertion fails.

THE MCP HARNESS GREW AN ENV-TAKING SPAWN (`spawn_daemon_with`) so a test can point a daemon at a config of its own without touching the environment its parallel siblings read -- `wire_client`'s `spawn_host_with` one crate over, applied where R258 left it. The live gate is what proves the tool makes its second host call at all: nothing in the arguments asks for the caveat, so a wiring that never made the call would satisfy every unit test of the wording.

Read from the code, the missing thing was narrower and worse: two surfaces ALREADY EXISTED that instruct a reader to edit the very file being silently refused, so what was owed was not a place to put a message but a caveat on advice already being given. An item's cost is in what its absence makes other code SAY, not only in what it leaves unsaid.

THE TUI IS AN EXCLUSION AND IT IS PRICED. It has no surface for a global message and never had one -- `global_commands` does not reach it either, and R257 already rejected a status row with its cost (a row leaves the window, the client reports a smaller area, `window-size` re-arbitrates, every pane reflows). WHERE AN ANSWER COMES FROM IS PART OF ITS CORRECTNESS. The cheap version of this slot was `global_commands_value`'s -- re-read the file and report what it says. It would have been wrong in a way no test of the sentence could catch: it describes the FILE while the client needs to know about the RULESET IN FORCE, and after a broken edit those differ by exactly the fact that matters. Copying a neighbour's mechanism copies its premise; this one's premise is that the file IS the answer.

R267.publishable_decision_summary: R267: the broken-manifest report path, which R266 priced exactly and R257 had already re-aimed once. The defect is not that a report was missing but that the surface which sends a user to fix the file is the same surface that cannot tell them the file was refused: `sprag agent PANE` prints "no agent (no manifest claims this pane)" and then instructs the reader to write an `[[agent]]` block in config.toml -- which is exactly what a reader HAS written when the daemon refused their file and fell back to the last list that worked. `agent_explain` carries the same instruction to an agent. So the fact had to reach those surfaces, not merely exist. THE DESIGN QUESTION was where the answer comes from, and the neighbouring slot answers it the wrong way for this fact: `global_commands` re-reads its file on every call, and a manifest slot doing the same would be a SECOND AUTHORITY reporting on a first -- after a broken edit the rules in force are neither the built-ins nor the file's but the last ones that PARSED, and only the waker that did the re-read knows that. So the report is published by the daemon's own holder into the clock every client already reaches, and the slot is a lock and a clone rather than a disk read. AND THE PUBLISH SITE IS THE WHOLE OF IT: a broken edit REPLACES NOTHING, so `AgentManifests::refresh` answers `false`, so the natural place to publish -- beside the `reload`, inside `if replaced` -- would have covered every case except the one the report exists for. That version was written, mutated back in, and measured red. ALSO RE-DERIVED rather than inherited: R266 recorded the shape as "paint in each client", and the TUI has no surface to paint on and never had one -- `global_commands` does not reach it either.
publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry` holds the RENDERED sentence beside the ruleset it explains, and `set_manifest_report` is deliberately NOT folded into `reload`. The two move on different events -- a broken edit moves the report and leaves the ruleset alone -- so one call taking both would be published in the branch the report is never in. The type still reads no file and holds no path: it is handed the sentence exactly as it is handed the Ruleset.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: `adopt_manifests` is the ONE publisher, called at boot synchronously (before the socket mounts, so a request cannot race a thread that has not been scheduled) and on every sweep. The reload stays inside `if replaced`; the report is published outside it, which is the whole content of the function and is written out as such.

crates/sprag-host/src/wire.rs + workspace.rs: `AGENT_MANIFESTS_SLOT`, a FIXED slot answering `{error}` or `null` -- the shape its two config neighbours use, so a client that meets all three parses one thing. crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs + sprag-client/src/wire.rs: `HostClient::agent_manifest_report() -> Option<String>`, defaulting to `None` -- and the default IS the in-process arm's real answer, `pane_agent`'s treatment: the manifests are read by the daemon's waker, so a host without one holds no verdict rather than withholding one. R268.decision_summary: R268: the three items R254 and R250 left owed, resolved rather than carried, and all three turned out to be claims already written down and never checked. The reload LATENCY read as a law - five runs at 4.997-5.039 s against a 5 s sweep - until a control moved it: a 1.3 s sleep before the edit shifted every reading to 3.698-3.710 s, so arrival is the next sweep BOUNDARY and the clustering at 5.0 was the fixture's phase, which means this test reaches the worst case by construction because the settle step before the edit is itself published by the pass that precedes it. That is what finally proves the sentence underneath it, that the re-read runs BEFORE the walk so the panes an edit invalidates are served by the very pass that invalidated them; moved after, it costs exactly a second interval, 10.013 s measured. The PENDING-candidate case was untested rather than broken: the restart guard is right because the settle window absorbs a sampling artifact of the SCREEN and the screen has not moved, but every reload test so far used a SETTLED pane, so the guard had never been asked about the one input that reaches it by a different route. And slice 1's two measured misses were closable from data sitting in this crate's own test fixtures since slice 1: both onboarding screens NAME the product, in the sentence each prints to explain itself.

DIALOG_WINDOW replaces the literal 12, now that four matches in two manifests must agree about the region.

sprag-detect/src/track.rs: three tests for interactions nothing had asked about - a reload mid-transition keeping the window its candidate already served, a reload the pane disagrees with starting a fresh one, and the onboarding SEQUENCE, where the fingerprint reaches a screen the memory could not have been seeded from and the memory then reaches a screen no fingerprint can match.

sprag-host/tests/wire_client.rs: the reload latency contract asserted rather than described, carrying the measurement, the control that interpreted it, and why the bound is a ceiling rather than a description of where this fixture happens to sit.

sprag-detect/src/lib.rs docs: the bounds paragraph rewritten from what slice 1 predicted to what now holds, including the residue - codex's trust dialog names nothing, and the post-esc hint is NOT closed and NOT closable by the memory, whose is_active filter is a measured decision rather than an oversight.

sprag-host/src/config.rs: a test asserting a built-in's fingerprint COUNT against a literal now reads it from the built-in - the claim was that a correction leaves the fingerprints alone, and the literal stated an incidental fact that went red the round a built-in gained one.
verification_bullets: THE CONTROL IS WHAT MADE THE MEASUREMENT MEAN ANYTHING. Five runs at 4.997-5.039 s against a 5 s sweep reads as always one interval, which is a law. THE ORDERING REVERT-PROOF LANDED ON THE PREDICTED VALUE: moving the manifest re-read after sweep_once produced 10.013 s against a bound of 7.5 s, with the assertion naming the cause. Mutated block printed both ways, file byte-restored from a copy.

THE PENDING GUARD'S REVERT-PROOF TOOK A CO-CASUALTY AND IT IS NAMED. Making the restart unconditional fails the new mid-transition test AND a_pane_that_keeps_repainting_settles_when_the_candidate_has_held_long_enough. The guard was already load-bearing for a pane whose SCREEN keeps moving; what had never been asked is whether it holds when the RULE LIST moves. Same for the is_active filter: three red, two of them pre-existing.

A DOC CLAIM WRITTEN THIS ROUND WAS WRONG AND WAS CAUGHT BY READING THE CODE. The bounds paragraph first said the post-esc hint was closed by the identity memory. It is not: a remembered identity is asserted only for an ACTIVE verdict and an esc-ed pane is at rest. Corrected, and pinned by a test written from the STRUCTURE the miss follows from - and slice 1's claim that BOTH misses were asserted by tests covered only one.

THE CAPTURE ENVIRONMENT IS A TRAP AND IS NOW ASSERTED. The codex trust-dialog fixture was captured under a path containing the string claude, so a fingerprint written on the bare NAME rather than on a phrase would read a codex pane as claude on any box whose scratch directory is named that way. The test asserts the string IS there and that the fingerprint does not fire on it.

carry_forward_bullets: A NUMBER THAT LOOKS LIKE A CONSTANT NEEDS A CONTROL THAT MOVES IT. Five identical readings are the most convincing possible evidence for the wrong conclusion: they say the mechanism is deterministic without saying WHICH mechanism. Perturb the one variable the hypothesis calls irrelevant and see whether the number follows. It did, by exactly the shift.

THE OWED ITEM WAS THE COMMENT, NOT THE CODE. All three resolved into claims already written down and never checked: an edit lands within one sweep, the re-read runs before the walk, both misses are asserted by tests. None was a missing feature and one of the three was false. When a carry-forward names a behaviour, look first for the sentence that already asserts it.

THE ANSWER TO A MEASUREMENT DEBT WAS IN THE FIXTURES. Slice 1 recorded the onboarding miss as needing a title-free fingerprint and left it, and the screens it captured to RECORD the miss carried the agent's own name in plain text. A test fixture is a measurement and can be read for more than the assertion it was written for.

The two residues - a resting pane that has lost its fingerprint, and a trust dialog that names nobody as a pane's FIRST screen - are properties of the screens rather than of this crate. Nothing else from H3 is owed.

R269.decision_summary: R269: herdr re-audited at source (its HEAD 26a7bc86, not a README), which moved sprag from 22 of 116 surface items to 36 and left 80 — and then the largest single block of those, 28 items of event stream, was built. THE RE-AUDIT'S FINDING is that the gap is not what its own title says: sprag ALREADY parks on scene/waitFor and already long-polls, so the mechanism exists and the INFORMATION does not. A woken client learns one number and re-reads the window list, the pane set and every pane in it to rediscover a change the daemon already knew, and a client that is not a display client cannot use the wake at all. So H6 is not a push transport; it is giving the wake a payload. THE DESIGN QUESTION was where a typed event can come from without a per-handler rule, because pinion bumps the revision inside its own dispatcher and sprag never writes that line — so there is no site to append at, and appending in each handler restores exactly the discipline notify.rs was built to remove. The answer is that dispatch_one's non-waitFor arm is the ONE place every mutating method passes, so the events are DERIVED there by diffing a cheap session shape, while the one event a dispatch cannot see — the agent verdict, which rests on the screen and on a clock nothing else runs — is EMITTED by the settle waker that already computes it. AND THE CURSOR IS THE SCENE REVISION, which is what collapsed the slice list from six to five: a client already parks on that token, so scene/waitFor IS the blocking read and herdr's two methods become one query field here.
changes_bullets: "sprag-host/src/events.rs (NEW): the change LOG behind a wake — a bounded ring whose cursor is the SCENE REVISION and never a counter of its own (pinion's waiter carries the scar: a private counter forked the version namespace). A group of records lands whole or not at all, because `record` takes the group and a reader takes the same lock, so a torn read is unrepresentable rather than forbidden. An event names its SUBJECT and never carries the new value: copying `PaneInfo`'s fifteen fields here would be a second definition of a pane's public shape, and a copied value is stale the instant a later mutation lands while an id stays true.",

"sprag-host/src/events.rs `SessionShape`: the structural fingerprint the diff is taken over — window names, current, layout_revision, sorted pane ids under one registry lock plus one workspace lock per window. `SessionJournal` binds the shape and the log behind ONE lock, so two observers cannot diff against the same predecessor and record one change twice.",

"sprag-host/src/rpc.rs: THE DERIVE SITE — one diff in `dispatch_one`'s non-waitFor arm, which is the single place every mutating wire method passes through. A method added later records what it changed without a line of its own, which is the structural property `notify`'s WAKE already had, extended to the wake's PAYLOAD.",

"sprag-host/src/wire.rs + workspace.rs: `EVENTS_FIELD = parametric(\"events.<since>\", …)`, served by `query` off `literal_prefix` and answering `{events, next, lost}`. A malformed member of an advertised family is `Null`, never absence — `cells.<offset>`'s taxonomy. `lost` travels even when false: it is a SAFETY answer, and a peer that cannot see the key would read a hole as a clean read.",

"sprag-host/src/sweep.rs + notify.rs: the settle waker EMITS `AgentStateChanged` for the panes whose `seq` moved — the same condition it already uses to decide whether to wake a session at all, so the record and the wake cannot disagree. `ChannelRegistry::announce` holds the journal lock ACROSS the bump, because the bump fires the wake synchronously and a record appended after it is one the woken client can race.",

"sprag CLI `events [-t SESSION] [--since N] [-f]` + MCP `wait_for_change {timeout_seconds}`: the capability, reachable. `-f` parks and prints, which is the shape `sprag events -f | while read` needs; the MCP tool replaces a poll loop with a park and holds its cursor as PROCESS state, because \"what changed\" is meaningless without \"since when\"."
verification_bullets: "THE ARC'S CENTRAL PROOF, and it is a NEGATIVE one: `a_spawned_pane_is_reported_without_the_action_emitting_anything`. The spawn action mentions no log, no module, and no event, and a pane appearing is still reported. Revert-proof: remove the `observe` call from `dispatch_one` and it goes red while `typing_into_a_pane_records_nothing` stays green — the site is load-bearing AND does not pollute the input path.",

"A CARRY-FORWARD I WROTE AS A CLAIM WAS FALSE, AND THE TEST CAUGHT IT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. The first shape gated the pane walk on each window's `layout_revision`. Measured: a spawn takes panes 1 to 2 and the revision 0 to 2 with `layout_rev` STILL 0. The number means a client's PROJECTION is stale, not that the pane set moved — its own docs say so — and a spawn reconciles the tree lazily. The gate was reading a real number for a question it does not answer; the carry-forward is gone.",

"READING MUST NOT BUMP, MEASURED RATHER THAN CLASSIFIED. Serving `events.<since>` from `invoke` instead of `query` makes one read advance the revision by exactly +1 (left: 2, right: 1) — the R152 livelock's mechanism, and worse here because reading events would generate events. Proven over a real socket against the shipped daemon, with the mutation applied to the daemon and byte-restored after.",

"THE FOLLOW LOOP HAD A BUG A MANUAL DRIVE DID NOT CATCH. `cursor = woken[revision]` skips whatever was recorded AT that revision, and the read is strictly greater so it is never offered again. It survived by luck: a spawn bumps TWICE, so the record lands above the wait's answer. It would have lost every agent transition, which `announce` publishes with a SINGLE bump. Regression test uses that case; with the bug restored it TIMES OUT at 30 s while the non-follow test stays green.",

"THE LIVE MCP GATE CAUGHT WHAT NO WORDING TEST COULD (R258's lesson). Nothing in `wait_for_change`'s arguments asks for a park or a cursor, so a wiring that made neither host call would satisfy every unit test. Driven against a real daemon it failed at once with `Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)`: a Linux socket read timeout is EAGAIN/`WouldBlock`, not `TimedOut`, so every quiet wait was being reported as a tool FAILURE.",

"THE DERIVE SITE'S COST, MEASURED WHERE THE DESIGN ARGUED. The design priced it \"user actions are infrequent\" and that was already false: `key`/`text`/`paste`/`mouse` are invokes, so this runs at TYPING rate. sprag-latency, release, three runs, no change to find: 0.121-0.142 us at one pane, 0.651-0.754 us at 64 — about 9-10 ns per pane, ~0.015% of one keystroke against R246's ~5 ms. NOT claimed: this is one window; a multi-window session takes one workspace lock each and no row measures that.",

"GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1610 to 1627 passed / 0 failed (+17 = exactly this arc), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0, rustdoc gate 16 crates (it caught a module doc still linking the deleted `PaneUpdated`), T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 116/116. Two in-tree list tests had to learn the new tool; the suite found both."
carry_forward_bullets: "AN INHERITED 'NOT DELIVERED' COST THE DESIGN A WHOLE SEAM, AND THE OWNER CAUGHT IT, NOT ME. R269.publishable_decision_summary: R269: herdr re-audited at source (its HEAD 26a7bc86, not a README), which moved sprag from 22 of 116 surface items to 36 and left 80 — and then the largest single block of those, 28 items of event stream, was built. THE RE-AUDIT'S FINDING is that the gap is not what its own title says: sprag ALREADY parks on scene/waitFor and already long-polls, so the mechanism exists and the INFORMATION does not. A woken client learns one number and re-reads the window list, the pane set and every pane in it to rediscover a change the daemon already knew, and a client that is not a display client cannot use the wake at all. So H6 is not a push transport; it is giving the wake a payload. THE DESIGN QUESTION was where a typed event can come from without a per-handler rule, because pinion bumps the revision inside its own dispatcher and sprag never writes that line — so there is no site to append at, and appending in each handler restores exactly the discipline notify.rs was built to remove. The answer is that dispatch_one's non-waitFor arm is the ONE place every mutating method passes, so the events are DERIVED there by diffing a cheap session shape, while the one event a dispatch cannot see — the agent verdict, which rests on the screen and on a clock nothing else runs — is EMITTED by the settle waker that already computes it. AND THE CURSOR IS THE SCENE REVISION, which is what collapsed the slice list from six to five: a client already parks on that token, so scene/waitFor IS the blocking read and herdr's two methods become one query field here.
publishable_changes_bullets: "sprag-host/src/events.rs (NEW): the change LOG behind a wake — a bounded ring whose cursor is the SCENE REVISION and never a counter of its own (pinion's waiter carries the scar: a private counter forked the version namespace). A group of records lands whole or not at all, because `record` takes the group and a reader takes the same lock, so a torn read is unrepresentable rather than forbidden. An event names its SUBJECT and never carries the new value: copying `PaneInfo`'s fifteen fields here would be a second definition of a pane's public shape, and a copied value is stale the instant a later mutation lands while an id stays true.",

"sprag-host/src/events.rs `SessionShape`: the structural fingerprint the diff is taken over — window names, current, layout_revision, sorted pane ids under one registry lock plus one workspace lock per window. `SessionJournal` binds the shape and the log behind ONE lock, so two observers cannot diff against the same predecessor and record one change twice.",

"sprag-host/src/rpc.rs: THE DERIVE SITE — one diff in `dispatch_one`'s non-waitFor arm, which is the single place every mutating wire method passes through. A method added later records what it changed without a line of its own, which is the structural property `notify`'s WAKE already had, extended to the wake's PAYLOAD.",

"sprag-host/src/wire.rs + workspace.rs: `EVENTS_FIELD = parametric(\"events.<since>\", …)`, served by `query` off `literal_prefix` and answering `{events, next, lost}`. A malformed member of an advertised family is `Null`, never absence — `cells.<offset>`'s taxonomy. `lost` travels even when false: it is a SAFETY answer, and a peer that cannot see the key would read a hole as a clean read.",

"sprag-host/src/sweep.rs + notify.rs: the settle waker EMITS `AgentStateChanged` for the panes whose `seq` moved — the same condition it already uses to decide whether to wake a session at all, so the record and the wake cannot disagree. `ChannelRegistry::announce` holds the journal lock ACROSS the bump, because the bump fires the wake synchronously and a record appended after it is one the woken client can race.",

"sprag CLI `events [-t SESSION] [--since N] [-f]` + MCP `wait_for_change {timeout_seconds}`: the capability, reachable. `-f` parks and prints, which is the shape `sprag events -f | while read` needs; the MCP tool replaces a poll loop with a park and holds its cursor as PROCESS state, because \"what changed\" is meaningless without \"since when\"."
publishable_verification_bullets: "THE ARC'S CENTRAL PROOF, and it is a NEGATIVE one: `a_spawned_pane_is_reported_without_the_action_emitting_anything`. Revert-proof: remove the `observe` call from `dispatch_one` and it goes red while `typing_into_a_pane_records_nothing` stays green — the site is load-bearing AND does not pollute the input path.",

"A CARRY-FORWARD I WROTE AS A CLAIM WAS FALSE, AND THE TEST CAUGHT IT BEFORE IT SHIPPED. The first shape gated the pane walk on each window's `layout_revision`. Measured: a spawn takes panes 1 to 2 and the revision 0 to 2 with `layout_rev` STILL 0. The number means a client's PROJECTION is stale, not that the pane set moved — its own docs say so — and a spawn reconciles the tree lazily. The gate was reading a real number for a question it does not answer; the carry-forward is gone.",

"READING MUST NOT BUMP, MEASURED RATHER THAN CLASSIFIED. Serving `events.<since>` from `invoke` instead of `query` makes one read advance the revision by exactly +1 (left: 2, right: 1) — the R152 livelock's mechanism, and worse here because reading events would generate events. Proven over a real socket against the shipped daemon, with the mutation applied to the daemon and byte-restored after.",

"THE FOLLOW LOOP HAD A BUG A MANUAL DRIVE DID NOT CATCH. `cursor = woken[revision]` skips whatever was recorded AT that revision, and the read is strictly greater so it is never offered again. It survived by luck: a spawn bumps TWICE, so the record lands above the wait's answer. It would have lost every agent transition, which `announce` publishes with a SINGLE bump. Regression test uses that case; with the bug restored it TIMES OUT at 30 s while the non-follow test stays green.",

"THE LIVE MCP GATE CAUGHT WHAT NO WORDING TEST COULD (R258's lesson). Nothing in `wait_for_change`'s arguments asks for a park or a cursor, so a wiring that made neither host call would satisfy every unit test. Driven against a real daemon it failed at once with `Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)`: a Linux socket read timeout is EAGAIN/`WouldBlock`, not `TimedOut`, so every quiet wait was being reported as a tool FAILURE.",

"THE DERIVE SITE'S COST, MEASURED WHERE THE DESIGN ARGUED. R270.decision_summary: R270: H's agent PUSH path, slice 1 — a pane's child is now told which pane it is in and where the daemon serving it listens, which is the fact every later half of that path rests on. THE RE-READ THAT SET THE SHAPE: sprag's one pane-spawn assembly site (sprag-terminal::command) sets TERM and nothing else, so a process inside a pane could be driven and scraped but could not name itself; herdr's hook, read at its own HEAD, is inert without exactly this (HERDR_ENV / HERDR_SOCKET_PATH / HERDR_PANE_ID, each absent meaning exit 0), and its 15 installable integrations all rest on the same three variables its `apply_pane_base_env` publishes. THE DESIGN PROBLEM was that the funnel and the fact were in different types: this crate owns the only two places a pane is born, but a Workspace does not know its session, and the pane id was minted AFTER the spawn — a child cannot be told a number that does not exist yet, since an environment is fixed at exec. The answer is a PaneEnvSource handed the PaneId and nothing else, consulted at both births, with the id reserved BEFORE the spawn; the session name is deliberately absent because an id is unique across the whole registry and a session name stored per pool would be a second authority that `sibling` copies — `new_session` builds its first pool as a sibling of the DEFAULT session's, so every pane of every later session would have published the wrong name. The daemon (the site that also mounts the endpoint) installs the concrete source, so publishing an address stays a promise to serve it and the GUI's in-process host publishes nothing.
changes_bullets: sprag-terminal/src/workspace.rs: `PaneEnvSource` (`Arc<dyn Fn(PaneId) -> Vec<(String, String)>`), modelled on `HistoryLimitSource` and consulted at BOTH birth sites (`spawn_with_dirty`, `spawn_restored`) so a caller cannot forget it. It returns PAIRS rather than editing the `CommandBuilder`: a closure handed the builder could change the program, and the authority a source needs is strictly 'add these variables'. Default publishes NOTHING, so a standalone pool and every unit test spawn exactly as before, and a child that finds no variable correctly concludes there is nobody to report to.

sprag-terminal/src/workspace.rs: the pane id is now minted BEFORE the spawn rather than after, because the id travels in the child's environment. The COST is stated rather than avoided — a failed birth consumes an id where it used to leave the counter untouched — and it is affordable because ids need uniqueness and monotonicity, not density: a snapshot stores the high-water mark rather than deriving it from live ids. Peeking the counter and minting after would let the published id and the pane's id disagree under a concurrent spawn, which this ordering makes unrepresentable.

sprag-terminal/src/registry.rs: `set_pane_env_source`, the registry-wide install, beside the history-limit one and for its reasons — seeding what exists now covers every window later made from it, because `sibling` inherits.

sprag-host/src/host.rs: `PANE_ENV_VAR = SPRAG_PANE` (tmux's `TMUX_PANE`; the value is the `id` every pane-addressing wire method takes) and `pane_env_source(&Path)`, which publishes that plus the endpoint under `HOST_SOCKET.path_env` rather than a second spelling of `SPRAG_HOST_RPC_SOCK` — so a client's override and this publication cannot drift. `Host::with_pane_env` installs and HOLDS it; `restore` re-installs on the pools it replaces.

sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs: the daemon installs it with the `sock` it resolved once for its own mount, so what a pane is told and what is bound cannot differ, and the module doc now states the pane contract where the socket policy is stated.
verification_bullets: THE PROOFS READ THE CHILD, NOT THE BUILDER. Every assertion here spawns a pane whose command PRINTS the variable and reads it back off the emulator's screen — a test that inspected the `CommandBuilder` would pass on a wiring that never reached an `exec`. Each is read TWICE with the input changed (two panes, each printing its own id), so a source consulted once and reused, or handed the wrong id, fails the second assertion while passing the first.

THREE REVERT-PROOFS RUN, NOT WRITTEN, each turning exactly one test red while its siblings stayed green. (1) Drop `with_pane_env` from `sprag-term`'s main: the new wire test fails and the other 33 in that file pass — the wiring is load-bearing and the test is not passing for another reason. (2) Drop the `set_pane_env_source` from `Host::restore`: `a_restored_pane_is_told_which_pane_it_is` fails while the other 13 restore tests pass, which is the asymmetry precisely — a pane unable to name itself ONLY after a reboot. (3) Make `sibling` default instead of inheriting: the sibling test fails alone. Files byte-restored from copies, never `git checkout`.

THE END-TO-END TEST IS THE ONLY THING THAT COULD SEE THE DAEMON'S WIRING (R258's lesson): a `Host` built without `with_pane_env` satisfies every unit test in the file, and a pane spawned by such a daemon looks identical from outside. It boots a real `sprag-term`, has the boot pane print both variables, and reads them back over the socket — taking the pane id from the same `panes` list a client reads rather than assuming 0, so the two cannot agree by coincidence.

AND ITS FIRST RUN FAILED FOR A REASON WORTH RECORDING: both values HAD reached the child, but the harness boots a 40-COLUMN pane and a temp-dir socket path is longer, so the emulator wrapped the line mid-path (`…/sprag-wire-it-0.so\nck`). The wrap is the terminal's, not the child's; the match now strips row breaks and says why. A screen is not a string.

WHAT IS ASSERTED AND WHAT IS NOT, since the harness lacks a control for half of it. `SPRAG_PANE` is a proof of INJECTION — nothing in the test process's environment sets it. The ADDRESS is asserted for agreement only: this harness hands the daemon `SPRAG_HOST_RPC_SOCK` to control its socket path, so the child would inherit the same string either way. That the source publishes it under the variable a client overrides is pinned where a control exists, against `HOST_SOCKET.path_env` rather than a literal — a literal would keep passing if the policy renamed its override, which is the drift that would leave a child pointed at a variable nobody honours.

GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1629 to 1639 passed / 0 failed (+10 = exactly this slice), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0 across all targets, rustdoc gate 16 crates, T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 116/116. Both commits passed pre-commit.
carry_forward_bullets: THE FUNNEL AND THE FACT WERE IN DIFFERENT TYPES, AND THE ANSWER WAS TO SHRINK THE FACT. The obvious shape — give a pool its session name so a pane can publish it — is the one that breaks, and it breaks SILENTLY: `SessionRegistry::new_session` builds a new session's first pool as a `sibling` of the DEFAULT session's, so every pane of every session created after boot would publish the wrong name, with nothing to fail. Handing the source only the id makes `sibling` inheritance correct instead of dangerous, and the session stays derivable because an id is unique across the registry. When a seam needs a fact its type does not hold, ask whether the fact is needed at all before threading it.

A COMMENT NAMED A PROPERTY THAT NOTHING TESTED, AND CHANGING IT WAS THE RIGHT MOVE. `spawn_with_dirty` minted the id after a successful spawn to keep the counter 'gap-free on failure' — a documented compatibility nicety with no test anywhere that would fail if it stopped applying (the class R264 named). The environment needs the id before the child exists, so the ordering flipped and the cost is now asserted BY a test: a failed birth consumes an id. The lesson is not that such comments are wrong, it is that their cost is unknown until something asks for the other ordering.

STILL OWED ON THIS PATH, and named so a later round does not read this slice as the whole of it: the identity is published and nothing CONSUMES it yet. The report methods (herdr spends five: `report_agent`, `report_agent_session`, `report_metadata`, `release_agent`, `clear_agent_authority`) and the AUTHORITY LADDER they need — a reported state outranking a scraped one, with `seq` freshness per source — are slice 2, and the hook INSTALLER that writes into an agent's own config directory is slice 3. Slice 3 writes under the user's HOME, which is a kind of side effect nothing in this tree does today; it is an owner decision, not a technical one.

THE RE-AUDIT DOC OVERCOUNTED herdr's installable integrations as 16. Its source says 15 (`IntegrationTarget::ALL: [Self; 15]`, and 15 asset directories); the 19 detection manifests are right, and the two numbers are different sets — 19 agents can be RECOGNISED, 15 can be INSTRUMENTED. Read a rival's count from its enum, not from a directory listing that happens to include a test file.

R271.decision_summary: R271: the agent PUSH path, slice 2 — a process inside a pane can now REPORT what it is doing, that report outranks anything the screen argues, and a release gives the pane back. THE DESIGN QUESTION was where the report may live, and the answer is decided by what already rests on the tracker's `seq`: the sweep's wake condition, the pane list's change detection and R269's journal all read "the published verdict moved" from one place, so a report kept beside the tracker would have been a second definition of a published change and the two would have drifted. So the report is a SECOND KIND OF EVIDENCE inside `sprag-detect`'s Tracker, which owns the published verdict — and it skips the settle window, because hysteresis exists for a property of SCREENS (a resting verdict rests on the absence of an animated signal, so an absence may be an artifact of the instant a sample was taken) and a process saying what it is doing is not a sample. THE EXPIRY IS NOT A CLOCK: herdr's own `HookAuthority` has no TTL either, and the thing that expires is the REPORTER, so a report is dropped when the pane's CHILD exits — which the daemon can see, and which is exactly the case a hook cannot cover because a killed process runs no hook. Freshness is per SOURCE: a reporter's `seq` is its own monotonic clock, so comparing across sources would let one integration's numbering silence another's, and a pane runs one agent, so the newest speaker owns the pane while a replay from the speaker already talking is refused. Reachable as two wire actions (herdr spends five), and as `sprag report-agent working` inside a pane, which is what slice 1's `SPRAG_PANE` was published for.
changes_bullets: sprag-detect/src/track.rs: `Tracker::report` / `release_report` / `reported_source` / `owes_look` — the authority, held where the published verdict and its `seq` already live. `observe` returns early for a reported pane AFTER refreshing the quiescence memory, so a reported pane is CHEAP rather than merely overruled: it runs no rules, and with the screen and the ruleset both recorded as seen it is neither stale nor skipped-with-a-lie, so it owes nothing until it reports again. `release` clears that memory, which is what makes the release take effect — without it a pane whose screen has not moved since the report is skipped by the exact-skip and keeps publishing a report nobody stands behind.

sprag-detect/src/lib.rs: `AgentState::from_wire`, `wire_str`'s inverse, so the vocabulary has ONE definition and a reporter cannot introduce a spelling a client could not read. `unknown` is REFUSED on purpose — it is a conclusion about the RULES rather than a state a reporter is in, and a reporter that no longer knows is asking to be scraped, which is a release.

sprag-host/src/agent.rs: `AgentRegistry::report` / `release` / `reported` / `owes_look` / `any_owes_look`, and RELEASED as the fourth reason in `owes_evaluation` — served on ANY wake rather than only a sweep, because a release is one pane's own event and invalidates its whole published state, where a ruleset edit is bulk and unhurried. `AgentClock::release` SIGNALS the parked waker: this is the arrival `AgentClock::observe`'s own docs anticipated, work asked for from another thread. `AgentFacts::source` publishes WHO said so, additively — a reported verdict carries no rule and a scraped one carries no source.

sprag-host/src/workspace.rs + wire.rs: `report_agent {id, source, state, name?, seq?}` → `{accepted, changed, seq}` and `release_agent {id}` → `{released}`. The report announces `agent_state_changed` only when the verdict MOVED — the same condition the settle waker uses, so the two publishers of an agent verdict cannot come to disagree about what a change is — and a pane the daemon does not hold is refused rather than remembered, or a reporter with a stale `SPRAG_PANE` would create a tracker nothing could ever prune.

sprag-host/src/sweep.rs: a pane whose child has EXITED loses its report, checked as one atomic `is_eof` per pane with the agent lock taken only when it holds. The same pass then re-derives the verdict, because the release makes the pane owe a look.

sprag CLI: `report-agent STATE [--pane N] [--source S] [--name AGENT] [--seq N]` and `release-agent`, both defaulting the pane to `$SPRAG_PANE` — so an agent's hook is `sprag report-agent working` with no argument to discover, which is what slice 1 published that variable for. The vocabulary is refused client-side, with `unknown` pointed at `release-agent`, and a refused replay is printed rather than exiting 0 on a report that vanished.
verification_bullets: THE LIVE TEST WAS A FALSE INSTRUMENT TWICE, AND THE REVERT-PROOF IS WHAT CAUGHT IT. First draft polled the pane list for the corrected verdict — but a pane-list query OBSERVES every pane it describes, so the test served the release itself and passed with the daemon's waker gutted. Second draft parked on `scene/waitFor` instead: also worthless, because pinion bumps the scene revision inside its own dispatcher, so the release's own invoke wakes the park whatever the daemon does. The third watches the JOURNAL (`events.<since>` is a query, so it reads the log and observes no pane), which only the waker's pass can move after a release. Two mutations now bite it: dropping `any_owes_look` from the waker's guard, and dropping the notify from `AgentClock::release`.

FIVE REVERT-PROOFS RUN, each red alone. (1) The guard without the released reason — live test fails. (2) The release without its signal — live test AND `a_release_wakes_a_parked_waker` fail. (3) The authority check out of `observe` — the screen overrules a report, two detect tests fail. (4) The EOF release out of the sweep — `a_report_dies_with_the_process_that_made_it` fails. (5) The announce out of `report_agent` — the report publishes without recording, and the wire test reads an empty journal.

THE CHEAPNESS CLAIM IS MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. `a_reported_pane_costs_no_evaluation` reads `sprag_detect::work`'s evaluation counter across one observe of a reported pane whose SCREEN HAS MOVED (so the quiescence gate is not what is being measured) and asserts the delta is zero — with the control that the same moved screen DOES cost an evaluation once the pane is released.

A TEST FOUND A DEFECT IN THE DESIGN BEFORE IT SHIPPED. Routing a report through the tracker's own `publish` runs its identity-clearing rule, so a `claude` pane whose hook reported `idle` WITHOUT repeating the name would come back from a release as nobody at all. A report that names an agent now SETS the identity and one that does not leaves it, the verdict falling back to what the pane already was — the same asymmetry `evaluate` already keeps, where the memory answers about WHO and never about what.

THE CLI IS TESTED AS A SURFACE, against a real daemon: the `$SPRAG_PANE` default, the error that names that variable when there is none, `unknown` refused client-side with `release-agent` named, a report reaching `sprag agent`'s reading of the pane list, a replay printed as REFUSED, and the second release saying there was nothing left to drop.

GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1639 to 1658 passed / 0 failed (+19 = exactly this slice), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0 all targets, rustdoc gate 16 crates (it caught a public doc linking to a private `consider`), T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 116/116.
carry_forward_bullets: A NEW AUTHORITY MUST ENTER WHERE THE OLD ONE PUBLISHES. The report's home was not a preference: the sweep's wake condition, the pane list's change detection and R269's journal all read 'the published verdict moved' from the tracker's `seq`, so a report held beside the tracker would have been a second definition of a published change — and the failure would have been silent, since every individual verdict still looks right. When adding a second source of truth, find what already reads the first one's CHANGE and enter there.

A BOUND IS AN INSTRUMENT ONLY IF SOMETHING ELSE CANNOT PRODUCE THE SAME OBSERVATION. Both false drafts of the live test measured a real thing that the daemon was not responsible for — the client's own observation, then pinion's own dispatcher bump. `Ask what ELSE produces the same number` applies to a WAKE as much as to a duration, and the only way this was settled was by mutating the daemon and watching the test stay green.

A BYTE-RESTORE IS ONLY AS GOOD AS WHEN THE COPY WAS TAKEN. Restoring `agent.rs` from a backup made before a later test was added silently DELETED that test, and the suite total was the only witness — 17 tests added, +16 measured. Re-take the copy after every change, or diff the restore against the working tree rather than trusting it.

THE EXPIRY QUESTION HAD A DERIVABLE ANSWER, AND READING THE RIVAL IS WHAT FOUND IT. A TTL for a report needs a number nobody can justify. herdr's `HookAuthority` has none either — it tracks the process's EXIT — and sprag can see exactly that, one atomic load per pane. The residue is named rather than hidden: an agent running as a GRANDCHILD (a shell that spawned it) can be killed while the pane's own child lives, and that report stands until something releases it. herdr has the same exposure.

STILL OWED ON THIS PATH: slice 3, the hook INSTALLER that writes into an agent's own config directory (herdr ships 15 installable targets). It writes under the user's HOME, which nothing in this tree does today — an owner decision, not a technical one. DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT here, with the reason: the agent SESSION id and token metadata herdr carries on its own report methods, because sprag has no resume feature and no token surface to consume them, so publishing them would be fields nothing reads.

R272.decision_summary: R272: the agent PUSH path, slice 3a — the hook INSTALLER, which is the first thing in this tree to write under the user's HOME, into a file it did not create. THE OWNER'S THREE DECISIONS SHAPED IT: preserve what is there, support uninstall, always ask. THE FIRST DESIGN MOVE was to drop the rival's shell script entirely. herdr installs one because its report carries a session id, a transcript path and a token count and its hook assembles them with python3; sprag's report is one verb with no metadata (slice 2's deliberate shrink), so a script buys nothing and costs a mode bit, a Windows twin, a second artifact to version, and an interpreter dependency whose absence makes an install SUCCEED and then report nothing forever. The agent's config names this binary directly. BUT THE PAYLOAD STILL HAS TO BE READ, and that is the rival-reading that paid: two payloads must be ignored rather than mapped — one carrying an `agent_id` (a subagent's event, not the pane's) and `SubagentStop`, a completion event that can arrive after the pane's own turn has stopped. This matters MORE here than there, because slice 2 made a report outrank the screen: a bad scrape is corrected by the next sweep, a bad report stands until something releases it. ONE TABLE SERVES BOTH READERS — the events an install writes and the mapping a payload is judged by are the same `Target::events`, so the state a hook reports can be corrected by a new sprag release WITHOUT rewriting the user's file, which is what a version ladder in the installed footprint would otherwise be for. WHAT "PRESERVE" ACTUALLY MEANT was the round's real cost: not "do not clobber other keys" (a parse/edit/serialise round trip already does that) but comment, ORDER and LAYOUT — the property herdr spends 870 hand-written lines of YAML and TOML line surgery on.
changes_bullets: Cargo.toml: `serde_json` gains `preserve_order`. Without it `Map` is a `BTreeMap`, so reading and rewriting an agent's `settings.json` ALPHABETISES every object in a file sprag does not own — the revert-proof shows the user's own `matcher` sorting behind `hooks` and `type` behind `command`. The blast radius is named rather than assumed: maps serialise in insertion order instead of alphabetically, which no consumer in this tree reads and JSON-RPC does not define.

sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: `Target` (name, label, agent, dir, file, events) as DATA, so a further agent is a further const rather than further code; `CLAUDE` wired to `~/.claude/settings.json` across six events; `report_for` deciding what a payload means; `plan_install` / `plan_uninstall` / `status` deriving an edit without applying it, and `Plan::apply` writing it with a `.sprag-backup` copy of anything it did not create. Indentation is read from the file's own first indent and re-emitted, so a four-space config comes back four-space.

sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: sprag's entry always sits in a group of its OWN. Not tidiness — a hook group can carry a `matcher` that filters every entry inside it, so joining an existing group would silently narrow the integration to whatever that group matched, with no symptom but a pane that stops reporting. It also makes the uninstall exact: a whole group it is sure of, rather than an entry picked out of somebody else's.

sprag-host/src/config.rs: `write_config` becomes `write_atomic`, `pub(crate)` and returning an `io::Error` so both callers can name their own file in it. The installer writes a user's file for the same reasons the config writer does, and a second answer to how that is done would be a second answer to what an interrupted write leaves behind.

sprag CLI: `install-hooks` / `uninstall-hooks` [AGENT...] [--yes] [--dry-run], `list-hooks`, and `hook AGENT` — the one the installed entry names, which takes its payload on stdin. Naming no AGENT covers every agent actually on this machine and PRINTS the ones skipped. Needs no daemon, exactly as `bind-key` does not.
verification_bullets: THE ASK IS TESTED AS A DECISION, NOT A PROMPT. With no terminal to ask on and no `--yes` the install REFUSES and writes nothing: not assumed yes (the promise was to ask) and not assumed no (exiting 0 having silently done nothing is the failure mode being avoided, and is exactly what the rival's missing `python3` produces). `--dry-run` prints the edit and leaves the disk untouched. The diff shown is rendered FROM the plan that will be written, so what a user is shown and what reaches the disk cannot come apart.

THE PRESERVATION CLAIM IS ONE BYTE-IDENTITY TEST, READ TWICE WITH THE INPUT CHANGED. Install then uninstall returns a two-space file and a four-space file each exactly as it went in. One fixture could not tell preserving the layout from happening to share it: pinning the indent to two spaces turns the four-space half red and leaves the two-space half green, and dropping `preserve_order` turns three tests red with the user's keys visibly sorted.

SIX REVERT-PROOFS RUN, NOT WRITTEN, each red alone. (1) `preserve_order` dropped. (2) The indent fixed at two spaces. (3) `ensure_event` allowed to join a foreign group — the `matcher` test fails. (4) The `agent_id` check out of `report_for` — the subagent test fails. (5) `hook` made loud — the live test fails on the silence. (6) `confirm` assuming yes with no terminal — the installer test fails on consent. Each restored by an exact reverse edit and confirmed by the tree's own diff rather than a byte copy taken at an unknown time (R271's lesson).

THE LIVE TEST IS THE WHOLE VERTICAL AND ITS FIRST ASSERTION IS THE NEGATIVE ONE: `sprag hook claude` fed a real payload OUTSIDE a pane exits 0 and prints nothing, with the pane as its control — without the control it would pass on a binary that does nothing at all. Then a subagent's `Stop` leaves the pane working while the pane's own moves it to idle, and `SessionEnd` hands it back. ON THE INSTRUMENT: a pane-list read does observe the pane it describes, so it cannot prove the daemon woke unprompted — that is not the claim and is proven where it belongs; what it cannot do is invent `working claude` for a pane running `cat`, which no manifest claims.

GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1658 to 1674 passed / 0 failed (+16 = exactly the tests this slice adds), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0 across all targets, rustdoc gate 16 crates (it caught an `io::Error` link in a module that imports no `io`), T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 117/117. Both commits passed pre-commit.
carry_forward_bullets: A `matcher` MADE THE OBVIOUS SHAPE UNSAFE, AND THE DESIGN HAD NOT SEEN IT. Adding our entry to the group already under an event is the natural edit and the wrong one: the group may carry a matcher, which filters everything inside it, so the integration would quietly narrow to one tool. The general form is worth keeping — when appending to a container somebody else owns, read what the CONTAINER asserts about its contents, not just what the contents are.

ONE PRESERVATION CLAIM WAS UNACHIEVABLE AND THE CODE NOW DOES THE OPPOSITE ON PURPOSE. The design said an already-empty event array is not ours to tidy away. Once our group is removed, a file whose array was already empty and one that never listed the event are in the SAME STATE — nothing can tell them apart without a record of what the install created, and such a record is a second source of truth about the user's config that goes stale the moment they edit it by hand. Pruning is chosen, the alternative being an empty array under every installed event forever; the test asserts the limit rather than the aspiration.

SURFACED, NOT CAUSED: A RELEASE WAITS OUT THE SETTLE WINDOW. Proving `SessionEnd` end to end turned up a property of R271 that nothing asserts and that the CLI's own `release-agent` shows identically — a released pane does not drop its verdict at once, because `working`/`idle` to `unknown` is a RESTING transition asserted by an absence, so the hysteresis that guards every such transition guards this one. Roughly two seconds here. The report skips the window on the way in (a report is not a sample) and the screen's answer does not skip it on the way out. Defensible, and arguable the other way since a withdrawn report leaves the state unknown BY CONSTRUCTION; it is R271's semantics, so it is named and left alone, with the live test polling and saying why.

STILL OWED ON THIS PATH: slice 3b, codex — the TOML half, through `toml_edit` and the `edit_config` precedent rather than the rival's hand-rolled line surgery. herdr's codex integration also flips `[features] hooks = true` in `~/.codex/config.toml`; that flag needs re-verification at codex's own HEAD before it is copied, because a rival's config claim is dated by the pin it was read at. Beyond it, further targets should be DATA and not code — that is the property that decides whether 3a's abstraction was right, and herdr's is not: it carries fifteen install-path structs and fifteen uninstall-result structs, one pair per target, because it grew target-first.

Indentation is read from the file's own first indent and re-emitted, so a four-space config comes back four-space.

sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: sprag's entry always sits in a group of its OWN. Not tidiness — a hook group can carry a `matcher` that filters every entry inside it, so joining an existing group would silently narrow the integration to whatever that group matched, with no symptom but a pane that stops reporting. It also makes the uninstall exact: a whole group it is sure of, rather than an entry picked out of somebody else's.

sprag-host/src/config.rs: `write_config` becomes `write_atomic`, `pub(crate)` and returning an `io::Error` so both callers can name their own file in it. The installer writes a user's file for the same reasons the config writer does, and a second answer to how that is done would be a second answer to what an interrupted write leaves behind.

sprag CLI: `install-hooks` / `uninstall-hooks` [AGENT...] [--yes] [--dry-run], `list-hooks`, and `hook AGENT` — the one the installed entry names, which takes its payload on stdin. Naming no AGENT covers every agent actually on this machine and PRINTS the ones skipped. Needs no daemon, exactly as `bind-key` does not.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE ASK IS TESTED AS A DECISION, NOT A PROMPT. With no terminal to ask on and no `--yes` the install REFUSES and writes nothing: not assumed yes (the promise was to ask) and not assumed no (exiting 0 having silently done nothing is the failure mode being avoided, and is exactly what the rival's missing `python3` produces). `--dry-run` prints the edit and leaves the disk untouched. The diff shown is rendered FROM the plan that will be written, so what a user is shown and what reaches the disk cannot come apart.

THE PRESERVATION CLAIM IS ONE BYTE-IDENTITY TEST, READ TWICE WITH THE INPUT CHANGED. Install then uninstall returns a two-space file and a four-space file each exactly as it went in. One fixture could not tell preserving the layout from happening to share it: pinning the indent to two spaces turns the four-space half red and leaves the two-space half green, and dropping `preserve_order` turns three tests red with the user's keys visibly sorted.

SIX REVERT-PROOFS RUN, NOT WRITTEN, each red alone. (1) `preserve_order` dropped. (2) The indent fixed at two spaces. (3) `ensure_event` allowed to join a foreign group — the `matcher` test fails. (4) The `agent_id` check out of `report_for` — the subagent test fails. (5) `hook` made loud — the live test fails on the silence. (6) `confirm` assuming yes with no terminal — the installer test fails on consent. Each restored by an exact reverse edit and confirmed by the tree's own diff rather than a byte copy taken at an unknown time (R271's lesson).

THE LIVE TEST IS THE WHOLE VERTICAL AND ITS FIRST ASSERTION IS THE NEGATIVE ONE: `sprag hook claude` fed a real payload OUTSIDE a pane exits 0 and prints nothing, with the pane as its control — without the control it would pass on a binary that does nothing at all. Then a subagent's `Stop` leaves the pane working while the pane's own moves it to idle, and `SessionEnd` hands it back. ON THE INSTRUMENT: a pane-list read does observe the pane it describes, so it cannot prove the daemon woke unprompted — that is not the claim and is proven where it belongs; what it cannot do is invent `working claude` for a pane running `cat`, which no manifest claims.

GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1658 to 1674 passed / 0 failed (+16 = exactly the tests this slice adds), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0 across all targets, rustdoc gate 16 crates (it caught an `io::Error` link in a module that imports no `io`), T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 117/117. Both commits passed pre-commit.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: A `matcher` MADE THE OBVIOUS SHAPE UNSAFE, AND THE DESIGN HAD NOT SEEN IT. Adding our entry to the group already under an event is the natural edit and the wrong one: the group may carry a matcher, which filters everything inside it, so the integration would quietly narrow to one tool. The general form is worth keeping — when appending to a container somebody else owns, read what the CONTAINER asserts about its contents, not just what the contents are.

ONE PRESERVATION CLAIM WAS UNACHIEVABLE AND THE CODE NOW DOES THE OPPOSITE ON PURPOSE. The design said an already-empty event array is not ours to tidy away. Once our group is removed, a file whose array was already empty and one that never listed the event are in the SAME STATE — nothing can tell them apart without a record of what the install created, and such a record is a second source of truth about the user's config that goes stale the moment they edit it by hand. Pruning is chosen, the alternative being an empty array under every installed event forever; the test asserts the limit rather than the aspiration.

SURFACED, NOT CAUSED: A RELEASE WAITS OUT THE SETTLE WINDOW. Proving `SessionEnd` end to end turned up a property of R271 that nothing asserts and that the CLI's own `release-agent` shows identically — a released pane does not drop its verdict at once, because `working`/`idle` to `unknown` is a RESTING transition asserted by an absence, so the hysteresis that guards every such transition guards this one. Roughly two seconds here. The report skips the window on the way in (a report is not a sample) and the screen's answer does not skip it on the way out. Defensible, and arguable the other way since a withdrawn report leaves the state unknown BY CONSTRUCTION; it is R271's semantics, so it is named and left alone, with the live test polling and saying why.

STILL OWED ON THIS PATH: slice 3b, codex — the TOML half, through `toml_edit` and the `edit_config` precedent rather than the rival's hand-rolled line surgery. herdr's codex integration also flips `[features] hooks = true` in `~/.codex/config.toml`; that flag needs re-verification at codex's own HEAD before it is copied, because a rival's config claim is dated by the pin it was read at. Beyond it, further targets should be DATA and not code — that is the property that decides whether 3a's abstraction was right, and herdr's is not: it carries fifteen install-path structs and fifteen uninstall-result structs, one pair per target, because it grew target-first.

R273.decision_summary: R273: four debts R272 left, paid, and the honest comparison that found them. Asked whether slice 3a was actually superior to the rival, the answer was NO on three counts, two of them defects in sprag's own code. FIRST, THE CORRECTION: R272 presented sprag's own hook group (a group's matcher filters everything inside it) as a place sprag diverges from herdr. It is not. herdr's ensure_command_hook already pushes a fresh group and never joins one; the hazard was real in sprag's first implementation and a test caught it, but the rival had solved it already, and the record now says so. SECOND, WHAT THE COMPARISON FOUND. (a) list-hooks reported installed for a config naming a sprag binary that had since moved or been deleted, every event wired and every hook failing, which is the worst answer a status can give: a confident wrong one. herdr checks its hook file exists and reads the version inside it. (b) sprag hook ran with NO read deadline, and it runs in the AGENT'S CRITICAL PATH: a daemon that accepts a connection and then wedges would stall somebody's editing session, a failure CONNECT_TIMEOUT cannot see because the accept succeeds. herdr writes a timeout into the entry so the agent can defend itself; sprag had neither half. (c) the reporter's seq was a wall clock, matching the rival rather than beating it, and NTP steps a wall clock, so a report arriving with a smaller seq than its predecessor is refused and the pane holds a stale state. THIRD, WHERE SPRAG IS GENUINELY AHEAD, checked rather than asserted: herdr depends on serde_json with no preserve_order and writes with to_string_pretty plus fs::write, so an install ALPHABETISES the user's settings.json, forces two-space indentation, and replaces the file non-atomically. The claim that its 870 lines of hand-rolled surgery preserve more than sprag's editor is true of its TOML and YAML targets and false of the JSON one.
changes_bullets: sprag-host/src/hooks.rs + bin/sprag.rs: AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECS written into every installed entry, and HOOK_DEADLINE set on the client's own connection right after connect. Two halves of one defence, deliberately ordered: the client's is tighter and trips first in silence, the agent's is the backstop for what a client-side deadline cannot cover (a sprag that wedges before it reaches the socket at all). HostConn::connect performs no handshake read, so setting the deadline immediately after it leaves no unguarded window.

sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: Target::program_of (the path back out of a command that owns recognises) and Status::missing_program. An entry is still recognised by its SUBCOMMAND rather than its path, the choice that lets a moved binary be repaired in place, and this is the cost of that choice paid: an absolute program that is not on disk makes list-hooks print BROKEN and name the command that repairs it. A bare program name is resolved on PATH at hook time and is not a claim a status can falsify, so only an absolute path is checked.

sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: report_seq, a boot-relative monotonic clock (CLOCK_BOOTTIME on Linux, CLOCK_MONOTONIC elsewhere), moved OUT of the bin so it can be tested at all. It restarts at zero on a reboot, which is sound because nothing survives one: the daemon holding the previous numbers dies with it, and durability deliberately does not persist a tracker's report.

sprag CLI agent: the line now prints source= for a reported verdict and rule= for a scraped one, the distinction R271 put on the wire and nothing surfaced. The ADVICE follows it, because telling somebody to redefine a manifest rule for a verdict a hook reported names a rule that never fired and an edit that would do nothing, so a reported pane is pointed at release-agent instead.

sprag-mcp: AgentInfo::source, parsed and rendered beside rule on the same additive discipline, so the two agent-facing surfaces cannot come to disagree about whether a verdict is an authority or an inference.
verification_bullets: THE CLOCK'S FIRST TEST WAS A FALSE INSTRUMENT AND THE REVERT-PROOF IS WHAT CAUGHT IT. It asserted report_seq() below SystemTime::now(), which passes on the wall clock too, since a realtime sample taken first is below a realtime sample taken second. Switching the implementation to CLOCK_REALTIME left it GREEN. It now measures against a FIXED anchor (2020-01-01 in epoch nanoseconds), a moment already past, so any wall clock reads above it while an uptime would have to exceed half a century to reach it. The same mutation now turns it red, printing the offending 1.78e18.

FOUR REVERT-PROOFS RUN on the four fixes, each red alone. (1) set_read_deadline dropped: the wedged-daemon test waits 20.0 s, exactly the stand-in's sleep, i.e. it waited for the daemon and not for the agent, and fails its bound. (2) The timeout out of the entry: two install tests fail. (3) The missing_program check stubbed to None: the unit test and the list-hooks CLI test fail. (4) CLOCK_BOOTTIME to CLOCK_REALTIME: the clock test fails.

THE WEDGED-DAEMON TEST BUILDS THE FAILURE A CONNECT TIMEOUT CANNOT SEE: a UnixListener that accepts and answers nothing, holding the stream rather than dropping it, because closing would give the client an EOF and an EOF is an answer of a kind. Being ignored is the case under test. It asserts the hook still exits 0, still prints nothing, and returns well inside the stand-in's own 20 s sleep.

THE BROKEN-INSTALL TEST HAS ITS CONTROL: one fixture installs against a path never created and asserts complete() AND missing_program together, every event wired and every one of them dead, while a second installs against a real file named sprag and asserts nothing is missing. The CLI half writes the settings file BY HAND, because a sprag that has since moved is not a state any install this test could run would produce.

GATES GREEN, suite by EXIT CODE: exit 0 across 44 targets, 1674 to 1680 passed / 0 failed (+6 = exactly the tests these fixes add), counted unanchored. fmt clean, clippy 0 across all targets, rustdoc gate 16 crates, T1/T3/T4 0, citation-gate 117/117. The commit passed pre-commit.
carry_forward_bullets: A SUPERIORITY CLAIM IS A CLAIM ABOUT SOMEBODY ELSE'S CODE, AND IT GETS READ FROM THEIR CODE. R272 recorded the matcher hazard as a divergence from the rival without opening the rival's function, and herdr had already solved it. The general form is the one this project keeps relearning, verify before you write it down, with the sharper edge that a comparison has TWO sides and only one of them was read. Where the same discipline was applied properly, against herdr's own manifest and its JSON writer, it produced three superiority claims that are true and checkable.

ASKING WHETHER THIS IS ACTUALLY BETTER FOUND TWO DEFECTS THAT NO TEST WOULD HAVE. Neither the stalling hook nor the lying status was a failing assertion; both were shapes the suite had no reason to exercise, and both surfaced from comparing sprag's behaviour to a rival's on axes sprag had not thought to have. A rival is not only a feature list to catch up with, it is a second design that already had to answer the questions this one has not been asked yet.

THE CRITICAL PATH WAS THE THING NOT MODELLED. sprag hook is the first code in this tree that runs inside SOMEBODY ELSE'S process while that process waits. Every other client here is a person or a display that can be kept waiting. Anything later that installs itself into an agent's lifecycle inherits the same obligation: bound every wait, and prefer answering nothing to answering late.

STILL OWED, unchanged by this round: slice 3b, codex, the TOML half. And a shape question it will settle: Target holds ONE dir and ONE file, while codex needs a hooks file AND a features flag in a second file of a different format. The claim that a further target is DATA rather than CODE is therefore already in doubt, and 3b should re-derive the type before extending the table.

R274.decision_summary: Slice 3b instrumented codex's own config.toml, and building a second target proved the "further targets are data" claim while exposing three things one target could not: a config-dir variable the first target had ignored, an agent switch that makes a complete install dead, and a trust gate that makes writing the file only half an install.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: `Format::{Json,Toml}` selects a private `Doc` (parse / ours_under / put / take_ours / render) rather than a code path, so the policy -- our own group, subcommand recognition, correct-in-place, prune-what-we-emptied, plan and backup -- keeps ONE definition across two documents; the TOML half goes through `toml_edit`, following `config.rs::edit_config`.

crates/sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: the `CODEX` target is a `const`. Its event table differs from Claude's by exactly one row -- `PermissionRequest` where Claude has `Notification` -- because codex's payload schema is Claude's with that substitution, `hook_event_name` and `agent_id` included.

crates/sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: `Target::home_var` honours `CODEX_HOME` and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Slice 3a read `$HOME/.claude` alone, so on a machine with the variable set it installed into a file Claude never opens and `list-hooks` still said `installed` -- R273's defect class, latent in the code R273 was fixing. A RELATIVE override is refused (`HookError::AmbiguousHome`) rather than resolved against the wrong directory.

crates/sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: `Status::disabled_by` reports the agent's own hook switch when it is off, and `Target::follow_up` says what the user must still do; `Status::inert()` folds both causes of a wired-but-dead install into one question. sprag writes NEITHER -- not `features.hooks` (already true; a flag that reaches a `removed` stage would rot in the user's file) and not codex's `trusted_hash` (forging the user's approval inside the mechanism that exists to ask them).

crates/sprag-host/src/hooks.rs: a `hooks` key holding something else is now REFUSED in both formats instead of silently replaced, and an uninstall drops a group only when removing OUR entry is what emptied it -- so a group somebody else left empty is not collateral.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `list-hooks` names the disabled switch and the pending review; the `deliver_hook` doc that still described a wall-clock `seq` was corrected to match the boot-relative clock R273 installed.
verification_bullets: Measured at codex-cli 0.146.0's own HEAD, never from a description: the embedded `<event>.command.input` JSON Schemas gave the event set and the `agent_id` optionality, and `codex features list` doubled as a live validator for the TOML shape (`type = "bogus"` and a handler with no `command` are REJECTED naming their own structs).

herdr's `[features] hooks = true` write is UNNECESSARY, verified with a control: an empty config reads `hooks stable true`, and `hooks = false` reads back `false`, so the flag is real, readable at `features.hooks`, and on by default. (`memories stable false` in the same listing shows `stable` does not imply `true`.)

P9, the live proof: the exact bytes sprag renders were handed to the installed codex and loaded without complaint -- the only check that can catch a misspelled event name, because codex accepts `[[hooks.NotAnEvent]]` SILENTLY. That text is pinned in `the_rendered_codex_entry_is_the_text_codex_itself_loads`.

10 new proofs, and all 9 revert-proofs RUN red: re-emitting TOML instead of editing in place kills the comment; a non-implicit table breaks the pin; joining a foreign group; comparing entries WITH their decor (which made every re-install rewrite the file -- the test caught this as a real bug, not a hypothetical); a status that stops reading the switch; treating a null `agent_id` as a subagent; ignoring the config-dir variable; overwriting rather than refusing; giving codex Claude's word for blocked.

Suite exit 0 / 44 targets / 1690 passed (1680 -> 1690 = exactly this slice's 10). fmt clean, clippy 0 all targets, doc gate 0 (it caught two public items linking to private ones). Live: install preserves a comment and two user tables, uninstall restores the file byte-identically, `features.hooks = false` reads BROKEN with the control reading `installed`, and a relative `CODEX_HOME` is refused by name.
carry_forward_bullets: A reverse edit is only exact if its OWN anchor is unique. The last revert-proof restored `("Notification", ...)` into the FIRST table that matched -- Claude's -- silently swapping both targets' blocked events. The script had checked the forward anchor's uniqueness and not the reverse one, and only re-running the suite caught it. Extends R271's byte-restore lesson: check uniqueness in BOTH directions.

The trust gate is REPORTED, not read. codex records approvals at `hooks.state."<identity>".trusted_hash`, whose key is a normalised internal identity with no stability promise; a status derived from misreading it would be exactly the confident wrong answer R273 was about. If codex ever documents that key, reading it would let `list-hooks` distinguish `installed` from `installed, awaiting review`.

Whether the `agent_id` filter is right for codex is read off its SCHEMA (optional exactly on the events a main agent can raise, required on the subagent pair) and not observed from a running codex, which needs an authenticated session. If it is wrong the pane reports nothing and falls back to screen inference -- a degradation, not a break.

Slice 3c is now the real test of the abstraction: a THIRD target must be a `const` and nothing else. Neither remaining candidate has been read at its own HEAD, and the two properties this slice added (a disable switch, a follow-up step) were both discovered from the target rather than predicted.

herdr's `[features] hooks = true` write is UNNECESSARY, verified with a control: an empty config reads `hooks stable true`, and `hooks = false` reads back `false`, so the flag is real, readable at `features.hooks`, and on by default. P9, the live proof: the exact bytes sprag renders were handed to the installed codex and loaded without complaint -- the only check that can catch a misspelled event name, because codex accepts `[[hooks.NotAnEvent]]` SILENTLY.
